question: A patient presented with jaw swelling and weight loss. Suspecting a malignancy, thesubmandibular gland was resected. Which is the most likely nerve to be damaged duringsubmandibular gland resection?
explanation: The most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection is the lingual nerve. It loops around the submandibular duct and hence is susceptible to injury during submandibulargland resection. Course: 227 The lingual nerve arises from the posterior trunk of the mandibular nerve (V3 branch of thetrigeminal nerve). The lingual nerve descends between the tensor veli palatini muscle and thelateral pterygoid muscle, where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve. It then descends acrossthe medial pterygoid muscle to enter the oral cavity. As the lingual nerve enters the floor of theoral cavity, it lies on the deep portion of the submandibular gland. It then passes into the tongueon the hyoglossus muscle where it is attached to the submandibular ganglion. The submandibular duct lies between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves, superficial to thehyoglossus muscle. As the duct reaches the anterior border of the hyoglossus, it is crossed by thelingual nerve and lies in close proximity to the nerve. Hence lingual nerve injury is the mostcommon. Injury: The lingual nerve is at risk to be injured during submandibular gland resection because dissectionof the submandibular duct from the nerve is required. Also, it is connected to the submandibularganglion which will lead to the nerve being exposed within the operating field. The manifestations of lingual nerve injury depend on whether the lesion is proximal or distal towhere it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve. • Proximal injury: There is loss of sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, gingivae,oral mucosa, lower lip, and chin. • Distal injury: In addition to features of proximal injury, secretion from the salivary glands belowthe oral fissure and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is also lost. Note: The cranial nerves that are at risk during submandibular gland resection include: • The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve • Lingual nerve • Hypoglossal nerve 228 Other options: Option A: Nerve to mylohyoid is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve and lies in the mylohyoidgroove inferior to the mandibular foramen, hence the risk of injury is less. Option B: Inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen, henceis unlikely to be injured during submandibular gland excision. Option D: Hypoglossal nerve injury is less common than lingual nerve injury as it only lies belowand parallels to the submandibular duct.

question: A patient underwent a coronary bypass graft with the great saphenous vein. The patient nowcomplains of paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Which ofthe following nerves is most likely to be involved?
explanation: The given clinical vignette in a patient with paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect ofthe leg and foot is suggestive of injury to the saphenous nerve. 229 Injury to the saphenous nerve is common following venous cut down for access to the greatsaphenous vein, in this case for coronary bypass graft. Saphenous nerve: It is the longest and largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve and is the longest nerve in thebody. It arises from the posterior division of the femoral nerve. It then enters the adductor canaland exits it by piercing the fascia lata between the gracilis and sartorius and supplies the skin overthe patella. The saphenous nerve then descends along the medial border of the tibia along withthe great saphenous vein (anterior to the vein) and supplies the skin on the medial side ofthe knee, leg, and foot as far as up to the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Saphenous nerve injury: When the great saphenous vein is being harvested for coronary bypass graft, injury to thesaphenous nerve is common as it closely travels with the great saphenous vein. Sensory loss overthe medial side of the knee, leg, and foot is observed in saphenous nerve injury. 230 Other options: Option A: Superficial peroneal nerve injury causes sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the legand the dorsum of the foot. Option C: Femoral nerve gives rise to anterior cutaneous branches, the saphenous nerve, andmotor supply to the quadriceps and sartorius. Anterior cutaneous branches supply the skin on theanterior thigh and knee. If the saphenous nerve was not an option in the question, the femoralnerve would have been the next best answer. Option D: Sural nerve injury causes sensory loss over the posterior and lateral aspects of the distalthird of the leg and lateral side of the foot and fifth toe. It is often used as an autologousperipheral nerve graft as it is readily identified and easy to harvest.

question: During the clinical examination of the nervous system, which of the following nerves can betested by touching the highlighted structure?
explanation: The structure marked in the given sagittal section of the head and neck is the uvula. The sensorysupply to the uvula is by the glossopharyngeal nerve and it is tested in this case. Nerve supply by glossopharyngeal nerve: • Sensory fibers to the uvula, tympanic cavity, pharyngotympanic tube, tonsils,fauces, nasopharynx, and posterior third of the tongue. • Motor fibers to the stylopharyngeus muscle • Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland • Gustatory fibers for the postsulcal part of the tongue. Pharyngeal plexus: The nerve supply of the pharynx is mainly from the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. It is formed bythe pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve. It also has contributionsfrom the superior cervical ganglion. The vagus nerve provides the motor supply and theglossopharyngeal nerve provides the sensory supply. Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve: • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division ofthe trigeminal nerve) • All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve) Note: Previously cranial root of the spinal accessory nerve was thought to contribute to the motorfunctions of the pharyngeal plexus, but recent evidence suggests that it is not a major part of themotor drive to the pharyngeal plexus. Innervation of the soft palate: General sensation - It is mostly carried by the lesser palatine nerve which is a branch of maxillarynerve. The sensation from posterior part is carried by the pharyngeal branches of theglossopharyngeal nerve and from the plexus around the tonsil which is formed by the tonsillarbranches of the glossopharyngeal and lesser palatine nerves. 231 Taste sensation - There are taste buds in the oral surface of soft palate and sensation from them iscarried by the lesser palatine nerve. Secretomotor supply - It is by the lesser palatine nerve via postganglionic fibres from thepterygopalatine ganglion. Motor supply - It is by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve except for tensor veli palatiniwhich is supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. 232

question: Arrange in sequence the structures involved in the direct pathway:
explanation: The sequence of structures involved in the direct pathway is cortex > striatum > globuspallidus > substantia nigra > thalamus. There are five parallel circuits that connect the frontal cortex to the striatum, pallidum, substantianigra, and thalamus. These circuits have both direct and indirect pathways. The direct pathwaystimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibit it. The cerebral cortex projects into the striatum. The striatum is seen projected into the pallidumand substantia nigra pars reticularis. Fibres originate from different striatal cells according totheir endings in the external and internal pallidum. In the direct pathway, striatalneurones project directly to the internal pallidum. Whereas some other fibres that arise from theneurons project to the external pallidum. This is called the indirect pathway. The sequence of structures involved in the indirect pathway is cortex > striatum > globuspallidus externa > subthalamic nucleus > globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra>Thalamus The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in theindirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. Putamen lies lateral and the internal capsule lies medial to the pallidum. It receives fibres fromthe striatum and subthalamic nuclei. It acts as the main output of the basal ganglia to thethalamus and superior colliculus. The substantia nigra is seen in each cerebral peduncle of themidbrain located deep to the crus cerebri. The levels of dopamine in the substantia nigra andstriata are seen reduced in parkinsonism disease. 249 In parkinsonism disease, due to the death of neurons in substantia nigra activity of the directpathway is reduced and the indirect pathway is increased. This results in bradykinesia inparkinsonism disease. Whereas in Huntington's disease, the activity of the indirect pathway isaffected resulting in choreic involuntary movements. 250

question: What is the volume of the prostate in normal adult males?
explanation: The volume of the prostate in normal adult males is 20cc. Prostate is an accessory glandular tissue embedded in the fibromuscular stroma. It usually weighs8 grams in the young adults and its weight ranges from 40-150 grams in men aged >50 years. The prostate gland is situated in the lesser pelvis and surrounds the prostatic urethra whichextends from bladder base to the membranous urethra. Pubic symphysis and pubic arch lieanteriorly to the prostate whereas rectourethralis and rectal ampulla lie posteriorly to it. The prostate has three distinct zones as follows: ZoneStructures enclosedClinical significance Transitional zoneUrethraMost common site for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) Central zoneEjaculatory ductsAtrophies secondary to BPH Peripheral zoneCentral and transitional zones Pre-prostatic urethraMost common site for prostatic carcinoma 251 The prostate is composed of 5 lobes. They are anterior, posterior, two lateral and one medial ormiddle lobe. The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae. It is an elevation found in the lower partof the bladder trigone. It is the most common site of adenoma. Microstructure of the prostate gland: The glandular tissue of the prostate gland is composed of many follicles with frequent internalpapillae. The follicular epithelium is either a single-layered or pseudostratified columnarepithelum. These follicles open into canals, which join to form the main ducts. Small eosinophiliccolloid amyloid bodies called corpora amylacea are frequently seen within a follicle. The prostatic ducts open into the prostatic sinus in the prostatic urethra. The ducts of the prostatefollicles are lined by bilayered epithelium (basal cuboidal and apical columnar). The secretions of the prostate are acidic and contain acid phosphatase, amylase, prostate-specificantigen (PSA), fibrin, and zinc. 252 The blood supply to the prostate is by the inferior vesical, internal pudendal and middle rectalarteries. It recieves nerve supply from the inferior hypogastric plexus.

question: Which ligament connects medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal?
explanation: The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal. Lisfranc ligament is a cuneometatarsal interosseous ligament. It is the strongest ligament amongthe three cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments. It passes from the lateral surface of the medialcuneiform to the adjacent angle of the second metatarsal bone. Deformity of this ligament can lead to instability and deformity of the tarsometatarsal joint. Other options: Option A: Chopart's ligament is related to both calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular joints. It isa strong Y-shaped band, having a proximal stem and 2 distal limbs. • The proximal limb is attached by a stem to the anterior part of the upper calcaneal surface. • The distal limb divides into calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular parts. 253 Option B: Spring ligament also known as the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament connectsthe sustentaculum tali to the navicular. It ties the calcaneus to the navicular and maintains themedial longitudinal arch of the foot. It is made up of the superomedial calcaneonavicular portionand the inferior calcaneonavicular portion. Option D: Deltoid ligament also called the medial collateral ligament is attached to the apex,anterior and posterior borders of the medial malleolus. It has 2 layers, superficial and deep: • The superficial layer consists of tibionavicular fibres anteriorly, tibiocalcaneal fibres in themiddle, and superficial posterior tibiotalar fibres posteriorly. • Deep layer consists of anterior tibiotalar fibres, tibiocalcaneal in the middle and deep posteriortibiotalar posteriorly. 254
subject: Anatomy

question: Fibres of the given structure originate from ?
explanation: The given structure is the fornix and its fibres arise from the hippocampus. The fornix is a part of the connecting pathways of the limbic system. It arises from thehippocampus which wraps around the thalamus and ends in the mammillary body. It connectsthe hippocampus with distal brain sites. The fornix has two types of fibres: • Association fibres: They connect the various cortical regions within the same hemisphere • Commissural fibres: They connect the corresponding regions of two hemispheres. It is seen inthe hippocampal commissure of the fornix. The blood supply of fornix is by the anterior communicating artery which arises from the anteriorcerebral artery. The limbic system is a group of structures seen between the cerebral cortex and thehypothalamus. It is involved in emotional and motivation activity, learning, and memory. 255 Other options: Option A: Amygdala is a part of the limbic system that consists of lateral, central and basal nuclei.It can Influence the body's response to enviromnental changes. In a fearful situation it can changethe heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate etc. Option C: Caudate nucleus is a C-shaped mass of grey matter. It is divided into a head, body, andtail. Degeneration of the caudate nucleus is seen in Huntington's disease.
subject: Anatomy

question: Which structure is supplied by the nerve causing this elevation?
explanation: Risorius is supplied by the facial nerve which causes the elevation marked. The image shows thefloor of the fourth ventricle and the facial colliculus is marked. 256 The fourth ventricle is located between the brainstem and the cerebellum. The rhomboid fossa is adiamond-shaped depression seen on the floor of the fourth ventricle. The superior and the inferiorpart of the floor is triangular in shape. It is divided by a longitudinal median sulcus into twohalves. Each half is again divided into the medial and lateral regions. The facial colliculus is present in the superior part, which presents as a small elevation producedby the root of the facial nerve winding around the nucleus of the abducens nerve. Columns areformed by groups of facial neurones, which innervate individual muscles and give branches of thefacial nerve. Dorsal neurones innervate muscles in the scalp and upper face and ventral neuronssupply the lower facial musculature. Risorius falls under the buccolabial muscle group and act as the elevator, retractor and evertor ofthe upper lip. Some of its peripheral attachments are the zygomatic arch, parotid fascia and fasciaover the mastoid process. It is involved in actions like grinning and laughing and is innervated bythe buccal branches of the facial nerve. Other options: 257 Option A: Lateral rectus is an extraocular muscle that arises from the lateral part of the commontendinous ring. It is innervated by the abducens nerve. Option B: Superior oblique is an extraocular muscle that arises from the body of the sphenoid. Itis innervated by the trochlear nerve. Option D: Levator palpebrae superiors is an extraocular muscle that arises from the lesser wing ofsphenoid. It is innervated by the oculomotor nerve. 258

question: Arrange lung hilar structures from anterior to posterior:
explanation: Lung hilar structures are arranged from the anterior to posterior in the order: • Pulmonary vein • Pulmonary artery • Primary bronchus • Bronchial artery The medial surface of the lung is connected to the heart and trachea by a group of structures thatenter or leave the hilum. It is called the pulmonary root. It is anteriorly related to the phrenicnerve, pericardiacophrenic vessels , and anterior pulmonary plexus. The vagus nerve andposterior pulmonary plexus form the posterior relation and the pulmonary ligament the inferior 259 relation. The superior vena cava and right atrium are seen in front of the right root and terminal part of theazygos vein superiorly. The hilar structures are arranged from the superior to inferior as: • Superior lobar bronchus • Pulmonary artery • Principal bronchus • Inferior pulmonary vein The aortic arch is seen superiorly and descending thoracic aorta posteriorly of the left root. Thehilar structures are vertically arranged as: • Pulmonary artery • Principal bronchus • Inferior pulmonary vein 260

question: Which is not a branch of facial artery in the face?
explanation: Mental is not a branch of the facial artery but the branch of the maxillary artery in the face. The first part of the maxillary artery gives rise to the mental artery as a terminal branch of theinferior alveolar artery. The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery which arises in the carotid triangle,above the origin of the lingual artery. It runs upwards in the neck and curves around theanteroinferior border of the masseter to enter the face. The premasseteric artery passes along the anterior border of the masseter and the surroundingtissues are supplied by it. The inferior labial artery mainly supplies the inferior labial glands. Itthen anastomoses with its controlateral fellow and with the mental branch of the inferior alveolarartery. The superior labial artery supplies the upper lip whereas the lateral nasal artery suppliesthe dorsum and alae of the nose. Both these arteries anastomose with its controlateral fellow. The image shows the branches of facial artery: Branches of facial artery in the neckBranches of facial artery in the face Ascending palatine arteryPremasseteric artery Tonsillar branchSuperior and inferior labial arteries Submental arteryLateral nasal artery Branches to submandibular glandAngular artery 261

question: Which of the following structures passing via jugular foramen has a separate canal?
explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve passing through the jugular foramen has a separate canal. The jugular foramen is formed by the occipital bone and the petrous part of the temporal bone.The spinal accessory nerve and vagus nerve also pass through this foramen. The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves the skull through the anteromedial part of the jugular foramenin a separate dural sheath. The branches of the nerve are tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar and lingualbranches. Infection, malignancy and postoperative inflammation of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa will causereferred pain in the ear. This is conducted through the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngealnerve. Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexusof nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superiorcervical ganglion. Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are: • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division ofthe trigeminal nerve) • All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve) Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotidgland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc. The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of theposterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palateetc. The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing,phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx. Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include: • Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”). • By assessing the strength of the cough The image below shows the base of the skull and foramina: 262

question: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image?
explanation: The median nerve supplies the 1st lumbrical which is marked. There are four lumbrical muscles. They originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorumprofundus. It passes to the radial side of the corresponding fingers and is inserted into the dorsaldigital expansion of the extensor digitorum. The action of lumbricals is flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joint and extension ofinterphalangeal joints. Lumbricals can be tested only along with interosseous muscle. The examiner will hold themetacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger in hyperextension. Then the patient is asked toextend the proximal interphalangeal joint against resistance. The test is repeated on other fingersas well. 263 The median nerve innervates the first and second lumbricals. The deep terminal branch of theulnar nerve innervates the third and the fourth. The median nerve is formed by the union of the lateral root (C6, 7) from the lateral cord, and themedial root (C8, T1) from the medial cord. On the hand, it is seen proximal to the flexor retinaculum and lateral to the tendons of flexordigitorum superficialis. It also lies between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and palmarislongus. Its cutaneous supply in hand is as follows: • Lateral 2/3rd of the palm by superficial cutaneous branch • Lateral 3½ fingers (palmar aspect and dorsal aspect of nailbeds) by palmar digital nerves 264 The muscles supplied by the median nerve in the hand are flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicisbrevis, and opponens pollicis The median nerve sometimes gets compressed under the fibro-osseous tunnel beneath the flexorretinaculum leading to carpal tunnel syndrome. Pen test is used to test the median nerve in the hand. It tests the abductor pollicis brevismuscle. The hand must remain flat with the palm facing upwards. A pen is held above the palmand the patient is asked to touch the pen with his thumb.
subject: Anatomy

question: A child lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Defective development of which of thefollowing structures is likely to be the cause?
explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. Defective development ofthe third pharyngeal pouch marked as 3 causes this condition. 265 A child with DiGeorge syndrome lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands due to defectivedevelopment of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch. The child can also lack superior parathyroid glands,due to defective development of the 4th pharyngeal pouch. It is caused by chromosome 22qdeletion and is characterized by the following (Mnemonic: CATCH-22) • Cleft palate • Abnormal facies • Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency and recurrent infections • Cardiac defects • Hypocalcemia, secondary to parathyroid aplasia. Derivatives of the Pharyngeal Pouches 1st Pouch • Tympanic cavity (middle ear cavity) • Auditory tube (eustachian tube) 2nd Pouch • Palatine tonsils • Tonsillar fossa 3rd Pouch • Inferior parathyroid glands • Thymus 4th Pouch • Superior parathyroid glands • Ultimobranchial body - gives rise to parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland 266 The medulla of the thymus has Hassall’s corpuscles. They are small rounded structures formedfrom whorls of medullary epithelial cells with a central partially keratinized core appearing as aneosinophilic-staining mass. question: Identify which of the following structure is a merocrine gland:
explanation: Sweat gland marked 2 is a merocrine gland. Eccrine and apocrine are the two types of sweat glands. Secretions of the sweat glands are byexocytosis hence they are also known as merocrine sweat glands. A histopathological image of the sweat gland is shown below: 267 The other structures marked are: 1- Hair follicle 3- Sebaceous gland 4- Hair shaft Glands are divided into holocrine, apocrine, and merocrine on the basis of the manner in whichtheir secretions are poured out of the cells. In holocrine secretions, the secretory cells themselves are disintegrated as part of their terminaldifferentiation. Afterwhich, the terminally differentiated cells filled with lipid products arereleased. The sebaceous gland and hair follicles are examples. A histopathological image of the sebaceous gland is shown below: 268 Merocrine uses exocytosis for secretions. Most of the exocrine glands are merocrine. In apocrine, product-filled areas of cells are released, the mammary gland is an example. Histopathological image of mammary gland is shown below: 269

options.c: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery
options.d: Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

explanation: Blood is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery as themarked structure is the anterior part of the corpus callosum. Corpus callosum is the largest fibre pathway of the brain. The parts of the corpus callosum are therostrum, genu, trunk or body, and splenium. The image below shows the parts of the corpus callosum: 270 Anterior cerebral artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery. The frontal branch of theanterior cerebral artery supplies the corpus callosum and the central branch which supplies therostrum. Central or perforating arteries arises from the circle of willis. They are again divided into theanteromedial, anterolateral, posteromedial and posterolateral groups. The anterior cerebral andanterior communicating artery give rise to anteromedial group which supplies the rostrum of thecorpus callosum. The image below shows the mid sagittal section of the brain:
subject: Anatomy

question: Superior gluteal nerve supplies all of the following structures except:
explanation: 271 All of the structures except pyriformis are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. Pyriformis issupplied by the nerve to the piriformis. The dorsal branches of the L4, L5, and S1 rami give rise to the superior gluteal nerve. It isaccompanied by superior gluteal vessels. This nerve leaves the pelvis via the greater sciaticforamen above piriformis and divides into superior and inferior branches. It supplies gluteusmedius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. The dorsal branches of the S1 and S2 rami give rise to the nerve to the piriformis. Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis onthe femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject tostand on one limb. If the ipsilateral abductors are normal, the pelvis remains in a horizontalposition. If the ipsilateral abductors are weak, then the pelvis tilts towards the opposite(unsupported) side. This is called positive Trendelenburg’s sign. 272
subject: Anatomy

question: Arrange the structures of the cubital fossa in sequence from medial to lateral.
explanation: The structures are arranged in the cubital fossa from medial to lateral as follows: • Median nerve • Brachial artery • Tendon of biceps brachii • Radial nerve The cubital fossa is a triangular depression in the anterior aspect of the upper forearm. It isrelated to the epicondylar line proximally, lateral border of pronator teres medially, and by themedial surface of brachioradialis laterally. Its roof is formed by the deep fascia of the forearm. The floor of the fossa is formed by thebrachialis and supinator. Veins like basilic, median cubital, and cephalic veins are arranged in thesuperficial fascia from medial to lateral side.
subject: Anatomy

question: Arrange the cells according to their positions from the basal layer towards the lumen in theseminiferous tubules.
explanation: From the basal layer towards the lumen in the seminiferous tubules, the cells are arranged in theorder of: • Myoepithelial cells • Spermatogonia • Primary spermatocyte • Spermatid • Spermatozoa Spermatogenesis is the process in which spermatogonia are transformed into spermatozoa. Itbegins at puberty. During puberty, the sex cords acquire lumen to become seminiferous tubules. 273 The primordial germ cells give rise to spermatogonial stem cells. The transformation ofspermatogonial stem cells to spermatozoa is given in the flowchart below. The process by which spermatids are transformed into spermatozoa is called spermiogenesis.
subject: Anatomy

question: Which skull foramen is formed by 3 bones?
explanation: Foramen lacerum is formed by three bones. The three bones involved in the formation of foramen lacerum are: • Petrous part of the temporal bone • Greater wing of the sphenoid bone • Basilar part of the occipital bone 274 The internal carotid artery enters the skull through this foramen. It ascends through the carotidcanal and from the upper end of the foramen lacerum. It is accompanied by venous and sympathetic nerve plexuses. It is also transversed by themeningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal artery and emissary veins from the cavernoussinus. On the anterior margin of the foramen lacerum pterygoid canal can be seen which leads to thepterygopalatine fossa. The nerve of the pterygoid canal and accompanying vessels are transmittedby them. The image below shows the base of the skull and foraminas: Other options: Option B: Foramen magnum is formed by the occipital bone. Option C: Foramen rotundum is a hole seen in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. 275 Option D: Foramen jugulare is formed by the petrous part of the temporal bone and occipitalbone. The image below shows superior and inferior views of the skull base:
subject: Anatomy

question: Which marked structure causes lateral rotation, flexion, and abduction at the hip joint, alongwith flexion at the knee joint?
explanation: Sartorius is involved in lateral rotation, flexion, and abduction at the hip joint, and flexion at theknee. The structure marked '2' is sartorius. The sartorius muscle is known as the tailor muscle and is also the longest muscle in the body. Theword "sartorius" is derived from the Latin word sartor, which translates to tailor, due to the waythe individual will position one's leg while working. Origin: Anterior superior iliac spine and the upper half of the notch below it. Insertion: Into the superior aspect of the medial surface of the tibial shaft near the tibialtuberosity (joins aponeurosis of gracilis and semitendinosus to form pes anserinus). Action: Flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation of the thigh; and flexion of the leg. Innervation: By femoral nerve (L2 and L3) 276 Other options: Option A: Rectus femoris is involved in flexion at the hip and extension at the knee. Option C: Gracilis is involved in adduction at the hip and flexion and medial rotation at the knee. Option D: Adductor longus is involved in adduction, flexion, and medial rotation at the hip.
subject: Anatomy

question: Which among the following statements is true regarding the course of the mandibular nerve?
explanation: The true statements are 2 and 3. The lingual nerve is a branch from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve, and it arcsaround the submandibular duct. The buccal branch is a branch from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve, and it emergesfrom behind the mandibular ramus. The other statements: 1. The auriculotemporal nerve emerges from behind the temporomandibular joint and is a branchfrom the posterior division of the mandibular nerve. 4. The ophthalmic nerve arises in the middle cranial fossa and is a division of the trigeminalnerve, along with the maxillary and mandibular nerves.
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair(s) of pharyngeal arch and its artery.
explanation: All the given pairs of pharyngeal arteries and their arteries are correctly matched except for 'v'(option C). The 6th pharyngeal arch has its blood supply on the left side from the left pulmonary artery andductus arteriosus, not from the aorta. 277
subject: Anatomy

question: The rupture of penile urethra does not cause extravasation of blood into which of thefollowing spaces?
explanation: Rupture of the penile urethra causes extravasation of blood into the superficial perineal pouch,scrotum, penis, and then up to the lower anterior abdominal wall. The superficial perineal pouch is a compartment of the perineum enclosed by the membranouslayer of the perineal fascia that surrounds the scrotum or labia and penis or clitoris. Anteriorly, the membranous layer of perineal fascia is continuous over the pubic symphysis andpubic bones. It is later continuous with the membranous layer of the anterior abdominal wall. Thus, the fluid that accumulates in the perineal pouch extends to the lower anterior abdomen. In the lower lateral abdominal wall, the abdominal fascia is attached to the deep fascia of thethigh, inferior to the inguinal ligament. Thus, on trauma at the penile urethra, urine does notextravasate into the anterior thigh. The superficial perineal pouch is closed posteriorly by attaching the membranous layer ofsuperficial fascia to the posterior margin of the urogenital diaphragm. Thus, commonly there is noextravasation into the deep perineal pouch and the ischiorectal fossa. Also, the membranous layer of superficial fascia attaches to the ischiopubic rami and forms thelateral borders of the urogenital triangle. Thus, the urine does not extravasate to the thigh. But, the ischiorectal fossa would be a better answer because of the following reasons: • Bulbourethral glands that lie in the deep perineal space open their ducts into the spongy urethra,which is related to the superficial perineal space. Also, the muscles surrounding these glands wererecently found to be a continuation of the deep transverse perinei and tail of the external urethralsphincter, both of which are components of the deep perineal space. Injury to the penile urethracan damage bulbourethral glands' ducts, which can lead to damage to the above-mentionedstructures and may cause extravasation of urine into the deep perineal space. • Previously, the perineal membrane was thought to be a triangular membrane. However, recentstudies show that it is contiguous anteriorly with the structures that support the urethra.Posteriorly, it is related to the support of the perineal body and lateral vaginal wall. So damage tothe urethra might damage the anterior part of the perineal membrane which can make way forextravasation of blood into the deep perineal space. • Deep perineal pouch: It was believed initially that the urogenital diaphragm was formed by 3layers: An inferior fascia (also called the perineal membrane), deep perineal space, and a superiorfascia. The superior fascia formed the inferior border of the ischioanal fossa. The Colles fascia alsoseparates the perineal membrane from the ischioanal fossa. So, extravasation of blood into thedeep perineal space is possible but extravasation into the ischioanal fossa due to penile urethralinjury is highly unlikely. Recent studies have shown that this might be a slightly more complexstructure. 278
subject: Anatomy

question: Which nerve is blocked when local anesthesia is given below the inguinal ligament duringfemoral vein catheterization?
explanation: Genitofemoral nerve is blocked when the local anesthetic is given below the inguinal ligamentduring femoral vein catheterization. The genitofemoral nerve originates from the L1 and L2 ventral rami. It divides into the genital andfemoral branches after crossing behind the ureter. The genital branch enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring and accompanies thespermatic cord or round ligament. It exits the superficial inguinal ring and supplies the cremastermuscle and skin of the external genitalia. The femoral branch descends lateral to the external iliac artery to pass behind the inguinalligament and enter the femoral sheath lateral to the femoral artery. It pierces the anterior wall ofthe femoral sheath and fascia lata and supplies them. 279 The genitofemoral nerve gives sensory supply to the anteromedial thigh via the femoral branch.The genital branch supplies skin of the scrotum in males and mons pubis and labium majus infemales. The genitofemoral nerve also innervates the cremaster muscle via the genital branch andis responsible for the cremasteric reflex. The image given below shows nerves related to the inguinal region: Other options: Option A: Femoral nerve arises from the posterior division of ventral rami of L2-L4 spinalsegments on the posterior abdominal wall. It enters the femoral triangle by passing under theinguinal ligament. In the femoral triangle, it lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside thefemoral sheath. Later, it is divided into anterior and posterior branches by the lateral circumflexfemoral artery. Option C: Lateral cutaneous nerve (a.k.a lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) of the thigh is mostcommonly injured at the site where it leaves the pelvis. An injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve ofthe thigh leads to pain and paresthesia over the anterolateral region of the thigh, a conditioncalled meralgia paresthetica. Option D: Ilioinguinal nerve is most commonly injured within the inguinal canal in open herniarepair due to traction or thermal injury. Injury causes loss of sensation in the root ofthe penis and adjacent part of the scrotum.
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the nerve passing around the marked structure.
explanation: The structure marked in the given image is the neck of fibula. The nerve passing around the neckof fibula is the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve). The common peroneal nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the ventral rami of L4, L5, S1,and S2. The sciatic nerve divides into the tibial nerve and the common fibular nerve. The common fibular nerve runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibularhead. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves 280 laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves. Superficial fibular nerve: Motor innervation: • Peroneus longus • Peroneus brevis Sensory innervation: • Lateral aspect of the lower leg • Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital webspace Deep fibular nerve: Motor innervation: • Extensor digitorum longus • Extensor hallucis longus • Tibialis anterior • Peroneus tertius Sensory innervation: • The first interdigital space 281 The common peroneal nerve is more prone to injury as it lies superficial at the level of the lateralaspect of the neck of the fibula. Injury results in foot drop (which causes high-stepping gait), lossof eversion of the foot, and sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot.
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following cells are present in the molecular layer of the cerebellum?
explanation: The molecular layer of the cerebellum contains stellate and basket cells. The molecular layer is the outermost layer that contains stellate cells and basket cells, anddendrites of Purkinje cells. They receive excitatory input from the parallel fibers andform inhibitory synapses on the Purkinje cells. This layer contains many myelinated andunmyelinated nerve fibers and appears pale on H&E staining. 282
subject: Anatomy

question: Bleeding as shown in the image is due to which of the following vessels?
explanation: The image showing a bleed over the arachnoid layer but under the dura is suggestive of a subduralhemorrhage. Most commonly, it results from the shearing of cortical bridging veins. Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid layers ofthe meninges. The causes of SDH include • trauma • anticoagulants, antiplatelets • alcohol abuse • battered baby syndrome. Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice. Other options: Middle meningeal artery rupture would result in an extradural hemorrhage. Lenticulostriate artery would lead to an intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Vertebral artery dissection leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage or sometimes intraparenchymalhemorrhage. 283 The given image shows types of brain hemorrhage:
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following statements are true about the internal capsule?
explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are true about the internal capsule. The charcot’s artery of hemorrhage is a larger lenticulostriate or lateral striate artery. Lateralstriate arteries supply the anterior limb, genu and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Thesearteries are also commonly involved in ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes. The retrolentiform part of the internal capsule carries fibers mainly from optic radiation. A lesionhere produces homonymous hemianopia, superior quadrantanopia, or inferior quadrantanopia. The anterior limb of the internal capsule carries fronto-pontine fibers. A lesion hereproduces confusion, impaired attention, agitation, and dysarthria. 284 The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries cortico-spinal motor fibers in the anterior partand the lesion here produces contralateral hemiparesis. The posterior part of the posterior limb ofthe internal capsule carries sensory fibers and lesions here may produce contralateralhemi-sensory deficits. The internal capsule predominantly contains projection fibers, not commissural fibers. Projectionfibers are the fibers that project from higher to lower centers or vice versa in CNS.
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following is not a branch of posterior division of internal iliac artery ?
explanation: The inferior gluteal artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. Branches of the anterior trunk of the internal iliac artery: • Obturator artery 285 • Superior vesical artery • Inferior vesical artery • Inferior gluteal artery • Middle rectal artery • Vaginal artery (in females) • Uterine artery (in females) • Internal pudendal artery Branches of the posterior trunk of the internal iliac artery: • Iliolumbar artery • Lateral sacral arteries • Superior gluteal artery
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the incorrect statement regarding the marked structure.

options.a: It is the meeting point of frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones.
options.b: Blow to the lateral side of the skull injures the marked structure.
options.c: Accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure.
options.d: It corresponds to site of anterolateral fontanelle of fetal skull.

explanation: The structure marked in the image is the pterion. The incorrect statement is statement 3, which isthe accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure. The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull: • Frontal bone • Squamous part of the temporal bone • Greater wing of the sphenoid bone • Parietal bone It is located approximately 4 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch. 286 The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and the lateral fissure ofthe cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin, and any injury to this area may lead torupture of the middle meningeal artery, leading to extradural hematoma. The pterion also corresponds to the site of the anterolateral (sphenoidal) fontanelle of theneonatal skull, which closes in the third month after birth. The accessory meningeal artery may be a branch of the middle meningeal artery or might arisedirectly from the maxillary artery. It reaches the cranium via the foramen ovale and distributesprincipally in the extracranial region. It is distributed over the medial and lateral pterygoids,tensor veli palatini, greater wing and pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone, mandibular nerve,and the otic ganglion. So, it supplies the trigeminal ganglion, dura mater and bone. But in somepeople, it may be replaced by small separate arteries. 287
subject: Anatomy

question: What are the derivatives of the marked cells?
explanation: The cells shown in the image are neural crest cells (NCC) present adjacent to the neural tube (NT).NCCs contribute to many organs and tissues, and the neural crest is sometimes referred to as thefourth germ layer: • In the trunk region, they form: • Melanocytes • Sensory ganglia • Sympathetic and enteric neurons • Schwann cells • Adrenal medulla cells • In the cranial region, they contribute to the: • Craniofacial skeleton • Neurons for cranial ganglia • Satellite glial cells • Melanocytes • Some of the other neural crest derivatives are • C cells of the thyroid gland • Conotruncal septum in the heart • Odontoblasts • Smooth muscle cells to blood vessels to the face and forebrain. The intermediate mesoderm is a longitudinal strip of intraembryonic mesoderm that connects theparaxial with the lateral plate mesoderm. The intermediate mesoderm develops into the genitalridge and nephrogenic cord. The majority of the heart, including the right ventricle and outflow tract, is derived from thebulbus cordis, which is further derived from the pharyngeal mesoderm. 288
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?
explanation: Iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus are parts of the pelvic diaphragm, which is also known as thelevator ani. The levator ani muscle is a complex unit that consists of 3 muscle components: • Pubococcygeus • Pubovaginalis - elevates the urethra and hence contributes to urinary continence • Puboperinealis - draws the perineal body towards the pubic symphysis • Puboanalis - elevates the anus and keeps the urogenital hiatus narrowed • Puborectalis • Iliococcygeus Levator ani muscles are the most important muscles in the pelvic floor and maintain a constantstate of contraction. They provide a stable floor and support the weight of the abdominopelviccontents against intra-abdominal forces. Weakening of levator ani and pelvic fascia fromstretching or tearing during childbirth, may decrease support for the vagina, bladder, uterus, orrectum or alter the position of the neck of the bladder and urethra. Other options: The obturator internus forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa and is not a part of the levatorani. The deep transverse perineal muscle is the content of the deep perineal space and contributes tothe formation of the perineal body. 289
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following arteries passes in close proximity to the area marked by the arrow inthe given image?

options.a: Anterior division of middle cerebral artery
options.b: Anterior division of the middle meningeal artery
options.c: Posterior division of middle cerebral artery

explanation: The area marked by an arrow in the given image is pterion and the artery that passes in closeproximity to this area is the middle meningeal artery. The pterion is an H shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull: • Frontal bone • Squamous part of the temporal bone • Greater wing of the sphenoid bone • Parietal bone. It is an important structure as it overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery andlateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this areamay lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma. 290
subject: Anatomy

question: Fracture of the jugular canal can present as

options.a: Loss of taste sensation in anterioir 2/3rd of tongue
options.b: Loss of taste sensation in posterior 1/3rd of tongue
options.c: Loss of general sensation in anterior 2/3rd of tongue
options.d: Loss of motor sensation in anterior 2/3rd of tongue

explanation: Fracture of the jugular canal affects glossopharyngeal nerve and presents as loss of taste sensationin the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue. The lingual nerve which is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve givesgeneral sensation, chorda tympani branch of facial nerve gives taste sensation for the anterior2/3rd of tongue. Both taste and general sensation of the posterior 1/3rd is by the glossopharyngealnerve. The muscles of the tongue, with the exception of palatoglossus, are supplied by thehypoglossal nerve. Palatoglossus is supplied via the pharyngeal plexus. The other nerves passing through the jugular foramen are glossopharyngeal(cranial nerve IX),vagus(cranial nerve X), and accessory nerve(cranial nerve XI). The following is an image of the base of skull showing jugular foramen: 291
subject: Anatomy

question: Injury of the lower brachial plexus leads to Klumpke's paralysis. What is the characteristicclinical finding seen in this lesion?
explanation: The characteristic clinical finding in Klumpke's paralysis is a complete claw hand. Klumpke's paralysis is caused by injury of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus-mainly T1 andpartially C8, due to traction injury of the lower trunk that may be seen in undue abduction of thearm (outstretched arm grabbing an object during a fall from height) or birth injury (traction of theextended arm during delivery) This leads to paralysis of the intrinsic muscles of the hand (T1) that are responsible for flexion atmetacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and extension at proximal and distal interphalangealjoints(PIP and DIP). The unopposed action of extensor digitorum at MCP causes hyperextension.The unopposed action of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus at PIP and DIP causesflexion. Thus giving rise to the characteristic claw hand. Other changes include anesthesia and analgesia along the ulnar border of the forearm, vasomotorchanges, absence of sweating, and trophic changes in long-standing cases. If the C8 is alsodamaged, the extent of anesthesia will be greater and will involve the medial side of the forearm,hand, and medial two fingers. Horner's syndrome (option D) may occur in one-third of the cases due to injury of sympatheticfibers to the head and neck that leave the spinal cord through nerve T1. The following image shows a complete claw hand in Klumpke's paralysis: Other options: Option A: Policeman tip deformity, also known as waiter's tip hand or porter's tip hand, is afinding of Erb's palsy due to injury of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus involving C5 and C6.The hand is adducted, medially rotated, and hangs by the side with the elbow extended andpronated. The following image shows policeman tip deformity in Erb's palsy: 292 Option B: Wrist drop is a feature of radial nerve injury in the axilla, radial groove, anterolateralside of the lower arm, or injury of the deep branch in the cubital fossa. Option D: Horner's syndrome is caused due to the disruption of sympathetic supply to the face. Itcauses ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, enophthalmos, and loss of ciliospinal reflex of the affected eye.It may occur in some cases of Klumpke's paralysis and is not a characteristic finding. The following image shows the ocular manifestation of Horner syndrome:
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the liver segment marked in the image below:
explanation: The liver segment highlighted in green in this CT section is segment V. The section of the CT givenis taken below the portal vein as the cross-section of the portal vein before its bifurcation can beviewed. 293 A horizontal plane known as the portal plane divides the liver where the portal vein bifurcates andbecomes horizontal. This divides each section of the liver into superior and inferior segments: • Left lateral section: segment II above and segment III below the portal plane • Left medial section: segment IVa above and segment IVb below the portal plane • Right anterior (or medial) section: segment VIII above and segment V below the portal plane • Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal plane Shown below is a section from below the portal plane. Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver isdivided into eight segments. It is based on the distribution of portal venous branches in the liverparenchyma. Each segment has its own vascular supply, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage. The Couinaud's liver segments are as follows: 294
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following lobes of the lung is affected when there is aspiration in supineposition?

options.b: Upper part of right inferior lobe

explanation: The upper part of the right inferior lobe is prone to aspiration in the supine position. It iscommonly seen in alcoholics. The posterior segment of the right superior lobe and the superior segment of the inferior lobes arethe most commonly involved lung sites when aspiration occurs in a recumbent patient. The location of aspiration depends on the position of the patient since it is gravity-dependent.Aspiration while standing leads to infiltration of bilateral inferior lobes because of larger andmore vertical corresponding bronchi, the middle lobes and the lingula. Aspiration of contents into foreign substances into the bronchial tree, usually oral or gastriccontents, produces aspiration pneumonia. Chemical (gastric acid) injury or bacterial infectioncomplicates the condition.
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the cranial nerve that arises from the marked part.
explanation: The structure marked in the image is the abducens nerve that arises from the pontomedullaryjunction. In the groove between the medulla and pons, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nervesemerge arranged medially to laterally. The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve that arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullaryjunction, passes through Dorello's canal, and enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to theinternal carotid artery. It then enters the orbit through the common tendinous ring in the superiororbital fissure to supply the lateral rectus.
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following are a part of the limbic system?
explanation: The amygdala, hippocampus, and thalamus are all a part of the limbic system. The limbic system refers to the interconnected neuronal circuit in the basal part of the brainthat controls emotional behavior and other vegetative functions such as body temperature, theosmolality of the body fluids, and the drives to eat and drink and to control body weight. The limbic system includes the following: • Subcallosal gyrus • Cingulate gyrus • Parahippocampal gyrus • Hippocampal formation • Amygdaloid nucleus • Mammillary bodies 295 • Anterior thalamic nucleus • Hypothalamus The connecting pathways for this system comprise the alveus, the fimbria, the fornix, themammillothalamic tract, and the stria terminalis.
subject: Anatomy

question: A 50-year-old male presented with a positive Trendelenburg test on the right side. Identifythe nerve injured.
explanation: Positive Trendelenburg test on the right side indicates a right superior gluteal nerve injury. When the patient stands on his right foot, there is drooping of the left pelvis, this is a PositiveTrendelenburg test on the right side. The gluteus medius and minimus are powerful abductors of the hip supplied by the superiorgluteal nerve. Normally, when the leg is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus on the opposite(unsupported) side exert traction on the hip bone. This results in a slight raising of the pelvis onthe unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk upright position. If the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis drops on the contralateral side. Thisis known as a positive Trendelenburg sign. It is positive in the paralysis of the hip abductors, andin developmental dysplasia of the hip. A characteristic lurching gait is seen. The image below shows the Trendelenburg test. 296 297
subject: Anatomy

question: The structure marked A in the image below gives rise to which of the following structures?
explanation: The structure marked A is ventral mesentery. The falciform ligament is a derivative of theventral mesentery. Mesenteries are double layers of the peritoneum that enclose an organ and connect it to the bodywall. They provide pathways for vessels, nerves, and lymphatics to and from the abdominalviscera. 301 • Ventral mesentery: Only the foregut has a ventral mesentery. It is attached to the terminal partof the esophagus, the stomach, and the upper part of the duodenum. The ventral mesentery isderived from the septum transversum. When the liver grows into the mesenchyme of the septumtransversum, it divides the ventral mesentery into 2 parts: • Lesser omentum- extends from the lower portion of the esophagus, the stomach, and the upperportion of the duodenum to the liver • Ligaments of the liver- all ligaments of the liver (falciform ligament, right and left triangularligaments, and coronary ligaments), except ligamentum teres • Dorsal mesentery: The foregut, midgut, and hindgut have a dorsal mesentery. This connects theorgans to the posterior abdominal wall. It runs from the lower end of the esophagus to the cloacalregion of the hindgut. It has the following special names in different regions: • Dorsal mesogastrium (or greater omentum)- stomach • Dorsal mesoduodenum- duodenum • Mesentery proper- jejunum and ileum • Mesoappendix- appendix • Transverse mesocolon- transverse colon • Sigmoid mesocolon- sigmoid colon • Gastrosplenic ligament (stomach to the spleen), lienorenal ligament (spleen to the left kidney),and gastrophrenic ligament (stomach to diaphragm) are derived from the dorsal mesentery. 302
subject: Anatomy

question: A patient underwent surgery for the varicose vein. He now complains of sensory loss over themedial aspect of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be injured?
explanation: The given clinical scenario in a patient with sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and footis suggestive of injury to the saphenous nerve. Injury to the saphenous nerve is common followingvaricose vein surgery. The saphenous nerve is the longest and largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve and is thelongest nerve in the body. It arises from the posterior division of the femoral nerve. It then entersthe adductor canal and exits it by piercing the fascia lata between the gracilis and sartorius andsupplies the skin over the patella. The saphenous nerve then descends along the medial border ofthe tibia along with the great saphenous vein (anterior to the vein) and supplies the skin on themedial side of the knee, leg, and foot up to the first metatarsophalangeal joint. During stripping of veins in varicose surgery, injury to the saphenous nerve is common as itclosely travels with the great saphenous vein. Sensory loss over the medial side of the knee, leg,and foot is observed in saphenous nerve injury. 303 Other options: Option A: Sural nerve injury causes sensory loss over the posterior and lateral aspects of the distalthird of the leg and lateral side of the foot and fifth toe. It is often used as an autologousperipheral nerve graft as it is readily identified and easy to harvest. Option B: Superficial peroneal nerve injury causes sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the legand the dorsum of the foot. It also causes weakness of foot eversion. Option C: Deep peroneal nerve injury causes weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension butnormal eversion of the foot.

question: A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, and excessivelacrimation. He also complains of hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth. On examination,pupillary reaction, light reflex, and accommodation reflex are normal. Which of the followingmarked nerves is involved in the above scenario?
explanation: The above patient presents with features suggesting an involvement of the trigeminal nerve. Thestructure marked 3 is the trigeminal nerve. Other marked structures: • 1- Optic nerve. The normal visual field and light reflex rules out the involvement of the opticnerve. • 2- Oculomotor nerve. Normal accommodation and pupillary reflex rule out the involvement ofthe oculomotor nerve. • 4- Facial nerve. Absence of motor involvement of the face rule out the involvement of the facialnerve. 306 The trigeminal nerve leaves the anterior aspect of the pons as a small motor root and a largesensory root. The large sensory root expands to form the crescent-shaped trigeminal ganglion,which lies within a pouch of dura mater called the trigeminal or Meckel's cave. The ophthalmic,maxillary, and mandibular nerves arise from the anterior border of the ganglion. Branches of the trigeminal nerve: • The ophthalmic nerve (V1) • Leaves the skull through the superior orbital fissure to enter the orbital cavity. • Contains only sensory fibers • Cornea (photophobia) • The skin of the forehead, scalp, eyelids, and nose • The mucous membrane of paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity • The maxillary nerve (V2) • Leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum. • Contains only sensory fibers from • Teeth of the upper jaw • The skin of the face over the maxilla • The mucous membrane of the nose, the maxillary sinus, and the palate • The mandibular nerve (V3) • Leaves the skull through the foramen ovale. • Contains both sensory and motor fibers. • Sensory from: • The skin of the cheek, over mandible, and side of the head • Teeth of the lower jaw and temporomandibular joint (hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth) • The mucous membrane of the mouth and anterior part of the tongue • Motor to: • Muscles of mastication (pterygoids, masseter, and temporalis) • Tensor tympani • Anterior belly of digastric • Mylohyoid

question: Identify the given structure:
explanation: The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part ofthe pancreas. 307 Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerousfenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than thesurrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum. The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas. The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types: • Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells: • α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon • β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin • δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin • PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreaticpolypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion ofgastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility. • Minor cell types: • D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis andhyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea. • Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that causecarcinoid syndrome. Other options: Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists ofan outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primaryfollicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center. The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullarysinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, whichcontains T lymphocytes. The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node. 308 Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wallis the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, andvisceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes. The glomerular tuft is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellularmesangial matrix. The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus. Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by redpulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery orarterioles. Lymphocytes surrounding the arteriole are called peri-arterial lymphatic sheath (PALS)and contain T cells. Follicles in white pulp contain B cells. The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It islike a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulpimmediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of 309 sinusoids. The image given below shows the histology of the spleen. 310

question: A student had his jaw locked while yawning. Which of the following muscles is attached to thearticular disc of the temporomandibular joint?
explanation: The muscle that is attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint is the lateralpterygoid. Lateral pterygoid muscle: • Origin - Upper head arises from the infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greaterwing of the sphenoid bone. The lower head arises from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoidplate. • Insertion - It is inserted into the pterygoid fovea, the capsule of the temporomandibular joint,and the articular disc. The action of lateral pterygoid muscle is depression, protrusion, and side-to-side movement of thejaw.

question: Identify the structure(s) in the following histological image.
explanation: The above histology image shows the glomerulus. Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium. Bloodenters the tuft through an afferent arteriole and leaves it through an efferent arteriole. It issupported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelialcells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain footprocesses. The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus. Option A: Leydig cells, also known as interstitial cells of Leydig, are present in the interstitialconnective between seminiferous tubules. 316 The testis contains numerous seminiferous tubules separated by connective tissue inbetween. Seminiferous tubules are lined by several spermatogonia cells, which producespermatozoa, and Sertoli (sustentacular) cells, which have a supportive function. The connective tissue in between the tubules is made up of Leydig cells, collagen fibers,fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, blood vessels, and lymphatics. Leydig cells are large, round,or polyhedral cells with eccentric nuclei. They are lightly stained and often have a foamyappearance. They secrete testosterone upon stimulation by luteinizing hormone from the anteriorpituitary. The image below shows seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells. Option B: Islets of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas. Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers and contain numerousfenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. The islet cells are paler thanthe surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum. The islet of Langerhans is mainly composed of three types of cells: • α or A cells - located peripherally and secrete glucagon • β or B cells - located centrally and produce insulin • δ or D cells - scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin The image given below shows the islets of Langerhans. 317 Option C: Hassall's corpuscles are small rounded structures present in the medulla of the thymus.Each corpuscle has a central core of degenerated epithelial cells and macrophages surrounded byconcentrically arranged epithelial cells. The degenerated cells ultimately give pink staining hyalinemass. The function of the corpuscles of Hassall is still not known. The image given below shows Hassall's corpuscle.

question: Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
explanation: The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causesfailure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also know ascommon peroneal nerve) 318 The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1stand 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to thefibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It thencurves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibularnerves. Superficial fibular nerveDeep fibular nerve Motor innervationPeroneus longusPeroneus brevisExtensor digitorum longusExtensor hallucis longusTibialis anteriorPeroneus tertius Sensory innervationLateral aspect of the lower legDorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital web-space The first interdigital space 319 Injury to the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve) at the level of the neck of the fibulacauses foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while theinversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot,including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

question: A defect in which of the following aortic arches causes the defect shown in the image?
explanation: The image above shows a patent ductus arteriosus due to a defect in the left side of the 6th aorticarch. Usually, in term infants, the ductus arteriosus closes within 72 hours of birth. Failure of theductus arteriosus to close results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). PDA usually presents with a hyperdynamic precordium, bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulsepressure, a machine-like continuous or systolic murmur, cardiomegaly, increased pulmonaryvascular markings, hepatomegaly, increasing oxygen dependence, carbon dioxide retention, andrenal failure. In a majority of cases, PDA closes spontaneously. If spontaneous closure fails to occur, COXinhibitors like indomethacin or ibuprofen can be used. Surgical ligation is indicated in case ofcontraindications to medical management or failure of the same. Other options Option A: The 4th right aortic arch gives rise to the proximal part of the right subclavian artery. Option B: The 4th left aortic arch gives rise to the arch of the aorta. Defects involving the 4th leftaortic arch could cause a variety of aortic arch anomalies, such as interruption of the aortic arch,but not PDA. Option C: The 6th right aortic arch forms the proximal part of the right pulmonary artery. 320

question: A patient presents with swelling under the left ear lobule and complains of pain. Which of thefollowing structures is the likely cause of the pain?

options.d: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia

explanation: The cause of the pain in this patient complaining of pain in the parotid region is likely to be thegreater auricular nerve. The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the parotid glandand the ear lobule. Pain associated with swelling and inflammation in the parotid region could betransmitted through the greater auricular nerve. The parotid gland is covered by a parotid capsulethat is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Any acute inflammation of thegland such as acute sialadenitis results in pain in the preauricular region. The pain is mainly dueto stretching of the capsule resulting in stimulation of the greater auricular nerve. Other options: Option A: The facial nerve is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling.The Hitzelberger sign(numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall of the external auditorycanal), associated with facial nerve involvement, is seen in acoustic neuroma and is not the causeof pain in this scenario. Option D: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is not the correct answer because the investinglayer of deep cervical fascia itself does not transmit pain sensation. The investing layer of deepcervical fascia is a layer of connective tissue that envelops the neck and extends to cover theparotid gland, forming the parotid capsule. While inflammation or swelling in the parotid glandcan stretch the capsule and cause pain, the actual transmission of pain sensation is mediated bysensory nerves, such as the greater auricular nerve, which innervates the skin over the parotidgland and the ear lobule. The greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a more appropriate answer in this context, as it isresponsible for carrying the pain sensation from the area of swelling and inflammation in theparotid region. Option C: The auriculotemporal nerve can cause referred pain due to caries tooth, ulcerativelesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia.However, it is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling. 322

question: Which of the following muscles are supplied by Superior Gluteal Nerve?
explanation: Gluteus Medius, Gluteus Minimus, and Tensor fascia lata are supplied by Superior Gluteal Nerve.Piriformis is supplied by the nerve to the piriformis. The dorsal branches of the L4, L5, and S1 rami give rise to the superior gluteal nerve. It isaccompanied by superior gluteal vessels. This nerve leaves the pelvis via the greater sciaticforamen above piriformis and divides into superior and inferior branches. It supplies gluteusmedius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. The dorsal divisions of the S1 and S2 rami give rise to the nerve to the piriformis. Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis onthe femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject tostand on one limb. If the ipsilateral abductors are normal, the pelvis remains in a horizontal 339 position. If the ipsilateral abductors are weak, then the pelvis tilts towards the opposite(unsupported) side. This is called positive Trendelenburg’s sign.

question: A 25-year-old male presented with symptoms of inability to flex the distal interphalangealjoint of the 4th and 5th digits. He was also not able to hold a piece of paper between hisfingers. What is the likely site of injury?
explanation: The given clinical situation with a positive card test and an inability to flex the distalinterphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits, suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely siteof injury would thus be medial epicondyle: site C Injury at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve, leading to paralysis of flexor carpiulnaris (loss of ulnar deviation) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (loss of distalinterphalangeal joint flexion). It leads to hypothenar paralysis (lead to atrophy) and sensory loss.Also, flexor digitorum superficialis (supplied by median nerve) and extensor digitorum (suppliedby the radial nerve) are still functional. Hence complete paralysis of the 3rd and 4th digits 340 is not seen. The positive card test is due to the weakness of palmar interossei leading to loss ofadduction. Ulnar nerve branches and supply: Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis, skin on the palmar surface of medial 1½ fingers.The deep branch runs within the concavity of deep palmar arch and supplies all intrinsicmuscles of the hand (except first 2 lumbricals and thenar muscles). Injury to the Ulnar nerve: Other tests seen in ulnar nerve lesions are as follows: • Claw hand deformity • Froment's sign positive • Wartenberg sign • Palmaris brevis sign High lesion(Elbow)Low lesion(Wrist) Site of injuryFracture/dislocation of themedial epicondyleCubital tunnel syndromeCompression between the two heads of FCUTardy ulnar nerve palsy (Valgus deformity) Wrist laceration/ slashingGuyon's canalsyndrome Motor lossClaw-handdeformityHypothenar & interosseous wastingLoss of:• Abduction & adduction of fingers(Card test- Positive)• Adduction of thumb(Froment sign-Positive)• Flexion of MCP jointsWeakness of wrist flexion (radial deviation) Claw-handdeformity(more pronounced)Hypothenar & interosseous wastingLoss of:• Abduction & adduction of fingers(Card test- Positive)• Adduction of thumb(Froment sign-Positive) Sensory lossOver palmar & dorsal aspect of themedial thirdof thehandOver palmar & dorsal aspect of themedial 11/2fingers No sensory lossover palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial third of the handOver palmar & dorsal aspect of themedial 11/2fingers The image below shows a positive card test. 341 Wartenberg's sign: (Weakness of palmar interossei), Sensory loss Palmar and dorsal surface of themedial third of hand and medial 1 and a half fingers. Other options: • Option A: Radial groove - Radial nerve • Option D: Neck of humerus - Axillary nerve • Option B: Lateral epicondyle – May lead to tardy ulnar nerve palsy after fracture but theincidence is less.

question: Which of the following muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?
explanation: 342 Iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus are parts of the pelvic diaphragm, which is also known as thelevator ani. The levator ani muscle is a complex unit that consists of 3 muscle components: • Pubococcygeus • Pubovaginalis - elevates the urethra and hence contributes to urinary continence • Puboperinealis - draws the perineal body towards the pubic symphysis • Puboanalis - elevates the anus and keeps the urogenital hiatus narrowed • Puborectalis • Iliococcygeus Levator ani muscles are the most important muscles in the pelvic floor and maintain a constantstate of contraction. They provide a stable floor and support the weight of the abdominopelviccontents against intra-abdominal forces. Weakening of levator ani and pelvic fascia fromstretching or tearing during childbirth, may decrease support for the vagina, bladder, uterus, orrectum or alter the position of the neck of the bladder and urethra. Other options: The obturator internus forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa and is not a part of the levatorani. The deep transverse perineal muscle is the content of the deep perineal space and contributes tothe formation of the perineal body.
