question: Given below is the image of a 33-hour chick embryo. Which of the following is derived fromthe marked structure?
explanation: The structure marked in the given image is the para-axial mesoderm. The ribs are derived fromthe para-axial mesoderm. During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, whichrefers to the formation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. This isfollowed by the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, which induces theformation of the neural tube above it. During the formation of the neural tube, some cells at thelateral border dissociate and form the neural crest cells, which is sometimes referred to as thefourth germ layer. 346 After the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, the mesoderm on either sidecan be seen to be organized into three layers as follows: 1. Para-axial mesoderm - Thickened plate of the mesoderm close to the midline, on either side ofthe notochord. This forms the somitomeres and somites, which have the following derivatives: • Dermatome: Forms the segmental dermis of the skin • Myotome: Forms the skeletal muscle • Sclerotome: Forms the vertebral column and ribs 2. Intermediate mesoderm - Longitudinal strip of mesoderm that connects the para-axial with thelateral plate mesoderm. The urinary (Option A) and genital systems are derived from theintermediate mesoderm. 3. Lateral plate mesoderm - A thinner layer of mesoderm that lies laterally. This layer develops alarge cavity called the intraembryonic coelom that gives rise to pericardial, pleural (Option C), andperitoneal cavities. The neural crest cells also contribute to the formation of structures as follows: In the trunk region, they form melanocytes, sensory ganglia (Option B), sympathetic and entericneurons, Schwann cells, and adrenal medulla cells. In the cranial region, they contribute to the craniofacial skeleton, neurons for cranial ganglia,satellite glial cells, and melanocytes.

question: Which of the following is false regarding the anatomy of the adrenal glands?

Each gland has one draining vein. • The right suprarenal vein drains into the IVC. • The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein. question: The sulcus located deep to the marked structure is?
explanation: 348 The area marked by an arrow in the given image is pterion and the stem of the lateral sulcus liesunder it. The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull: • Frontal bone • Squamous part of the temporal bone • Greater wing of the sphenoid bone • Parietal bone. The surface of the cerebrum consists of folds called gyri separated by fissures called sulci. Thelateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian Fissure, is present on the infero-lateral surface of eachcerebral hemisphere and separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. The lateral sulcusconsists of a stem which divides into three rami, which are, the anterior horizontal, anteriorascending, and the posterior rami. The structures lying deep to the pterion are: • The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery • The middle meningeal vein • The stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) The bone in this area is thin and an injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middlemeningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma. 349

question: Given below is an illustration of a transverse section of the heart. Identify the markedstructure.
explanation: The marked structure is the sub-aortic curtain. It is also called the trigonum fibrosum sinistrum. The fibrous skeleton of the heart is formed by fibrous tissue that is continuous between theatrio-ventricular and arterial orifices. They exist to keep the valves competent, allow attachmentof cardiac musculature, and act as an insulating layer for the conducting system of the heart. Thefibrous rings of importance are: • The atrioventricular fibrous rings - existing in a figure of 8 configuration, connecting the atria,ventricles and the membranous part of the interventricular septum. • The trigonum fibrosum dextrum - between the atrioventricular rings and the aortic ring. • The trigonum fibrosum sinistrum - between the mitral valve and the aortic valve. 350

question: Identify the structure marked as A.
explanation: The arrow-marked structure in the given image is the terminal bronchiole. It can be identified bythe absence of cartilage, which would be present in the bronchus, and the presence of cilia andstratified columnar epithelium, which would not be seen in respiratory bronchioles and alveolarsac. The following is a summary of the intrapulmonary passages: Trachea → Main Bronchi → Lobar Bronchi → Segmental Bronchi → Terminal Bronchiole →Respiratory Bronchiole → Alveolar Duct → Alveolar Sac → Alveoli Bronchi and bronchioles can be distinguished by the presence of cartilage and glands in thebronchi which are not present in the bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles represent the most distal parts of the conducting passage. Each terminalbronchiole ends by dividing into respiratory bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles contain cilia andstratified columnar epithelium, whereas respiratory bronchioles contain few or no cilia, andsimple cuboidal epithelium. Another differentiating point between the two is that terminalbronchioles would not communicate with the alveoli but respiratory bronchioles would have acommunication with the alveoli. Each respiratory bronchiole ends by dividing into a few alveolar ducts. Each alveolar duct ends ina passage, the atrium, which leads into a number of rounded alveolar sacs. Each alveolar sac isstudded with a number of air sacs or alveoli. A: Terminal Bronchiole, B: Respiratory Bronchiole, C: Alveolar Sac, D: Alveolar Duct The coloured strips in the following illustration represent the location of different cells/structuresin the trachea and bronchial tree. 351 Note - The image in the question has been updated for better clarity

question: The fibres of the internal oblique muscle and transverse abdominus muscle contribute towhich boundaries of the inguinal canal walls:
explanation: The fibres of the internal oblique muscle and transverse abdominus muscle contribute to the roofand posterior wall of the inguinal canal walls. The boundaries of the inguinal canal walls are as follows: • Anterior wall: Formed by the external oblique aponeurosis. • Roof: Formed by the arched fibres of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. • Floor: Formed by the grooved upper surface of the Abdomen and Pelvis inguinal ligament. • Posterior wall: Consists of the transversalis fascia and conjoint tendon (the lowest fibres of thetransverses abdominis muscle fuse with the lowest fibres of the internal oblique to form theconjoint tendon).

question: Which of the following is a function of the marked layer?
explanation: The image shows a histological section of the adrenal gland and the layer marked is the outermostlayer, ie, the zona glomerulosa, which secretes the mineralocorticoid - aldosterone, responsible forsodium and water retention. Based on structure and function, the adrenal cortex has three zones, which from outer to inner,are: • Zona glomerulosa: Secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) - which acts in response to theactivation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system (RAAS) and acts at the distal convolutedtubule and the collecting ducts favouring sodium and water retention and potassium excretion. 352 • Zona fasiculata: Secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol and corticosterone) - which has multiplefunctions that include metabolic effects which induce hyperglycemia inducing gluconeogenesis(Option A) and mediates anti-inflammatory and immunosuppresive effects by interacting with thecells of the immune system (Option D). • Zona reticularis: Secretes sex steroids (dehydroepiandrosterone, androstenedione, estrogens,and glucocorticoids) (Option C)

question: A patient's right hip drops when he takes the right foot off the ground. Which of the followingwould not be involved in the patient?
explanation: A patient with dropping of the right hip on lifting the right foot off the ground, has a positiveTrendelenburg’s sign. The sciatic nerve would not be involved. A positive Trendelenburg's sign is seen in the paralysis of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimusmuscles, both of which are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. In the scenario mentioned,since the patient has dropping of the hip on the right side, the structures on the left side would beaffected. 353 Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus: • When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, making it the unsupported side, gluteusmedius and minimus muscles on the opposite side, which is the supported side, exert traction onthe hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in slight raising of the pelvis on theunsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position. • When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis on the unsupported side sinkswhen the patient lifts the foot off the ground. This causes the patients to have a characteristiclurching gait.

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the anomaly shown below?

options.a: It occurs due to the persistance of prechordal plate
options.b: It occurs due to the defective migration of primordial cells to the genital ridge
options.c: It contains skin, cartilage and bone
options.d: It is a benign tumor of coccyx

explanation: 354 The image shows a sacrococcygeal teratoma, which occurs due to the persistence of pluripotentcells of the primitive streak in the sacrococcygeal region. During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, whichrefers to the formation of the three germ layers. These germ layers are formed from theprimordial germ cells of the epiblast, which are pluripotent. The process begins with theformation of the primitive streak on the epiblast, which develops into the primitive node in thecranial region, and a primitive pit. The cells from the epiblast, migrate towards the primitivestreak and invaginate into the primitive pit and organizes itself into cells arranged in three layers,which eventually develop into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The prechordal plate simplyrefers to the cells that have invaginated in the cranial region. Sacrococcygeal teratomas occur due to remnants of pluripotent cells from the primitive streak dueto defective migration of the cells (Option B). As these cells are from the epiblast, teratomascontain tissues from all germ layers which may include skin, hair, cartilage and bone (Option C).These tumors are benign in nature (Option D), but may rarely become malignant. If they occur inthe cranial end of the primitive streak, they form oro-pharyngeal teratomas (as shown below),whereas if they occur in the caudal end of the primitive streak in the coccygeal region, they arecalled sacro-coccygeal teratomas. 355

question: What is the role of the marked structure in the given image?
explanation: The marked structure is the subthalamic nucleus, which is a part of the basal ganglia and isconcerned with motor function. The basal ganglia refers to the mass of grey matter located within the cerebral white matter and isresponsible for a number of coordinated functions including the control of extra-pyramidalpathways for motor coordination. There are two major pathways involved which are, the directand indirect pathways. The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathwayinhibits it. The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and inthe indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. The subthalamic nucleus is a part of the indirectpathway. A lesion at subthalamic nuclei leads to loss of inhibitory effect of the indirect pathwayresulting in dopaminergic overactivity responsible for features of hemiballismus. 357 Other Options: Option B: Reward-punishment is associated with the prefrontal area and the dopaminergicconnections linked to it from the ventral tegmental area. Option C: Judgement is controlled by the frontal lobe. Option D: Memory is controlled by the hippocampus.

question: Which of the following muscles are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve?
explanation: From the given list, the muscles supplied by the lateral plantar nerve are the flexor digitorumaccesorius and the first interossei. 358 The sole of the foot is supplied by the medial and lateral plantar nerves which are both branchesof the tibial nerve. All the muscles of the sole of the foot are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve, except for thefollowing four muscles which are supplied by the medial plantar nerve: • Abductor hallucis • Flexor digitorum brevis • Flexor hallucis brevis • First lumbrical The sensory supply of the sole of the foot is as shown in the illustration below. The muscles of the sole of the foot are arranged in 4 layers as shown below: 1st layer: It consists of the abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi. 359 2nd layer: It consists of flexor accessorius and the four lumbrical muscles,the tendons of flexorhallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus run in the same plane as the muscles of the secondlayer. 3rd layer: It consists of the shorter intrinsic muscles of the toes, which are flexor hallucis brevis,adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis. 4th layer: It consists of plantar and dorsal interossei and the tendons of tibialis posterior andfibularis longus. 360

question: The marked structure sends efferents to which nucleus of the thalamus?
explanation: The marked structure in the given coronal section of the brain is the fornix. question: On neurologic examination, a patient is not able to identify an object but is able to recognizethe object from its texture, colour and pattern. Which of the following is likely to have beenaffected?
explanation: The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvementwould be the inferior temporal lobe. • Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia.According to De Jong, visual agnosia is further classified into: • Apperceptive visual agnosia - the visual image appears distorted to the patient and hence theyare unable to recognise it. This occurs due lesions in the parieto-occipital region • Associative visual agnosia - inability to visually identify objects in the absence of visualimpairment, with ability to identify the object using other sensory modalities (as suggested in thescenario). This occurs due to lesions of occipito-temporal junction, which is present in the inferiortemporal lobe. Prosopagnosia is a type of associatetive visual agnosia which refers to theinability to visually identify faces. The occipital lobe acts as the primary visual area and a lesion in this region would result incortical blindness and achromatopsia, which is the inability to visualise colour. In the givenscenario, as the patient is also able to identify colour, it indicates that the occipital lobe (Option A)is unaffected and (hence inferior temporal lobe is the better answer). Stereognosis is the ability to identify an object by a perception of the form and nature of an objectwithout looking at it. In the given scenario, the patient is able to recognize the object from itstexture and pattern which indicates that stereognosis is intact. Loss of this ability is known asastereognosis which occurs in lesions of the superior parietal lobule (Options B and C) and dorsalcolumn pathways.

question: Apocrine glands are present in which of the following?
explanation: Apocrine glands are present in the axilla. 362 Exocrine glands can be classified into three subtypes, based on the manner in which theirsecretions are poured out of the cells: • Apocrine • Merocrine • Holocrine In apocrine glands, the apical parts of the cells are shed off to discharge the secretion. Examplesof apocrine glands are : • Secretion of milk fat by mammary glands • Atypical sweat glands in the axilla, perianal region, periumbilical skin, mons pubis. • Ceruminous glands of the external auditory meatus are modified apocrine glands Apocrine glands are large glands found in the dermis or subcutaneous fat. They are a type ofsweat gland. It consists of a basal secretory coil followed by a straight duct that opens intothe pilary canal above the duct of the sebaceous gland. In hairless skin, it directly opens onto theskin surface. Apocrine activity is minimal before puberty, after which it is androgen-dependent and responsiveto emotional stimuli. It is controlled by adrenergic nerves and is sensitive to adrenaline andnoradrenaline. The secretion is initially sterile and odorless, but it undergoes bacterialdecomposition to generate odorous and musky compounds. Obstruction of apocrine sweat ductsand associated upper hair follicles in the axillae, breast areolae, and pubic region, mainly inwomen, is thought to cause Fox–Fordyce disease. It is also implicated in the causation of apainful, occasionally debilitating condition called hidradenitis suppurativa. The given image shows an illustration of apocrine secretion. 363

question: Which of the following is a tributary of the inferior vena cava?
explanation: The left inferior phrenic vein is a tributary of the inferior vena cava (IVC). From inferior to superior, the following vessels are direct tributaries of the IVC: • Common iliac veins (left and right common iliac veins merge to form the IVC) • Median sacral vein • Four pairs of lumbar veins • Right gonadal vein • Renal veins (both left and right) • Right supra-renal vein 364 • Hepatic veins • Inferior phrenic veins (both left and right) Other Options: Option B: The left supra-renal vein drains into the left renal vein. Option C: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein. Option D: The right ascending lumbar vein joins the subcostal vein on the right side to form theazygos vein. The left ascending lumbar vein joins the subcostal vein on the left side to form thehemi-azygos vein. 365

question: Which of the following joints is not formed by the structure shown in the picture?
explanation: 377 The provided image depicts a thoracic vertebra, which does not participate in forming asynchondrosis-type joint. The example for a synchondrosis is the costochondral joint formedbetween the ribs and the costal cartilage. A vertebral bone participates in the following joints : • Intervertebral joint - secondary cartilaginous joint ( symphysis type ) • Costovertebral joint - plane synovial joint • costotransverse joint - plane synovial joint • Facet joints or zygapophysial joints - synovial joint A syndesmosis is a type of complex fibrous joint between two bones connected by ligaments and astrong membrane[1] with slight movement allowed.The vertebra is connected by a anterior andposterior ligament where some degree of syndesmosis type of joint is seen. question: The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve has 2nd order neurons to carry whichsensation?
explanation: The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well asmotor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic(V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions. The first-order neurons for each divisionoriginate from different sensory ganglia: 1.Ophthalmic Division (V1): First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunaror Gasserian ganglion). 2. Maxillary Division (V2): First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion. 3. Mandibular Division (V3): First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion. 378 These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Uponentering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei: 1. Principal Sensory Nucleus (Main Sensory Nucleus): a.Receives input from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve. b.Located in the pons. c.Second-order neurons here carry discriminative touch and proprioceptive information. 2. Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus (Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal): a.Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions. b.Located in the medulla. c.Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations. After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centersfor processing and perception.

question: Which of the following is not seen in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?
explanation: The tail of the caudate nucleus is not seen on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.It is present on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. The inferior horn is the largest compartment of the lateral ventricle and extends up to 2.5 cmfrom the temporal pole. The relations are: Roof - Tapetum of corpus callosum laterally and tail of caudate nucleus medially. Floor (lateral to medial) - Collateral eminence produced by collateral fissure, hippocampus. The floor of the temporal horn consists of the hippocampus medially and the collateral eminence,formed by the infolding of the collateral sulcus, laterally. The inferior part of the choroidal fissure,located between the fimbria of the fornix and the inferolateral aspect of the thalamus, lies in themedial wall. The lateral ventricle is divided into the body and 3 horns. The locations of the parts are: • Body - parietal lobe • Anterior horn - frontal lobe • Posterior horn - occipital lobe • Inferior horn - temporal lobe. 379 The anterior horn extends from the genu of the corpus callosum up to the interventricularforamen. The relations of the anterior horn are: • Anteriorly - Genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum • Roof - Anterior part of the body of the corpus callosum • Floor and lateral wall - Caudate nucleus • Medial wall - Septum pellucidum and anterior column of fornix The body or central part extends from the interventricular foramen to the splenium of the corpuscallosum. The relations of the body are: • Roof - Body of the corpus callosum • Medial wall - Septum pellucidum • Floor (from lateral to medial) - Caudate nucleus, stria terminalis, thalamostriate vein, thalamus,choroid plexus, and body of the fornix The posterior horn extends from the splenium to the occipital pole. The relations are: • Roof and lateral wall - Tapetum of corpus callosum • Medial wall - Forceps major and calcar avis (calcarine sulcus Note: There is no lateral wall for the lateral ventricle. 380

question: Which of the following marked areas in the histopathological specimen shows calcification?
explanation: The given specimen is that of an epiphyseal cartilage, where zone 3 corresponds to the zone ofcalcification. Epiphyseal cartilage is divided into five zones : • The resting zone consists of hyaline cartilage without morphological changes in the cells (option1) • In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and form columns of stacked cells parallelto the long axis of the bone (option 2) • The hypertrophic cartilage zone contains large chondrocytes whose cytoplasm has accumulatedglycogen. The resorbed matrix is reduced to thin septa between the chondrocytes. • Simultaneous with the death of chondrocytes in the calcified cartilage zone, the thin septa ofcartilage matrix become calcified by the deposit of hydroxyapatite. • In the ossification zone, endochondral bone tissue appears (option 4). Blood capillaries andosteoprogenitor cells formed by mitosis of cells originating from the periosteum invade thecavities left by the chondrocytes. The osteoprogenitor cells form osteoblasts, which are distributedin a discontinuous layer over the septa of the calcified cartilage matrix. Ultimately, the osteoblastsdeposit bone matrix over the three-dimensional calcified cartilage matrix. The epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for the growth in the length of bone and it disappears inadults, which is why bone growth ceases in adulthood. 381

question: At what vertebral level does the part marked in the image lie in a normal anatomicalposition?

options.d: Disc space between L4 and L5

explanation: In the right pelvic bone given above the marked structure is the ischial spine which liesapproximately at the level of the fifth sacral vertebrae in a normal anatomical position. As the tipof the coccyx is the closest option relating to the spine , it can be the most appropriate answer. The ischial spine is a bony prominence found on the ischium, one of the three bones that make upthe hip bone. The ischial spine forms a part of the plane of least pelvic dimensions or narrowpelvic plane which comprises of : • lower border of the symphysis pubis • the tip of ischial spines • fifth sacral vertebra The interspinous distance is the distance between the tip of two ischial spines. ( Bispinousdiameter = 10.5 cm or 4.5" ) The important events occurring at the narrowest plane in the pelvis : • It corresponds roughly to the origin of levator ani muscles. • The internal rotation of the fetal head occurs during labour at this plane. • It marks the beginning of the forward curve of the pelvic axis • This level of ischial spines indicates station ‘O’ • When the fetal head station is at ‘O’, the head is considered to be engaged. • Deep transverse arrest occurs at this plane. • The ischial spine can serve as a landmark in pudendal anaesthesia, as the pudendal nerve liesclose to the ischial spine The image given below highlights the interspinous distance seen through the pelvic inlet. 383

question: The nerve related to the area marked in the picture has its root value from?

explanation: The above is an image of the left lung with the arrow pointing at the nerve passing anterior to theleft hilum. question: The structure marked as 'X' in image A has a direct connection with which of the followingstructures marked in image B?
explanation: Image A shows a section of the cerebellum and image B shows a section of the midbrain. Thestructure labeled as 'X' represents the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum, which has a directconnection with the structure marked as '1', which is the red nucleus. The dentate nucleus is the largest of the cerebellar nuclei. It has the shape of a crumpled bag withthe opening facing medially. The interior of the bag is filled with white matter made up of efferentfibers that leave the nucleus through the opening to form a large part of the superior cerebellarpeduncle. question: Which of the following statements is true concerning the anatomy of the breast?

options.a: Inner quadrants contain most breast tissue
options.b: Ligaments of cooper are found only in lower quadrants
options.c: Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold

explanation: The tail of Spence extends across the anterior axillary fold and is a small extension of the upperlateral quadrant of the breast. The breast lies in the superficial fascia of the pectoral region. It is divided into four quadrants, i.e.upper medial, upper lateral, lower medial and lower lateral. Vertically, it extends from the second to the sixth ribs. Horizontally, it extends from the lateralborder of the sternum to the midaxillary line. A small extension of the upper lateral quadrant,called the axillary tail of Spence, passes through an opening in the deep fascia and lies in theaxilla. The opening is called the foramen of Langer. 387 The breast lies on the deep pectoral fascia covering the pectoralis major and serratus anteriorsuperiorly, the external abdominal oblique and its aponeurosis inferiorly, and the clavipectoralfascia laterally. Fibrous strands or sheets consisting of condensations of connective tissue extendbetween the posterior lamina of the superficial fascia and the dermis. These suspensory ligaments(retinacula or Cooper’s ligaments) are often well-developed in the superior parts of the breast andsupport the breast tissue, helping to minimize drooping. The breasts normally comprise up to 20 discrete lobes that contain ductal-glandular tissueconsisting of branching ducts and terminal secretory lobules in a connective tissue stroma. Eachlobe is derived by branching from one central lactiferous duct in the nipple. The terminal ductlobular unit (TDLU or lobule) is the functional milk secretory component of the breast. The upper outer quadrant of the breast contains a greater volume of tissue than the otherquadrants. This is the reason for the majority of the carcinomas arising in the upper outerquadrant. 388
subject: Anatomy

question: A professor underwent a left parotidectomy. Post surgery she complains of left lower lipparalysis. Which structure is involved?
explanation: Lower lip paralysis is caused by damage to the cervical branch of the facial nerve. The cervical branch of the facial nerve is responsible for innervating the platysma muscle, which isone of the muscles involved in the movements of the lower lip. Damage to this nerve canpotentially lead to paralysis of the lower lip. The facial nerve is the motor nerve of the face. Its five terminal branches emerge from the parotidgland and diverge to supply the various facial muscles as follows : • Temporal — frontalis, auricular muscles, orbicularis oculi • Zygomatic — orbicularis oculi (lower eyelid part) • Buccal — muscles of the cheek and upper lip • Marginal mandibular — muscles of the lower lip • Cervical — platysma
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the normal anatomical variation given in the following CT image.
explanation: The CT finding in the image is suggestive of an aberrant right subclavian artery. An aberrant right subclavian artery occurs when the right fourth aortic arch and right dorsal aortainvolute cranial to the seventh intersegmental artery. This artery arises distal to the left subclavian artery and crosses the midline posterior to theesophagus. Because of the absence of a normal right subclavian-carotid junction to pull down theright recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) during embryologic development, the right RLN follows astraight path from the vagus to the larynx and is called a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve. Most patients with this anomaly are asymptomatic, and the aberrant subclavian artery is of noclinical consequence. Dysphagia caused by compression of the esophagus by an abnormalsubclavian artery is called dysphagia lusoria. 389
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the marked structure
explanation: The marked structure is superficial temporal artery. The superficial temporal artery is one of the terminal branches of the external carotid artery,along with the maxillary artery. It ascends in front of the ear, passing over the zygomatic arch andtravels superficially, supplying the scalp and areas around the temple. Other Options: Option B: The posterior auricular artery is smaller and located posterior to the ear. Option C: The middle meningeal artery is deep within the cranial cavity and supplies themeninges. Option D: The occipital artery lies posteriorly and supplies the scalp at the back of the head. 390
subject: Anatomy

question: The marked structure serves as a surface landmark for which anatomical structure?
explanation: The marked structure indicates the pterion and it serves as a landmark for the stem of the lateralsulcus. The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion. It is a landmark for thestem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), the most prominent sulcus of the cerebral hemisphere.It separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. Deep to the lateral sulcus lies the insularcortex. Pterion marks as a surface landmark for the following structures: • Middle meningeal artery and vein: fractures in this area can rupture the middle meningealartery, leading to an epidural hematoma. • Broca’s area: Located in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) in the inferior frontal gyrus, itlies in proximity to the pterion • The insular cortex and parts of the basal ganglia, such as the putamen, are located deep to thepterion, beneath the lateral sulcus. • Stem of the lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian fissure. It houses the middle cerebral artery andits branches, playing a crucial role in brain vascularization and cortical organization. During surgeries, the pterion is a common site for trephining (making a hole in the skull). Other Options: Option A: The pineal gland is located in the posterior aspect of the cranial fossa in the brain. It islocated deep in the brain, near the midline. Option B: Wenicke's area is in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant cerebral hemisphere.It is found in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus. 391 Option D: The internal carotid artery siphon is a part of the internal carotid artery's course.Characterized by its S-shaped curvature as it traverses the cavernous sinus and enters the cranialcavity. This configuration helps dissipate pulsatile energy, reducing stress on cerebral vessels, andallows adaptability to cranial movements while maintaining cerebral perfusion.
subject: Anatomy

question: A 60-year-old male recovering from facial nerve palsy complains of food getting stuckbetween the cheek and teeth while eating. What is the muscle affected in this case?
explanation: This patient, recovering from facial nerve palsy, getting food stuck between the cheek and teethwhile eating, is because of the buccinator being affected. The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression. It is innervated by the facial nerve. It is known asthe whistling muscle. The buccinator muscle is primarily responsible for keeping food between the teeth duringmastication by pressing the cheek against the teeth (involved in flattening the cheeks against thegums and teeth). In facial nerve palsy, paralysis of the buccinator muscle can lead to food accumulating in thecheek pouch, as the muscle is unable to contract properly. Other options: Option B: Levator Labii Superioris: This muscle elevates the upper lip and contributes to facialexpressions like showing the upper teeth and dilates the nostrils. It is not involved in keeping foodin place during chewing. Option C : Zygomaticus Major: Responsible for pulling the corner of the mouth upward andoutward, contributing to smiling. It does not influence food placement during mastication. Option D : Orbicularis Oris: Encircles the mouth and helps in closing the lips. While it is involvedin mastication and speech, its paralysis would not cause food to accumulate in the cheek.
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following is not a derivative of neural crest cells?
explanation: Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm. The RPE develops from theouter layer of the optic cup, a structure that arises from the neural tube (neuroectodermal origin),not from neural crest cells. Neural crest cells are a group of cells that migrate during embryonic development and give rise tovarious structures, including parts of the nervous system, face, and heart. Neural crest cells (NCC) are present adjacent to the neural tube and are sometimes referred to asthe fourth germ layer. It contributes to the formation of many organs and tissues: In the trunk region, they form: • Melanocytes (Option D) • Sensory ganglia • Sympathetic and enteric neurons 392 • Schwann cells • Adrenal medulla cells In the cranial region, they contribute to the: • Craniofacial skeleton • Neurons for cranial ganglia-Ciliary ganglion (Option C) • Ciliary muscles (Option A) • Satellite glial cells • Melanocytes Some of the other neural crest derivatives are: • C cells of the thyroid gland • Conotruncal septum in the heart • Odontoblasts • Smooth muscle cells to blood vessels to the face and forebrain.
subject: Anatomy

question: The cranial component of the neural crest cells leads to the formation of?
explanation: The cranial component of neural crest cells (NCC) leads to the formation of Conotruncal septum. The conotruncal septum is also known as the aortopulmonary septum. The formation of theaortopulmonary septum in the truncus arteriosus divides the outflow channel of the heart into theventral aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Persistent truncus arteriosus results when the conotruncalridges fail to form. The development of the heart begins in the third week of embryogenesis with the formation of thecardiogenic mesoderm. The heart tube forms through fusion of paired endocardial tubes, whichthen undergo looping and septation to establish the four chambers. By the end of the eighth week,the heart achieves its definitive structure, with separate atria, ventricles, and major vessels. The heart develops from mesodermal origins, with different parts deriving from specificembryonic structures: • First Heart Field (Primary Heart Field): Forms the left ventricle and part of the atria. • Second Heart Field: Contributes to the right ventricle, outflow tract (conus arteriosus andtruncus arteriosus), and part of the atria. • Neural Crest Cells: Contribute to the septation of the outflow tract and the formation of theaorticopulmonary septum. • Proepicardium (Epicardial Cells): Forms the epicardium and contributes to coronary vessels. • Sinus Venosus: Forms part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) and the coronary sinus. • Endocardial Cushions: Form the atrioventricular valves and contribute to septation. Other options: 393 Option A: SA node is derived from the primary heart field - sinus venosus. Option B: AV cushions are derived from adjacent endocardial cells. The endocardial cells alongwith the epicardium and mesenchyme, form the AV cushions. Option D: Chordae tendineae are formed from mesenchymal tissue within the heart.
subject: Anatomy

question: A 15-year-old boy underwent splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura. During theprocedure, the surgeon noticed bleeding while separating the spleen from the stomach.Which vessels are most likely implicated in this bleeding?
explanation: This patient, undergoing splenectomy, while separating the spleen from the stomach, is likelybleeding from the short gastric vessels. In an open splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament is opened and short gastric vessels are ligatedand divided. The spleen is attached to the stomach through the gastrosplenic ligament. The gastrosplenicligament attaches the greater curvature of stomach to the upper pole of the spleen. 394 Contents of the gastrosplenic ligament include: • Short gastric vessels • Left gastroepiploic vessels Hence, while separating the spleen from the stomach, there are maximum chances of bleeding ifthere is injury to the short gastric vessels. Other Options: Option A: Left gastric vessels: Left gastric vessels run along the lesser curvature of the stomach. Itis unlikely to be the source of bleeding in this case. Option C: Right gastro-epiploic vessels: The right gastroepiploic vessels run along the pylorus andinferior region of the greater curvature of the stomach. It is not a part of the gastrosplenicligament. Option D: Splenic vessels: The splenic artery and vein run along the superior border of thepancreas. They are not directly involved in the separation of the spleen from the stomach.
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the marked structure
explanation: The marked structure is the primitive streak. The primitive streak appears in the early stages of gastrulation, a process that reorganizes theepiblast into three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. It appears as a linearthickening on the dorsal surface of the epiblast in the bilaminar embryonic disc. It is found in thecaudal (tail-end) region of the developing embryo. 395 Functions of the primitive streak: • Serves as the site where cells migrate inward to form the mesoderm and endoderm. • Marks the beginning of gastrulation. • Defines the body axis (head-to-tail, left-to-right). Other Options: Option B: Notochord: A rod-like structure derived from mesoderm that forms after the primitivestreak and is crucial for the development of the neural tube. Located cranially relative to theprimitive streak. Option C: Neural Groove: A depression in the ectoderm that forms during neurulation, leading tothe development of the neural tube. It appears after the primitive streak. Option D: Secondary Neural Plate: Part of the neural plate involved in the later stages of neuraltube development. It is not directly related to the primitive streak. 396
subject: Anatomy

question: Which of the following is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along theprimitive streak?
explanation: Endoderm is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak. Gastrulation is when the single-layered blastula reorganizes into a multi-layered structure calledthe gastrula. This process establishes the three primary germ layers that give rise to all tissues andorgans of the body. During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak toform the three germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm. Cells from the epiblast migrate inward (invagination) through the primitive streak. The first group of migrating epiblast cells replaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm.The endoderm gives rise to structures like the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and lungs. Subsequent migrating cells spread between the epiblast and the newly formed endoderm to createthe mesoderm, which forms structures like muscles, bones, and the cardiovascular system. Remaining epiblast cells that do not migrate through the primitive streak form the ectoderm,which gives rise to the epidermis and the nervous system. Other Options: Option B: Cardiac Mesoderm: The mesoderm forms after the endoderm and differentiates laterinto subtypes, including the cardiac mesoderm. Option C: Epidermis: The epidermis arises from the ectoderm, which forms after both theendoderm and mesoderm. Option D: Neural Groove: The neural groove is part of the ectoderm and forms duringneurulation, which occurs much later than the formation of the endoderm.
subject: Anatomy

question: During walking, the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg is raised by the action of whichmuscle present in the supporting leg?
explanation: 397 Gluteus Medius of the supporting leg is responsible for raising the hip bone on the side of thesuspended leg. Actions of Gluteus Medius: • Hip abduction • Stabilizes the pelvis during gait. • Assists the internal rotation of the thigh. Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis onthe femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject tostand on one limb. Trendelenburg Sign: Trendelenburg sign is a clinical sign used to assess the function of the gluteus medius. It is positive when the pelvis drops on the opposite side of the stance leg, indicating weakness ordysfunction of the gluteus medius on the supporting leg. In a healthy individual, the gluteus medius contracts to prevent the pelvis from tilting when oneleg is lifted. If the gluteus medius is weak or paralyzed, the pelvis tilts toward the side of thesuspended leg. Option B: Gluteus Maximus: Extends and externally rotates the hip; key for climbing stairs andrising from sitting. Weakness causes difficulty in hip extension, affecting activities like standingup or climbing. Option C: Obturator Internus: Externally rotates and stabilizes the hip joint; abducts the thighwhen the hip is flexed. Dysfunction can impair hip rotation, commonly affected in pelvic injuries. Option D: Quadratus Femoris: Externally rotates and adducts the hip. Injury or entrapment of thenerve to quadratus femoris can cause deep hip pain and weakness in rotation. 398

question: Identify the marked structure?
explanation: The structure shown in the above image is the oculomotor nerve. The oculomotor nerve (CN III)passes through the superior orbital fissure, which lies within the region of the cavernous sinus. Option B: The abducens nerve (CN VI) also passes through the cavernous sinus and superiororbital fissure. However, it is located more medially in the sinus and the fissure compared to theoculomotor nerve. Option C: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) passes through the superior orbital fissure as well, but it isthe smallest cranial nerve and follows a higher and more lateral path than the oculomotor nerve. Option D: The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve enters the lateral wall of the cavernoussinus, below the oculomotor nerve and trochlear nerve. 399

question: Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve leads to?

options.b: Loss of extension of the wrist

explanation: Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve leads to loss of extension of digits. The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is a continuation of the deep branch of the radial nerve. Itoriginates from the radial nerve in the cubital fossa, near the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.After passing through the supinator muscle, it transitions into the PIN. The PIN is purely a motor nerve and supplies the posterior compartment of the forearm. Clinical correlation based on location of lesion: Monteggia fracture involves a fracture of the proximal ulna with a dislocation of the radial head.The radial nerve, especially its posterior interosseous branch, is at risk due to its proximity to thefracture site and leads to loss of extension of digits. Level of lesionNerve affectedCauseClinical feature LowPosterior interosseous nerveand Superficial CutaneousFracture or dislocations of the elbow.- Commonly seen in Monteggia fracture Cannot extend the MCP joint (digits)(Option A).Weakness in the extension of the thumb. HighRadial nerve in spiral grooveHumerus fracture.Wrist drop (Option D)"Saturday night palsy" due to compression of the radial nerveThumb drop, finger drop Very HighRadial nerve properLesions around the shoulder joint & axilla and crutch palsy Loss of extension of the wrist and hand.(Option B)Inability to extend elbow 400
