question: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to which of the following nerves?
explanation: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) and the vagus nerve(X). The afferent nerve for the gag reflex is the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the efferent nerveconsists of both the glossopharyngeal (to the stylopharyngeus muscle) and vagus. Both thesenerves pass through the jugular foramen and damage to them may be the cause for loss of gagreflex. Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexusof nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superiorcervical ganglion. Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are: • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division ofthe trigeminal nerve) 405 • All the muscles of the pharynx(except the stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngealnerve). The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of theposterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate,etc. Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotidgland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Sensory supply includes uvula, posteriorone-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc. The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing,phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx. Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include: • Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”). • By assessing the strength of the cough
subject: Anatomy

question: If a tumor compresses the structures passing through the opening marked in the given image,which of the following sensations would be affected?

options.c: Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose

explanation: The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure. If a tumour compresses the structures passingthrough this foramen, it would impair sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose, asthis would affect the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve. The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows severalcritical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliarynerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1),which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face. The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of thenose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity. Therefore, if atumour or lesion compresses the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure, it wouldlikely affect the sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose because these areas areinnervated by the branches of the trigeminal nerve that pass through this fissure. Other options: Option A: Sensation of the nasopharynx is innervated by other branches of the trigeminal andglossopharyngeal nerve, not by structures passing through the superior orbital fissure. Option B: While some sensation from the nasal cavity comes from the trigeminal nerve, thespecific branches affected by a lesion in the superior orbital fissure are more focused on theanterior areas of the face. Option D: Sensation of the chin is primarily innervated by the mandibular branch (CN V3) of thetrigeminal nerve, which passes through the foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure.
subject: Anatomy

question: A chronic tobacco consumer went to the dental clinic with bleeding lesions on his tongue andwas diagnosed with carcinoma of the tongue. Which of the following papillae, which do nothave taste buds, is least likely to be involved in such a cancer?
explanation: Among the different types of papillae on the tongue, the one that does not have taste buds is thefiliform papillae. 406 Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on thedorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. The filiform papillae do not contain taste buds.They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Other papillae of the tongue are: Circumvallate papillae are 8-12 in number which are large cylindrical structures. They form aV-shaped row just in front of the sulcus terminalis. Usually, the entire papillae are covered bynon-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Taste buds are present in the lateral wall of thesepapillae which surrounds the papillae circumferentially. Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red and are mainly present on the lingual margins andalso on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamousepithelium. They are supplied by the facial nerve. Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at thesides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratifiedsquamous epithelium. A diagrammatic representation of the various papillae of the tongue is given below: Below is the image showing the various parts of the tongue. 407 The given image depicts the histology image of filiform papillae: The given image depicts the histology image of circumvallate papillae: 408 The given image depicts the histology image of foliate papillae: The given image depicts the histology image of fungiform papillae: 409
subject: Anatomy

question: Which artery is used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein forhemodialysis, and is located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of thetendocalcaneus?
explanation: The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of thetendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein forhemodialysis. The posterior tibial artery is situated behind the medial malleolus and approximately 2.5 cm infront of the tendocalcaneus, making it a suitable site for creating an AV fistula with the greatsaphenous vein. This location allows for optimal access and ensures that the shunt can handle thenecessary blood flow for effective dialysis with the great saphenous vein. However, they are notcommonly used for AV shunting in common practices. Arteries used for AV shunting include the radial artery and the brachial artery in the upper arm,which are frequently employed for hemodialysis access. In the lower leg, the anterior tibial arteryand the peroneal (fibular) artery are less commonly used for this procedure. Other options: Option A: In comparison, the anterior tibial artery is located on the anterior aspect of the leg andruns down the front of the tibia, not behind the medial malleolus. Option C: The peroneal (fibular) artery is situated on the lateral side of the leg, travellingalongside the fibula, and is also not located behind the medial malleolus. Option D: The fibular circumflex artery is a small artery and is not commonly used forhemodialysis access. It is not a standard choice and does not fit the anatomical location described,as it is a branch of the anterior tibial artery.
subject: Anatomy

question: What is the outer covering of the condition shown in the image?
explanation: The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion. 410 Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrudethrough the umbilicus. In this condition, the herniated organs are covered by both peritoneumand an amnion. The umbilical cord inserts directly into this sac, which helps in identifying thecondition. The defect occurs due to the failure of the physiological hernia to return to the bodycavity by the 11th week of gestation. The size of an omphalocele can vary significantly. It may be relatively small, containing only thegut, or it can be classified as a giant omphalocele if it measures 4 cm or more in diameter,encompassing the gut, liver, and other abdominal organs. The condition is often associated withother congenital anomalies such as trisomies 13, 15, 18, or 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome,exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, and pentalogy of Cantrell. Treatment for omphalocele involves covering the exposed organs to prevent fluid loss and protectthem from infection. Prophylactic antibiotics may be administered in case of rupture. Surgicalcorrection is usually performed once the baby is stable. In omphalocele, since the umbilicus iscovered by a reflection of the amnion, this membrane also covers the omphalocele itself,differentiating it from other types of abdominal wall defects. Note : Gastroschisis is a condition where the intestinal loops herniate through the defect in theabdominal wall. The defect usually lies on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly). Theloops of the bowel are not covered by amnion. It is associated with elevated alpha-fetoproteinlevels.
subject: Anatomy

question: Identify the marked structure.
explanation: The marked structure in the image is the medial pectoral nerve. The given image shows the medial pectoral nerve arising from the medial cord of the brachialplexus. It also shows the axillary artery traversing inferior to the median pectoral nerve and thethoracoacromial artery. The medial pectoral nerve and the thoracoacromial artery both contributeto the neurovascular supply of the pectoral muscles. 411 After originating from the medial cord, the medial pectoral nerve passes anterior to the axillaryartery. This nerve is specifically known for its anatomical path of piercing the pectoralis minormuscle before branching out to supply both the pectoralis minor and the pectoralis majormuscles.
subject: Anatomy

question: A patient presents with sciatica and tenderness in the hamstring muscles. Which nervesupplies the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition?
explanation: The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition. In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and thecommon peroneal nerve. The adductor magnus muscle is an example of a hybrid muscle with dualinnervation: • The adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve. • The hamstring part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the tibial nerve. During sciatica, the tibial nerve is often affected, which would impact the hamstring part of theadductor magnus. However, because the adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated bythe obturator nerve, it remains functional and is likely to be spared. The obturator nerve arises from the anterior division of the ventral rami of L2-L4. Near theobturator foramen, it divides into anterior and posterior branches. • Anterior division supplies pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis • Posterior division supplies adductor magnus, obturator externus. It also supplies adductor brevisif the muscle is not supplied by the anterior division The image given below shows the course of the obturator nerve. 412 Other options: Option A: The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and can also be affected insciatica. It is responsible for innervating muscles in the anterior and lateral compartments of theleg. Option B: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is often affected in sciatica. Itsupplies the hamstring part of the adductor magnus, which would be impacted during sciatica. Option C: The femoral nerve is not involved in sciatica. It supplies the quadriceps and othermuscles in the anterior compartment of the thigh, and does not innervate the adductor magnus.
subject: Anatomy

question: Where will you find the epithelium shown in the image?
explanation: The epithelium shown in the above image can be found in the ureter. The ureter is lined by transitional epithelium (also called urothelium), similar to the urinarybladder. This specialized epithelium allows stretching, which is crucial as the urine passesthrough. The presence of transitional epithelium is characteristic of structures in the urinarysystem, such as the ureters, bladder, and part of the urethra. Given below is a cross-section of the ureter showing the transitional epithelium and the layer ofsmooth muscle. 413 Other options: Option A: Gall bladder: The gall bladder is lined by simple columnar epithelium, which facilitatesthe absorption of water and electrolytes from bile. Option B: Trachea: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium withgoblet cells, which helps trap and remove particles from the respiratory tract. Option D: Duodenum: The duodenum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells,aiding in digestion and nutrient absorption.
subject: Anatomy

question: During the examination of a patient, a professor asks the patient to invert his foot and pointsto a prominent tendon located behind the medial malleolus. Which tendon is beinghighlighted?
explanation: The tendon being highlighted here is of the tibialis posterior. It passes behind the medial malleolus and is a key muscle responsible for foot inversion. Thetendon of this muscle becomes prominent in this area during foot inversion. Dysfunction of thistendon can lead to flatfoot deformity. The given image shows the tarsal tunnel and position of the tendon of tibialis posterior: 414 Other options: Option A: Tibialis anterior lies anterior to the medial malleolus and aids in dorsiflexion andinversion of the foot but is not located behind the medial malleolus. Option B: Extensor digitorum is involved in extending the toes and runs anteriorly to the foot, notbehind the medial malleolus. Option D: Extensor hallucis longus extends the big toe and runs along the anterior portion of thefoot, also not behind the medial malleolus.
subject: Anatomy

question: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness duringdaily activities. On examination, she is unable to make an 'O' shape by opposing her thumband index finger. Which of the following muscles is most likely involved?
explanation: The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggestthe involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle. This is a case of anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome. The AIN is a purely motor branch ofthe median nerve that affects specific muscles in the forearm, the flexor pollicis longus and flexordigitorum profundus leading to difficulty in performing tasks requiring fine motor control, such asthe "OK" sign. Among the options provided, the abductor pollicis brevis is uniquely andconsistently innervated by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve, making it susceptibleto dysfunction in conditions affecting the median nerve. Other options: Option A: The opponens pollicis is innervated primarily by the lateral terminal branch of themedian nerve, with some contributions from a branch of the deep terminal branch of the ulnarnerve. While it plays a role in thumb opposition, it is not consistently affected in anteriorinterosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome, which primarily impacts deeper flexor muscles like the flexorpollicis longus. Therefore, it is less likely to be the cause of the patient’s inability to perform the"OK" sign. Option B: The palmar interossei muscles are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.Because they do not receive any innervation from the median nerve, they are not implicated in 415 AIN syndrome. Their primary function involves the adduction of the fingers. Option C: The flexor pollicis brevis has dual innervation: the superficial head is supplied by therecurrent branch of the median nerve, while the deep head is innervated by the deep branch of theulnar nerve. This dual supply makes it less likely to be solely affected in AIN syndrome. 416
subject: Anatomy

question: Given below is the demonstration of tetanization in the gastrocnemius muscle of a frog.Identify the tetanising frequency.
explanation: Tetanizing frequency demonstrated by the muscle is 33Hz. In the above graph, we know, • The speed of the paper is 1000mm/sec. • The y-axis represents millivolts, the x-axis represents time. • The scale on the x-axis is 10mm. • The area under the graph represents the muscle contraction. Contraction period (latent period to maximum force of contraction) includes 3 scales = 30 mm. As paper speed is 1000mm/sec, Contraction period = 30mm = (30/1000) = 30 msec. Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1000/30 = 33Hz. Tetanization The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. Theadding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall musclecontraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways: • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple Ibersummations. • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead totetanization. When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventuallyfuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous,this is called tetanization. Tetanization occurs in two ways: • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli. • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summatedstimuli. 425
subject: Physiology

question: The oxygen carrying capacity of a 18 year old boy with haemoglobin of 14g/dl is
explanation: The oxygen carrying capacity of a boy with haemoglobin 14g/dl is 18. When blood is saturated with 100% O2, the haemoglobin is also 100% saturated and each gram ofnormal haemoglobin contains 1.39 mL of O2. However, blood normally contains some inactive haemoglobin derivatives, and the measuredvalue in vivo is thus slightly lower hence, each gram of haemoglobin in vivo contains 1.31 mL ofO2 (Hufner’s constant). According to the above question, when Hb=14g/dl, O2= 1.31*14= 18.34 The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve • Demonstrates a progressive increase in the percentage of haemoglobin bound with oxygen asblood Po2 increases, which is called the percent saturation of haemoglobin. • Blood leaving the lungs and entering the systemic arteries usually has a Po2 of about 95 mm Hg,the usual oxygen saturation of systemic arterial blood averages 97 per cent. • Conversely, in normal venous blood returning from the peripheral tissues, the Po2 is about 40mm Hg, and the saturation of haemoglobin averages 75 per cent.
subject: Physiology

question: A 30-year-old patient with respiratory volume of 500 mL. The intraplueral pressure measured-4 before inspiration and -8 at the end of inspiration. The pulmonary compliance of thepatient is
explanation: Pulmonary compliance of this patient is 125 mL/cm of H2O. Compliance is developed due to the tendency for tissue to resume its original position after anapplied force has been removed. 426 After an expiration during quiet breathing, the lungs have a tendency to collapse and the chestwall has a tendency to expand. The interaction between the recoil of the lungs and recoil of thechest can be measured through a spirometer and a curve of airway pressure plotted againstvolume is the pressure-volume curve of the total respiratory system (Ptr). Compliance of the lung and chest wall is measured as the slope of the Ptr curve, or, as a change inlung volume per unit change in airway pressure (∆V/∆P). Compliance = Change in lung volume / Change in pressure Compliance = 500/4 Compliance = 125 ml/cm H20
subject: Physiology

question: The function of the Golgi tendon organ is to _________

options.c: Sense changes in position of the muscle
options.d: Sense changes in length of the muscle

explanation: Golgi tendon organ sense changes in muscle tension. Golgi tendon reflex (Inverse myotatic/ Inverse stretch reflex) is disynaptic, is the opposite of thestretch reflex. When the tension in a contracted muscle is significantly elevated, the inhibitory effect from theGolgi tendon organ leads to instantaneous relaxation of the entire muscle. This effect is calledthe lengthening reaction. It is a protective mechanism to prevent tearing of the muscle or avulsion of the tendon from itsattachments to the bone. Note: Muscle spindles senses changes in muscle length (stretch). 427
subject: Physiology

question: Difference in trajectory between inspiratory loop and the expiratory loop in the curve is dueto:

options.a: Difference in alveolar pressure during inspiration and expiration
options.b: Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration
options.c: Difference in airway resistance during inspiration and expiration
options.d: Inspiration is active and expiration is passive

explanation: The difference between the inflation and the deflation paths is called hysteresis. It exists because a greater transpulmonary pressure is required to open a previously closedairway, due to a deficit of surfactant at the air-water interface, than to keep an open airway fromclosing, as then it has abundant surfactant.
subject: Physiology

question: Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is:
explanation: Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is Bainbridge Reflex. The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferentsignals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain. Then efferent signals are transmittedback through vagal and sympathetic nerves to increase heart rate and strength of heartcontraction. Thus, this reflex helps prevent damming of blood in the veins, atria, andpulmonary circulation. Other options: Option A: Bezold–Jarisch Reflex: Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers in thecardiopulmonary region causes profound bradycardia, hypotension and a brief period of apnoeafollowed by rapid shallow breathing. Option C: Cushing Reflex: When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply toRostral Ventro-Lateral Medulla (RVLM) neurons is compromised. The local hypoxia andhypercapnia cause an increase in discharge from the neurons, producing hypertension,bradycardia, and irregular respiration. Option D: J Reflex: The stimulation of the J-receptors (C receptors/juxta-pulmonary capillaryreceptors) causes apnea followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia, and hypotension. 428
subject: Physiology

question: Identify the hormone from the picture
explanation: The image depicts the fluctuations of secretion of growth hormone throughout the day. • Growth hormone is found at relatively low levels during the day unless specific triggers such asstrenuous exercise are present. • During sleep, on the other hand, large pulsatile bursts of growth hormone secretion occur. Stimuli that Affect Growth Hormone Secretion in Humans Note: The early morning surge of Growth Hormone during sleep, as seen in the image, plays a role inthe Dawn Phenomenon Stimuli that Increase SecretionStimuli that Decrease Secretion ExerciseGoing to sleepFasting/HypoglycemiaStressful stimuli (including various psychological stresses)High Protein MealGlucagonEstrogens and androgensPyrogen GlucoseCortisolFFAMedroxyprogesteroneGrowth hormone and IGF-I
subject: Physiology

question: Feed forward control system is employed during the regulation of
explanation: Feed forward control system is employed during regulation of temperature. Feed forward control 429 There is a control system in our body when no stimulus is required but still the system anticipatesand makes corrective changes. Such a system is called Feed forward or Anticipatory or Adaptive Control. Examples include • Temperature control – Thermoregulatory responses are initiated by hypothalamus BEFORE thechanges in environmental temperature have succeeded in changing the body’s core bodytemperature • Cephalic phase of gastric secretion- Just thinking about food increases gastric acid production • Thinking about exercise itself increases heart rate & respiratory rate • Role of cerebellum in motor coordination
subject: Physiology

question: Cellular junctions present in a cardiac muscle are all except:
explanation: Zonula occludens is the other name for the tight junction. It is absent in a cardiac muscle. Cardiac muscle cells are connected by Fascia adherens (a structural analog of zonulaadherens), Gap junctions and Macula adherens. Cardiac muscle fibers are made up of many individual cells connected in series and parallel to oneanother. The areas where the end of one muscle fiber abuts on another are called intercalateddisks. At each intercalated disc, the plasma membrane fuses with one another forming gapjunction which provides low resistance bridges for the spread of excitation from one fiber toanother permitting the cardiac muscle to function as a syncytium.
subject: Physiology

question: Efferent arteriolar constriction causes all except:

options.c: Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries
options.d: Increases hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries

explanation: Efferent arteriolar constriction increases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries. Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic response on GFR depending on the severity ofresistance. Moderate efferent arteriolar constriction causes increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure andslightly increased GFR. However, in cases of severe efferent arteriolar constriction (more than threefold increase inefferent arteriolar resistance), the renal blood flow is significantly reduced. This results inincreased plasma protein concentration, thereby increasing the glomerular colloid oncoticpressure. As the increase in colloid oncotic pressure exceeds the increase in hydrostatic pressure,the net force for filtration decreases, resulting in decreased GFR. 430
subject: Physiology

question: Absolute refractory period is due to:

options.c: Closure of active gates of sodium channel
options.d: Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel

explanation: Absolute refractory period is due to closure of inactive gates of sodium channel. Voltage-gated sodium channels have 3 states that you can find them in. They can either be closed,open, or inactive. When the stimulus causes activation of the open gates, sodium rushes into the cell causing themembrane potential to become more positive. After 0.5 to 1 millisecond, the inactive gateautomatically closes and no stimulus, no matter how strong, can excite the nerve. This is calledthe absolute refractory period. 431
subject: Physiology

question: X, Y, Z are three permeable ions. X = -50 and Y = -30. At RMP, if there is no net electrogenictransfer, what is the value of Z?
explanation: No net electro genic transfer at RMP means X + Y + Z = 0 Since X = -50 and Y = -30, then Z must be +80 since (-80 +80 = 0)
subject: Physiology

question: Slow waves are generated by:
explanation: The interstitial cells of Cajal undergo cyclic changes in membrane potential due to unique ionchannels that periodically open and produce inward (pacemaker) currents that generateslow-wave activity. Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the GIT that initiate the basic electricalrhythm (BER). These are stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells with smooth muscle-like features. In the stomach and the small intestine, these cells are located in the circular smooth muscle layernear the myenteric plexus. In the colon, they are at the submucosal border of the circular musclelayer. The slow waves usually do not by themselves cause muscle contraction in most parts of thegastrointestinal tract, except perhaps in the stomach. Instead, they mainly excite the appearanceof intermittent spike potentials, and the spike potentials in turn actually excite the musclecontraction. Note: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal.
subject: Physiology

question: A patient has a Iblood glucose level of 200 mg/dL and GFR of 90 ml/min. What is theamount of glucose excreted if the transport maximum of the patient is as shown below?
explanation: The amount of glucose excreted in the above scenario is 30 mg/min. Calculation: Step 1: Calculate total filtered glucose: In this question, • GFR = 90 ml/min • Plasma glucose concentration = 200 mg/dL= 2 mg/ml (1 dL=100 ml). • Total filtered glucose = GFR X Plasma glucose concentration. = 90 ml/min X 2 mg/ml = 180 mg/min. Step 2: Check transport maximum: In the above question transport maximum is 150 mg/min. Step 3: Calculate the excretion: Excretion = Total filtered glucose - Total reabsorbed glucose (Transport Maximum) = 180-150 mg/min 432 = 30 mg/min
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following can be responsible for Bezold-Jarisch reflex?
explanation: Serotonin can be responsible for Bezold–Jarisch reflex. Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers located in the cardiopulmonary region (ex: ventricles,atria, great veins, pulmonary artery, juxtacapillary region of alveoli) causes profound bradycardia,hypotension, and apnea followed by rapid shallow breathing. This response is calledBezold-Jarisch reflex. Other substances that can cause Bezold–Jarisch reflex are capsaicin, phenyl biguanide, andveratridine.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following is the constituent of the marked area in the electron microscopicpicture of muscle?
explanation: Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area. The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line. Alpha actinin binds actin toZ-lines. The orderly arrangement of actin, myosin, and related proteins that produces this pattern. Thearea between two Z-lines is called sarcomere. The thick filaments, which are about twice the diameter of the thin filaments, are made up ofmyosin, which are lined to form A bands; the thin filaments are made up of actin, tropomyosin,and troponin. The array of thin filaments extends out of the A band and into the less densestaining I bands. The lighter H bands in the center of the A bands are the regions where, when the muscle isrelaxed, the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments. The Z lines allow for anchoring of 433 the thin filaments. Actinin, titin and desmin are additional structural proteins.Titin connects Z-lines to the M lineand provides the scaffolding to the sarcomere. Desmin adds structure to Z-lines by connectingZ-line to plasma membrane. Note: Some sources say that even titin is a component of Z-disc so if alpha actinin is not given inthe options titin is the second best answer.
subject: Physiology

question: The fourth heart sound is caused by:

options.a: Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves
options.b: Vibrations in the ventricular wall during systole
options.d: Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves

explanation: The fourth heart sound is caused by ventricular filling. A fourth sound is heard immediately before the first sound when atrial pressure is high or theventricle is stiff in conditions such as ventricular hypertrophy. It is due to ventricular filling and israrely heard in normal adults. 434
subject: Physiology

question: “a” wave on JVP is for
explanation: "a" wave in JVP represents atrial contraction. Waves of JVP : • a- atrial systole pushing the blood to the ventricles. • c- isovolumetric contraction of ventricles causing the tricuspid valve to bulge. • x'- fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to pull of valve leaflets. • v- venous filling which creates an increase in atrial pressure. • y- passive filling of ventricles by a passive flow of the blood from the right atrium.
subject: Physiology

question: In the 2 vessels shown below, assume the pressure along both the vessels is the same andboth follow linear flow pattern. What will be the amount of blood flow in A compared to B
explanation: The relationship between the flow in a long narrow tube, the viscosity of the fluid, and the radiusof the tube is expressed mathematically in the formula called as Poiseuille's law : 435 Blood flow (F) inside the vessel depends on: • Pressure difference: directly proportional • Viscosity: inversely proportional • Radius: directly proportional to the fourth power • Length of the vessel: inversely proportional Here, the radius is doubled so the flow increases by 2 to the power of 4 = 16. the length of the vessel is also doubled, so the flow decreases by half (÷2) = 8
subject: Physiology

question: A 13-year-old boy presents with involuntary dancing movements of his right hand. He wasdiagnosed with rheumatic fever. What constitutes the ganglia involved in the presentingcomplication?
explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Sydenham's chorea, a complication of rheumatic fever.The choreic movements are caused by the destruction of D2 neurons of the striatum. Theneostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen. The image given below shows Sydenham's chorea in a patient. 436 Nomenclature of basal ganglia: • Corpus striatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen+ globus pallidus • Lentiform nucleus: Putamen + globus pallidus • Neostriatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen 437 438
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following is the diluting segment of the kidney?
explanation: The ascending thick limb of the loop of Henle is called the diluting segment. In the ascending limb, there is the movement of Na+ and Cl– out of the tubular lumen, and thetubular fluid becomes more dilute. When the fluid reaches the top of the ascending limb, it becomes hypotonic to plasma.
subject: Physiology

question: Identify the ions A and B based on conductance graph of a neuron shown below:
explanation: Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+ Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential. 447 K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels. Theyare responsible for repolarization phase of action potential. Also, the postassium channels returnslowly to their closed state, which is responsible for after-hyperpolarization. The sequence of events during the action potential occur in 7 steps as described below. 1. Resting state - Both channels are closed 2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters into the cell. Themembrane reaches threshold potential. 3. The sodium influx causes opening of more sodium channels through positive feedbackmechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs. 4. Sodium conductance decreases. 5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Repolarization occurs. 6. Sodium channels are reset, and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relativerefractory period). During this phase, the potassium channels remain open and slowly return toclosed state causing after-hyperpolarization. 7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP. 448
subject: Physiology

question: How is an electrical synapse different from a chemical synapse?

options.a: No cytoplasmic continuity between presynaptic and postsynaptic membrane
options.c: Connexons are involved in electrical synapse
options.d: Electrical synapse has more latent period than chemical synapse

explanation: In electrical synapses, the cytoplasm of adjacent cells is directly connected by gap junctions(connexons) that allow free movement of ions from the interior of one cell to the interior of thenext cell. The transmission in electrical synapses is bidirectional and there is no synaptic delay. Unlikechemical synapses, electrical synapse has cytoplasmic continuity. Note: Most of the synapses used for signal transmission in the central nervous system are chemicalsynapses.
subject: Physiology

question: Hormone degradation as an important mechanism for regulating local concentrations is seenin _________.

options.c: Degradation of retinoic acid by Cyp26b1 in primordial germ cells of males

explanation: Hormone degradation as an important mechanism for regulating local concentrations is seen inall of the above. 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase inactivates glucocorticoids in renal tubular cells, preventingactions through the mineralocorticoid receptor. During development, degradation of retinoic acid by Cyp26b1 prevents the primordial germ cellsin the male from entering meiosis, which occurs in the female ovary. The thyroid hormone deiodinases convert T4 to T3 and can inactivate T3. All the three are henceexamples of local hormone degradation being utilized as a method for regulation of hormoneconcentration locally. 449
subject: Physiology

question: The factors that can cause a person to drink water due to stimulation of thirst mechanismis/are ___________.
explanation: Dehydration, hemorrhage, and prandial drinking: All three can cause increased thirst resulting inwater drinking. Increased osmolality acts via osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus. The decreased plasma volume, as in hemorrhage, acts via 1. Renin-angiotensin system 2. Baroreceptors in heart and blood vessels. The intake of liquids during a meal is known as prandial drinking. The increase is known aslearned or habit response but is not understood completely. The following factors are thought to play a role 1. Increase in plasma osmolality due to food absorption 2. Action on hypothalamus by one or more gastrointestinal hormones
subject: Physiology

question: On performing a histamine test on an individual with brachial plexus trunk injury, you canexpect ________.

options.a: Central capillary dilatation → wheal → Surrounding flare
options.b: Central capillary dilatation → wheal without surrounding flare
options.c: Central capillary dilatation → wheal with exaggerated surrounding flare

explanation: Brachial plexus trunk injury leads to anesthetized skin over the region. On performing a histaminetest on such an individual, one can expect central capillary dilatation → wheal withoutsurrounding flare. The incomplete triple response over the anesthetic skin is characteristic ofpostganglionic lesions. Intradermal injection of histamine usually causes a triple response in the surrounding skin i.e, redreaction→ flare → wheal • Red reaction is independent of innervation and is due to histamine-mediated relaxation of theprecapillary sphincters • Flare reaction (Flush, Axon reflex) is due to Substance P mediated arteriolardilatation (antidromic conduction of afferent impulses via collaterals of the sensory nerve fiberthat lead to the release of vasoactive mediators) • Wheal (skin edema) is due to histamine-mediated increased capillary permeability • The triple response persists after total sympathectomy • Flare is absent in locally anesthetized skin
subject: Physiology

question: GFR is increased by all except
explanation: Ureteric stone causes a reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Following ureteral obstruction, there is a progressive fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) due toa reduction in a single-nephron glomerular filtration rate (SNGFR) and a reduced number offiltering nephrons. All the other factors/options increase GFR. 450
subject: Physiology

question: Baroreceptor provides ________
explanation: Baroreceptors provide negative feedback in response to an increase in blood pressure. Increased baroreceptor discharge inhibits the tonic discharge of sympathetic nerves and excitesthe vagal innervation of the heart. Baroreceptor reflex • Increased BP → stimulation of baroreceptors → stimulation of NTS → inhibition of RVLM →inhibition of sympathetic system • Stimulation of NTS also stimulates CVC → parasympathetic stimulation • Net effect = sympathetic inhibition and parasympathetic stimulation → decreased HR and BP NTS - Nucleus tractus solitarius CVC - Cardiovagal center RVLM - Rostral ventrolateral medulla HR- Heart rate BP - Blood pressure
subject: Physiology

question: The diagram below shows the pressure-volume curves for 3 different lungs. Which of thefollowing is the best representation of compliance between the three lungs?
explanation: • The pressure-volume relationship is the fundamental relation between the work of breathing andlung mechanics. • The diagram depicts the change in volume with respect to the change in intrapleural pressure,which is compliance. Here, the change is more (steep curve) with B and least (flat curve) with C. • The “stiffer” lung displays a more horizontal curve (C), meaning that it takes a greater pressure toachieve the same inflation volume compared with a normal lung (A). These lungs are called lesscompliant. • Curve (B) is more compliant as it takes lesser pressure to achieve the same inflation volumecompared to normal (A). Applied aspect: Compliance is increased in emphysema. The mechanism is shown in the flow chart below. 451 Compliance is decreased in case of pulmonary edema or fibrosis.
subject: Physiology

question: Identify the site which is responsible for relieving pain when pressure is applied to the painfularea.
explanation: It is a cross section of brain stem at pons. • A is a periaqueductal gray matter which also consists of raphe nucleus. • Descending pathways from the mesencephalic periaqueductal gray matter inhibit transmissionin nociceptive pathways. This descending pathway includes a synapse in the ventromedial medulla(Raphe nucleus) and the release of endogenous opiates. So periaqueductal gray matter releasesendogenous opiates. Other marked structures are B: Corticospinal tract 452 C: Medial lemniscus D: Medial longitudinal fasciculus
subject: Physiology

question: Inhibitory control by the hypothalamus is exerted on:
explanation: Inhibitory control by the hypothalamus is exerted mainly on prolactin and growth hormone. The major hypothalamic releasing hormones are: • Thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH) • Corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH) • Growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH) • Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) The major hypothalamic inhibitory hormones are: • Prolactin inhibitory hormone or dopamine • Growth hormone inhibitory hormone (GHIH), also called Somatostatin.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following hormones play a permissive role in the attainment of puberty?
explanation: The hormone that plays a permissive role in the attainment of puberty is leptin. It now appears that leptin may be the link between body weight and puberty. Leptin is asatiety-producing hormone secreted by adipocytes. High leptin levels reduce appetite and increaseenergy expenditure. Evidence for which is given by: • Obese ob/ob mice that cannot make leptin are infertile, and their fertility is restored byinjections of leptin. • Leptin treatment also induces precocious puberty in immature female mice. • However, the way that leptin fits into the overall control of puberty remains to be determined. Leptin also accelerates GnRH pulsatility in neurons, fastening puberty.
subject: Physiology

question: Weber-Fechner law relates magnitude of sensation to ____.
explanation: Weber-Fechner Law states that the magnitude of sensation felt is proportionate to the log of theintensity of the stimulus. Other Laws in Physiology: • Doctrine of specific nerve energies - When the nerve pathways from a particular sense organ arestimulated, the sensation evoked is that for which the receptor is specialized no matter how or 453 where along the pathway the activity is initiated. • Law of projection - No matter where a particular sensory pathway is stimulated along its courseto the cortex, the conscious sensation produced is referred to the location of the receptor. Thisprinciple is called the law of projection.
subject: Physiology

question: The following Darrow Yannet diagram is suggestive of which condition? Note : The solid lineis the original fluid compartment and the colour shaded compartment within the dotted linedenotes the change caused by the condition.
explanation: In adrenal insufficiency there is hypo-osmotic volume contraction. Aldosterone deficiency leads toincreased sodium loss (loss of hyperosmotic fluid). • The osmolarity of ECF decreases. • ECF volume decreases because of the loss of volume. • Water shifts into ICF; as a result of the shift, ICF osmolarity decreases until it is equal to ECFosmolarity, and ICF volume increases. • So, loss of hypertonic fluid causes hypotonic volume contraction. Please note that in the diagram, the horizontal axis represents volume and vertical axis representsosmolarity. 454 The Darrow Yannet diagrams of various conditions are shown above.
subject: Physiology

question: The mechanism by which glucose is absorbed in the intestine is:
explanation: Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitialfluid. This depletes sodium inside the cell. Because of this Na+ concentration difference, moreNa+ binds to the SGLT on the luminal side. This increases the affinity of SGLT for glucose andglucose binds to it. Then, both the Na+ and glucose are transported together to the interior of the cell. Thus, glucoseis absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. The energy for glucose transport isprovided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell. The glucose moves out of thecell into the blood across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion mediated via GLUT. 455
subject: Physiology

question: The earliest stage at which erythropoietin is effective in red blood cell formation is?
explanation: BFU is the earliest stage of hematopoiesis where erythropoietin (EPO) acts Under the influence of EPO, both BFU and CFU grow in semisolid culture media and give rise tocolonies of well-hemoglobinized erythroblasts. Erythroid burst-forming unit (BFU-E) is the most primitive single lineage committed erythroidprogenitor. In addition to EPO, they form the sub-population of Erythroid Colony Forming Units(CFU-E). CFU is derived from burst-forming units. Note: While CFUs have the highest number of receptors for EPO, the earliest stage at which it actsis on the BFU.
subject: Physiology

question: Integrin connects with:
explanation: Integrin connects with fibronectin. Integrins are transmembrane glycoproteins (integral proteins) that allow cells to attach toextracellular matrix constituents such as laminin, fibronectin and collagen. It helps in linking theintracellular cytoskeleton functionally and structurally with the outside world.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following organelles is absent in the area of the cardiac muscle marked:
explanation: The area of the cardiac muscle marked is devoid of nuclei. Lysosomes are commonly observed inperinuclear areas. Other organelles are present in abundance throughout the cell.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following fibres reach the Purkinje cell directly?
explanation: The fibres of inferior olivary nucleus (climbing fibres) reach the purkinje cell directly. Note: The input from the Purkinje cells to the deep nuclei is inhibitory. However, the deep nuclei output is always excitatory.
subject: Physiology

question: Calculate the net filtration pressure across the GBM for a patient with Glomerularultrafiltration coefficient = 6 Glomerular hydrostatic pressure =45 Glomerular capillaryoncotic pressure =20 Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure =10 Bowman’s capsule oncoticpressure =0
explanation: 456 Net filtration pressure = Hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries - Pressure in Bowman'scapsule - Oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillaries. Net filtration pressure= [PG -PB- πG+ πB] Therefore, Net filtration pressure = (45-10-20+0) = 25-10 = 15 mmHg Note: Here, just the net filtration pressure is asked and not the GFR. GFR= Kf [PG -PB- πG+ πB]
subject: Physiology

question: In a 100-m dash, most of the energy consumed by skeletal muscles to replenish ATP isderived from _______
explanation: In a 100-m dash that takes 10 s, 85% of the energy consumed is derived anaerobicallyby phosphocreatine, which is hydrolyzed to creatine and phosphate groups with the release ofconsiderable energy. The ATP concentration in a muscle is low enough (4 millimolar) to sustain contractions for 1-2seconds after which ATP is dephosphorylated into ADP. The ADP is re-phosphorylated byphosphocreatine for the next 5 to 8 seconds. ADP is re-phosphorylated by 3 sources. • Phosphocreatine after 2 seconds upto 10 seconds. • Glycolysis (anaerobic) after 10 seconds upto a minute • Oxidative metabolism - after a minute upto 2-4 hours.
subject: Physiology

question: In the homunculus, which of the following has maximum representation?
explanation: In a homunculus, the more the representation of an area, the more precise the movements are. • The relative sizes of the cortical receiving areas of the sensory homunculus are proportionate tothe use of the part. • The sizes of these areas are directly proportional to the number of specialized sensoryreceptors in each respective peripheral area of the body. • Some body parts are represented by large areas in the somatic cortex—the lips the greatest of all,followed by the face and thumb, whereas the trunk and lower part of the body are represented byrelatively small areas. 457
subject: Physiology

question: What is the usual position of the Golgi apparatus in serous acinar cells?
explanation: Golgi complex is located in supranuclear cytoplasm in serous acinar cells. Serous acinar cells aregenerally found in pancreas and the submandibular salivary glands. 458
subject: Physiology

question: The function of the Golgi tendon organ is to _________

options.c: Sense changes in position of the muscle
options.d: Sense changes in length of the muscle

explanation: Golgi tendon organ sense changes in muscle tension. Golgi tendon reflex (Inverse myotatic/ Inverse stretch reflex) is disynaptic, is the opposite of thestretch reflex. When the tension in a contracted muscle is significantly elevated, the inhibitory effect from theGolgi tendon organ leads to instantaneous relaxation of the entire muscle. This effect is calledthe lengthening reaction. It is a protective mechanism to prevent tearing of the muscle or avulsion of the tendon from itsattachments to the bone. Note: Muscle spindles senses changes in muscle length (stretch). 463
subject: Physiology

question: Which is the first-order neuron in the optic pathway?
explanation: Photoreceptors - rods and cones are the first-order neurons in the visual pathway.
subject: Physiology

question: Pacemaker generating the rhythm for breathing is ________

options.b: Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla

explanation: Pre-Botzinger complex generates the rhythm for automated breathing. • These are also known as pacemaker cells located in the medulla. • These are the first set of neurons that initiate inspiration. 464 • These neurons discharge rhythmically, and they produce rhythmic discharges in the phrenicmotor neurons. Breathing is under the control of both the following: • Voluntary control: Located in the cerebral cortex (via corticospinal tract) • Automatic control: Driven by pacemaker cells in the medulla (Pre-Botzinger complex). Theseactivate motor neurons via cervical (Phrenic nerve innervating diaphragm) and thoracic spinalcord (external intercostal muscle). There is a reciprocal innervation to expiratory and inspiratory muscles in that motor neuronssupplying expiratory muscles are inactive when motor neurons supplying inspiratory muscles areactive, and vice versa. Inspiration InitiationPre-Botzinger complex (Pacemaker cells) in Medulla MaintenanceApneustic center in lower Pons stimulates Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla TerminationApneustic center inhibited by Vagus and Pneumotaxic center Regulation of expiration: During quiet breathing, expiration is a passive process; there is no firingof neurons. Ventral respiratory group of neurons are involved in forceful expiration like duringexercise. Mnemonic DIVE: Dorsal respiratory group for Inspiration and Ventral respiratory group forExpiration.

question: Which of the following is not an example of feed forward control mechanism?

options.d: Exercise resulting in heart rate increase

explanation: Exercise resulting in heart rate increase is not an example of feedforward control mechanism.However, thinking about exercise and it resulting in a heart rate increase would be an example offeedforward control mechanism. Feedforward control is that which makes an anticipatory or adaptive response without a specificstimulus. Temperature control - Thermoregulatory responses are initiated by the hypothalamus before thechanges in environmental temperature changes the core body temperature. Thus, shivering inresponse to cold environment would be an example of feedforward control. In the cephalic phase of gastric secretion, the thought of food itself and not food per se produces agastric secretion. The cerebellum has a feed-forward inhibition that limits the duration of the excitation producedby any given afferent volley. 465

question: Single breath nitrogen method is used for measuring ____
explanation: Anatomical dead space can be measured by the single-breath N2 curve (Fowler's method). • Anatomical dead space is the respiratory system volume exclusive of alveoli. • Alveolar dead space is the volume of gas not equilibrating with blood i.e. wasted ventilation. • Physiological/total dead space is the sum of anatomical and alveolar dead space. • The equation used for the calculation of total/physiological dead space is the Bohr’s equation. The patient takes a deep breath of O2 From mid-inspiration, then exhales steadily. The changes inthe N2 concentration of expired gas during expiration are plotted. Region I - Dead Space (DS) From I–II is a mixture of DS and alveolar gas. The transition from III-IV is the closing volume (CV). End of IV - Residual Volume (RV). Factors affecting dead space: Option B: Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is measured using body plethysmography. Option C: Tidal volume (TV) is measured using spirometry. Option D: Diffusion Capacity is measured using carbon monoxide diffusion capacity (DLCO). question: Which of the following hormones is exclusively secreted by adrenal gland but not by theovaries of females?
explanation: DHEAS is exclusively secreted from the adrenals but not by ovaries because ovaries lack theenzyme dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphotransferase needed to form DHEAS. 90% of DHEA is synthesised by the adrenals and 10% comes from the ovaries.

question: Which hormone crosses the plasma membrane for its action?
explanation: Thyroxine crosses the plasma membrane for its action. Thyroid hormones enter the nucleus and bind to thyroid hormone receptors. Thehormone-receptor complex in the nucleus binds to DNA via zinc fingers. This increases theexpression of a variety of different genes that code for proteins regulating cell function. Althoughthyroxine is an AA derivative, there are transporters to move it into the cell, hence they areintracellular receptors acting on the nucleus. Epinephrine, glucagon, and insulin bind to cell surface receptors.

question: Afferent fibers from baroreceptors for blood pressure control goes to?
explanation: Afferent fiber for blood pressure control goes to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS). Increased BP stimulates the baroreceptors which provide negative feedback in response to theincrease in blood pressure. Baroreceptor reflex: 467 • Increased BP → stimulation of baroreceptors → stimulation of NTS → excitation of CVLM →inhibition of RVLM → inhibition of sympathetic system • Stimulation of NTS also stimulates CVC → parasympathetic stimulation • Net effect = sympathetic inhibition and parasympathetic stimulation → decreased HR and BP NTS - Nucleus tractus solitarius CVC - Cardiovagal centre CVLM - Caudal ventrolateral medulla RVLM - Rostral ventrolateral medulla HR - Heart rate BP - Blood pressure

question: If the lung is allowed to undergo elastic recoil without the chest wall, the resultant volume ofthe lung would be?
explanation: If lung is allowed to undergo elastic recoil without the chest wall, the resultant volume of the lungwould be minimum volume as the opposing force by the chest wall would be non existant. question: You are an intern and want to determine the quantity of IV fluids needed for a patient. Howmuch amount of transient loss/insensible loss per day would you account for in yourcalculations?
explanation: 500-600 ml of transient loss/insensible loss per day would have to be accounted for in thecalculation. question: A soldier posted in Siachen is brought to you in the ER. In order to rule out hypothermia,how do you best measure his temperature?
explanation: In the given clinical scenario rectal temperature would be the preferred site to measure the corebody temperature. During low or high temperatures like in Siachen, the axillary and the oral temperatures are highlymisleading and should not be used to measure the core body temperatures Infrared tympanic thermometer measures the temperature of the eardrum which is representativeof core body temperature. However, more often the thermometer is not inserted adequately or forsafety reasons, they are manufactured in such a way that they do not reach deep into the earcanal, or the ear canal contains cerumen which can disturb the measurement. Hence the infraredthermometer more commonly delivers the temperature of ear canal cerumen and hence not areliable method of measuring the core body temperature.

question: "Vasopressin escape" in SIADH results due to:
explanation: Vasopressin escape in SIADH (Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion) results due todownregulation of aquaporin 2 production. 469 Prolonged exposure to elevated levels of vasopressin (ADH) leads eventually to downregulation ofaquaporin-2 receptors. This prevents excessive reabsorption of water, despite high serum ADHlevels and hence maintains euvolemia. This is known as vasopressin escape. This helps preventexcessive dilutional hyponatremia in SIADH.

question: Which of the following hormones do not act on the pancreas?
explanation: Gastrin does not act upon the pancreas. Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastricmucosal growth. question: A 65-year old patient visits his family practitioner for a yearly examination. On examination,his BP was 190/100 mm Hg. His pulse pressure was 90 mm Hg. What would have decreasedresulting in this increase in pulse pressure?
explanation: Pulse pressure increases with age due to decreased arterial wall compliance. With advancing age, there is an increase in systolic blood pressure. Whilst diastolic blood pressurefalls after 60 years of age due to increased arterial stiffness (decreased compliance). As a result ofthese two changes, pulse pressure increases (↑PP = ↑SBP - ↓DBP).

question: Which of the following curves represents gamma-globin chain production?
explanation: In the given image, the Orange curve represents the gamma-globin chain production. Gammaglobin chain is produced in the fetal period and drops to undetectable levels 6 months postpartumwhich is the pattern represented by the Orange curve. Hemoglobin in blood has different variants throughout life, in different proportions. The type ofhemoglobin essentially depends on the combination of globin chains. Adult hemoglobin is madeof 2 alpha and 2 beta chains, whereas fetal hemoglobin is made of 2 alpha and 2 gamma-globinchains. Other combinations of chains can be found in embryonic hemoglobin. question: Transcutaneous electric nerve stimulation is used to reduce pain. What is the mechanismbehind this?
explanation: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) used for pain relief is based on the gatetheory of pain. This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibers near the injury to relievepain. Gate control theory is based on the inhibition of pain pathway in the spinal cord. Various sensoryinputs from a particular dermatome reach the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. The pain istransmitted via A-delta and C fibers, whereas, A-beta fibers carry tactile sensations (touch,pressure) and A-alpha fibers carry proprioception. When these large-diameter A-beta/A-alpha fibers are stimulated, they inhibit the pain pathway inthe spinal cord. This inhibition is thought to result from the local lateral inhibition ofinterneurons in the spinal cord. Gate control theory operates at the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. The given image depicts the gate control theory of pain: 479

question: Which of the following is not required for calculation of creatinine clearance?

options.d: Volume of serum passing through kidney in 24 hours

explanation: The volume of plasma passing through the kidney in 24 hours is not used in the calculation ofcreatinine clearance. The parameters used to calculate creatinine clearance (CCr) are: • Urine creatinine • Serum creatinine • 24hr urine output The formula used to calculate creatinine clearance (CCr) is: UCr × V ⁄ PCr where, UCr - Urine creatinine(mg/dl) PCr - Serum creatinine(mg/dl) V - Urine volume(ml/24 hrs) Creatinine is a metabolite of muscle metabolism and is cleared from the body mostly byglomerular filtration. Therefore, the clearance of creatinine is used to assess GFR. Urine collection for the measurement of creatinine clearance may be subject to practicalconstraints. Therefore, approximate changes in GFR can be obtained by measuring the serumcreatinine concentration, which is inversely proportional to GFR.
subject: Physiology

question: A neuron is receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons. This is an example of?
explanation: A single neuron receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons is an example of convergence. 480 Convergence means signals from multiple inputs uniting to excite a single neuron. It can be of 2types: • Convergence from a single source • Convergence from multiple sources The importance of convergence is that neurons are almost never excited by an action potentialfrom a single input terminal. However, action potentials converging on the neuron from multipleterminals provide enough spatial summation to bring the neuron to the threshold requiredfor discharge.
subject: Physiology

question: Calculate the ECF volume in a volunteer in whom 10 gm of mannitol was injected in venousblood. At equilibrium urinary excretion of mannitol was found to be 10% and the plasmaconcentration of mannitol was 65 mg/100 ml.
explanation: ECF volume of the above volunteer is calculated to be 14 L. The ECF volume can be calculated using the formula: Where, • V = ECF volume • Amount injected = 10 gm • Amount of mannitol excreted = 10% of 10 gm = 1gm • Plasma concentration of mannitol = 65 mg/100mL = 0.65 gm/L Calculation: ECF Volume = (10-1)/0.65 = 13.8 L = approximately 14 L Mannitol cannot cross cell membranes, hence, it will be distributed in ECF but not in ICF. Thusmannitol is a marker for ECF volume and therefore calculating the volume of distribution ofmannitol gives the value of ECF volume.
subject: Physiology

question: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium is mainly due to?
explanation: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium is mainly due to intracellular proteins. Donnan and Gibbs showed that "When an ion on one side of a membrane cannot diffuse throughthe membrane, the distribution of other ions to which the membrane is permeable is affected in apredictable way". According to this, in the presence of intracellular proteins, which are negatively chargednon-diffusable ions, the distribution of other ions to which the membrane is permeable is affectedin a predictable way (Donnan Effect) so that at equilibrium their concentration ratios are equal.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of these hormones have intracellular receptors?
explanation: 481 Thyroxine hormone act by binding to intracellular nuclear receptors. All other hormones mentioned in the options bind to receptors on the cell membrane.

question: Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by?
explanation: Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by Exosome. In the last decade, a class of small, heterogeneous, secreted vesicles, broadly termedas extracellular vesicles have been identified. These extracellular vesicles have been implicated as a new and important mediator of cell-cellcommunication that likely contributes importantly to both normal and pathologic physiology. These vesicles are enclosed by a lipid bilayer. They are heterogeneous in size (30-2000 nm diameter), and are generated by at least two distinctmechanisms: • Microvesicles are generated by budding from the plasma membrane of a source cell. • Exosomes are generated from the multivesicular body (MVB). Note: The terms microvesicle and exosome are often lumped together as simply exosomes.
subject: Physiology

question: In skeletal muscle, dihydropyridine and ryanodine receptors are coupled by?
explanation: In skeletal muscle, dihydropyridine and ryanodine receptors show mechanical coupling involvingstructural interaction between the two. Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the T tubule membrane. The ryanodine receptor (RyR) is a ligand-gated Ca2+ channel with Ca2+ as its natural ligand. Skeletal muscle excitation-contraction (E-C) coupling is thought to occur by a "mechanicalcoupling" mechanism involving protein-protein interactions that lead to activation of thesarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor by the voltage-sensing transverse (T-) tubuledihydropyridine receptor.
subject: Physiology

question: In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity is seen in which of the following?
explanation: In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity could be seen in blood volume control by thekidney. When the blood volume falls below the equilibrium, the renal–body fluid mechanism causes theblood volume returns back to the equilibrium point resulting in zero error and hence the gain ofkidney in its ability to regulate blood volume is infinity (∞). The degree of effectiveness with which a regulatory system maintains constant conditions isdetermined by the gain of the negative feedback system. 482 Gain= Correction/Error Example: If an external or internal factor led to a decrease in mean blood pressure from 100 mmHg to 80 mm Hg. Activation of a negative feedback mechanism i.e. baroreflex leads to acorrection of blood pressure to 96 mm Hg. So in this case, • Correction = 16 mm Hg • Error = 4 mm Hg • Gain = Correction/Error = 16/4 = 4 Note: A gain of 0 would imply a total failure of the regulatory system and a gain of infinity (∞)would indicate complete restoration of the regulated variable.
subject: Physiology

question: The image below shows simple muscle twitch along with the time trace, recorded in a froggastrocnemius muscle. Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency. (The time tracer wasmade with a 100Hz tuning fork).
explanation: The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second. Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period. It is the frequency at which individual muscle fibrestwitch that fuse and cause sustained muscle contraction, where the contraction period is the timetaken from latent period to maximum force of contraction. In this case, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracerrecorded 100 waves per second. Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds. In the image given in the question, between the point B (end of latent period) to point C(maximum force of contraction), there are about 5 waves. Hence, the duration of contraction = 5 x 0.01 = 0.05 seconds. Substituting the value in the formula, we get: Tetanizing frequency = 1/0.05 sec = 100/5 = 20/sec. 483 Tetanization: The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. Theadding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall musclecontraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways: • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple Ibersummations. • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead totetanization. When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventuallyfuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous,this is called tetanization. Beyond this point, a further increase in the frequency, will not result inincreased force of contraction. Tetanization occurs in two ways: • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli. • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summatedstimuli.
subject: Physiology

question: Least frequency of slow waves is seen in:
explanation: Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min). The Basal electrical rhythm (BER) also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membranepotential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle. It is initiated by the interstitial cells of Cajal. Themembrane potential fluctuates between -65mV and -45mV. The BER is seen in all sites of gastrointestinal smooth muscle except in the esophagus andproximal stomach. The rate of BER in various sites is as follows: • Stomach: 4/min • Duodenum: 12/min • Distal ileum: 8/min • Cecum: 2/min • Sigmoid colon: 6/min The BER does not cause contraction of the smooth muscle. However, when the BER issuperimposed by the spike potentials, it increases muscle tension. Acetylcholine causes an increase in the number of spike potentials and muscletension. Epinephrine causes a decrease in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension. 484 Muscle contraction can occur only when the motor stimulus is provided during the depolarisationpart of the BER. Thus, BER does not cause muscle contraction by itself, but controls the rate and organization sitesof the muscle contractions, as in coordination of the peristaltic activity and setting the rhythm ofsegmentation.
subject: Physiology

question: Macula densa is formed by which part of the nephron?
explanation: Macula densa is formed by specialized tubular epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule. The juxtaglomerular apparatus consists of the following parts: • Macula densa: At the end of the thick ascending limb of Henle, and at the beginning of the distaltubule, the tubular epithelial cells are specialized to form the macula densa. They detect sodium 485 concentration of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium, themacula densa cells trigger the contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing the flow of blood tothe glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate. This happens as follows: When there isincreased sodium, there is increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity which leads to increasedATP hydrolysis causing more adenosine formation. The adenosine receptors on the macula densacells stimulate it to release more calcium, so that there is vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole,thereby decreasing the GFR. • Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole. • Granular cells/JG cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole, they secreterenin. Fall in pressure in afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, inturn, increases blood pressure.
subject: Physiology

question: As filtrate flows through PCT, the concentration of all of the following decreases except:
explanation: As the filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the concentration of the chlorideincreases. • The concentration of chloride in the early part of the pCT is ≈105 mEq/L. • As the sodium is reabsorbed, it preferentially carries glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate. • This leaves behind the solute, that has a higher concentration of the chloride, which as it reachesthe second half of the PCT is ≈140 mEq/L.
subject: Physiology

question: This is the graph depicting the filterability of dextran through the kidney, 1 representingcomplete filtration and 0 representing no filtration. Choose the substance A, B, Crespectively.
explanation: In the given graph, the order of filterability is A>B>C, which likely indicates that thesubstances are Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic. The glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged, which will repel most of the negativecharged (anionic substances). Whereas, the cationic substances are easily filtered. Hence, the order of filterability would be: Polycationic > Neutral > Polyanionic, representedby A, B, and C in the graph shown. The glomerular filtration barrier consists of: • Endothelium of the capillary • Basement membrane: • Lamina densa - electron-dense layer. It contains type IV collagen • Lamina rara interna - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge • Lamina rara externa - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge • Layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basementmembrane 486 The capillary endothelium is perforated by thousands of small holes called fenestrae, whichmeasure from 4 nm up to 8nm. Therefore, neutral substances with molecular diameters of lessthan 4 nm are freely filtered, and filtration of those with diameters of more than 8 nm approacheszero. However, in addition to the size of the particles, the filtration also depends mainly on the chargeof the particle being filtered. The glomerular capillary wall consists of highly negatively chargedproteins called sialoproteins, which repel the negatively charged substances (anions). Theproperty can be studied by using charged dextran. When the filtration of the negatively and positively charged dextrans was studied, the resultsindicated that the negatively charged dextrans in the blood are repelled, with the result thatfiltration of anionic substances 4 nm in diameter is less than half that of neutral substances of thesame size. This explains, why albumin despite having an effective molecular diameter of approximately 7nm, has a very low filtration rate.
subject: Physiology

question: Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ) in a patient with 50kg body weight, if the CO2 exhaledis 200ml/min and O2 consumed is 250 ml/min.
explanation: The respiratory quotient is 0.8. The respiratory quotient is the ratio of carbon dioxide production to oxygen utilization. In the given question, the CO2 production is 200mL/min, while the O2 consumption is250mL/min. Therefore, Respiratory quotient = 200/250 = 0.8 The respiratory quotient (RQ) is used for determining the metabolic utilization of various foods. • When carbohydrates are metabolized with one molecule of oxygen, one carbon dioxide moleculeis released. Therefore, the RQ of carbohydrates = 1. • When fats are oxidized, for every 100 molecules of oxygen consumed, 70 molecules of CO2 arereleased. Therefore, the RQ of fats is 0.70. • Similarly, the respiratory quotient for proteins is 0.80.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following types of amino acids are present in the transmembranous part of themembrane receptor?
explanation: The transmembranous part of the membrane receptor consists of hydrophobic amino acids. A membrane protein can be either integral protein (spans the thickness of the cell membrane) orperipheral protein (attached to the peripheral side of the membrane). The membrane-spanningsegment of integral proteins are usually hydrophobic alpha-helices. The central core of the cell membrane is hydrophobic. Integral proteins have their hydrophobicportions usually in the interior of the membrane and the hydrophilic portions towards thesurfaces. The presence of these hydrophobic amino acids in the interior is a special adaptation 487 that allows the protein to remain stable in the hydrophobic milieu of the cell membrane.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following is not a cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism?
explanation: Parathyroid adenoma is a benign tumor of the parathyroid gland, which causes primaryhyperparathyroidism (not secondary). Secondary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by high levels of parathyroid hormone, tocompensate for the low levels of serum calcium, due to some other underlying condition. Causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism, include: • Chronic kidney disease: The damaged kidneys are unable to produce sufficient amounts of theactive form of vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. This further causes hypocalcemia andtriggers PTH secretion. • Vitamin D deficiency: Causes hypocalcemia, which triggers the increased secretion of PTH. • Lithium: May cause an increased set-point of calcium for parathyroid hormone suppression,which leads to parathyroid hyperplasia.
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following events occur immediately when a person changes his/her posture fromsupine to standing?

options.b: Vagal output to cardiac fibres increase

explanation: There is a decreased firing from the baroreceptors. • When a person stands up from a lying down position, it causes pooling of the blood in the legs,due to gravity. This reduces the venous return and causes a decrease in cardiac output. • Reduced cardiac output, leads to a fall in blood pressure, which in turn causes reduced firingfrom baroreceptors. • As a result, the vagal tone is suppressed leading to increased heart rate. 488
subject: Physiology

question: Which of the following statements is true about skeletal muscle contraction?
explanation: During the contraction of the skeletal muscle, the Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmicreticulum. Only statement 3 is correct. Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of themuscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle. The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows: • Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, which bindsto the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. • This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane, leading to thegeneration of end-plate potential, which is a local potential. • When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fibre, and an actionpotential is generated. • The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules, leading to the spread ofdepolarisation. • The depolarization of the muscle fibre causes the release of Ca2+ from terminal cisterns ofsarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments. • The calcium released, binds to troponin C, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin. • The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filamentscauses contraction of the skeletal muscle. Steps in relaxation: • The cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, by the action ofSERCA (sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase). • Once the calcium concentration is lowered, the interaction between actin and myosin ceases, andthe muscle relaxes. Other options: Statement 1: Incorrect - Extracellular calcium levels play an important role in muscle contraction.When there is a decrease in extracellular calcium as in hypocalcemia, the voltage-gated sodiumchannels are activated, which causes sodium influx. The increased intracellular sodiumconcentration causes sustained depolarization, which may lead to tetany. Statement 2: Incorrect - Ca2+ is not released from mitochondria. It is released from thesarcoplasmic reticulum. Statement 4: Voltage-gated calcium channels on T-tubules (part of sarcolemma) are activated by adepolarizing stimulus, which causes the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
