question: Which of the following is true?
explanation: Of the given statements, 2 and 3 are true. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene and MYC is aproto-oncogene. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 17q21 and its function is to repair thedouble-stranded breaks in DNA. It is associated with familial breast and ovarian carcinoma.BRCA1-associated breast cancers are commonly poorly differentiated. All breast cancers are separated into 3 major groups based on the expression of two proteins, ERand HER2 (also known as ERBB2). HER2 cancers are defined as cancers overexpressing HER2and can be either ER-positive or ER-negative. Thus HER2neu is expressed only in a fraction ofpeople with breast cancer. EGF-receptor family has two proto-oncogenes: ERBB1 that codes for EGFR and ERBB2 that codesfor HER. Mutation in EGFR results in adenocarcinoma of the lung, which is one of the mainsubtypes of non-small cell lung carcinoma. MYC is a proto-oncogene, that is expressed in all eukaryotic cells and belongs to theimmediate-early response genes, which are rapidly induced by RAS/MAPK signaling followinggrowth factor stimulation of quiescent cells. Normally, MYC protein concentration are tightlycontrolled at the level of transcription, translation and protein stability. The mechanisms bywhich MYC promotes neoplastic cell growth may be follows: • MYC activates the expression of many genes like D cyclins, that are involved in cell cycleprogression • MYC regulates the expression of telomerase • MYC is one of the transcriptional factors that can act together to reprogram somatic cells intopluripotent stem cells MYC gene is deregulated in a number of cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma, breast, colon, lungand other cancers. The functionally identical NMYC and LMYC genes are also amplified in 2021 neuroblastomas and small cell cancers of the lung, respectively.

question: Identify the given condition.
explanation: The given histologic picture shows a suprabasal blister suggesting the diagnosis of pemphigusvulgaris. It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3. Rarely antibodiesagainst desmoglein 1 can also be found. The antibodies are commonly IgG antibodies. Desmoglein 3 is mainly present in the basal and suprabasal layers of the skin and mucosa. Thepatients, therefore, present with flaccid bullae over the skin and mucosal ulcerations. Oral mucosais commonly affected. Other areas where ulceration can be seen are conjunctiva, nasopharynx,larynx, etc. Cutaneous lesions are more common over the scalp, face, neck, upper chest, and back. Direct immunofluorescence will show the deposition of antibodies around the keratinocytes in theepidermis. It is treated with steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, etc. 2022 Other options: B) Leprosy: Tuberculoid leprosy shows granulomatous lesions, without much bacilli. Hence calledpaucibacillary leprosy. Lepromatous lesions contain large aggregates of lipid-laden macrophages(lepra cells), often filled with masses (globi) of acid-fast bacilli. Because of the presence ofabundant bacteria, it is also called as multibacillary. Given below are the images that depict lepromatous lesion showing foamy macrophages withglobi of pink/red acid-fast bacilli and tuberculoid leprosy showing granulomatous lesions,respectively. 2023 C) Mycosis fungoides: Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, characterized bypolymorphic patches and plaques with fine scaling usually present on the limbs, breast, andbuttocks. The lesions may be pruritic or even asymptomatic. Histological hallmarks include: 1.Sézary-Lutzner cells - cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/ hyper-convoluted nuclearmembrane), 2. Pautrier's microabscesses - tumor cells invade the epidermis as single cells andsmall clusters, forming a collection of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis and 3.Epidermotropism - pronounced invasion of the tumor cells into the epidermis. Given below is the image of Sezary-Lutzner cells. Given below is the arrow pointing at Paurtier's microabcess. 2024 D) Visceral leishmaniasis: In visceral leishmaniasis, parasites invade and activate themacrophages throughout the mononuclear phagocyte system. Hence, these phagocytic cells areenlarged and filled with leishmania species; many plasma cells are also present. question: A karyotyping image is given below. What are the clinical features most likely to be expectedin such patients?
explanation: The given karyotyping image shows ‘47, XXY’ abnormality, which is seen in Klinefelter’ssyndrome. Gynecomastia and long limbs are seen in Klinefelter's syndrome. Other clinical features seen in Klinefelter’s syndrome are: 2025 • Disproportionately long arms and legs, • Gynecomastia • Eunuchoid body habitus • Mitral valve prolapse • Mental retardation; IQ: 60-80, • Minor developmental and learning disabilities, • Lack of secondary sexual characteristics (due to a decrease in androgen production) • Higher risk of breast carcinoma • Testicular dysgenesis with small penis • Infertility/azoospermia • Type 2 diabetes mellitus • Metabolic syndrome • Higher risk of extragonadal germ cell tumors Klinefelter syndrome: • Most common sex aneuploidy in males • Classically karyotype is 47, XXY. question: A 20-year-old athlete suddenly collapsed while playing football and was taken to the hospitalwhere he was declared dead. His autopsy image is given below. Which of the following is themost likely cause of death?

options.a: Valvular heart disease due to RHD
options.b: Sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia
options.c: Sudden cardiac death due to Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
options.d: Sudden cardiac death due to atherosclerosis

explanation: The given image shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and along with the scenario, it issuggestive of sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathyhave an increased risk of sudden cardiac death from ventricular tachyarrhythmias. In fact,arrhythmias are the most important/most common cause of death in hypertrophiccardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the most common causes of sudden, otherwiseunexplained death in young athletes. HCM is characterized by reduced stroke volume due toimpaired diastolic filling, which is a consequence of the massively hypertrophic left ventricle.There is a dynamic obstruction to the left ventricular outflow as the anterior mitral leaflet movestowards the ventricular septum during systole. This compromised cardiac output in combinationwith a secondary increase in pulmonary venous pressure is the reason for exertional dyspnea attimes of increased oxygen demand. Major clinical problems in HCM are atrial fibrillation, stroke, intractable cardiacfailure, ventricular arrhythmias and also sudden death. There is a harsh systolic ejection murmurcaused by the ventricular outflow obstruction. Mutations causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy(HCM) are most commonly seen in the genes encoding β-myosin heavy chain(MHC/MYH7) or myosin-binding protein C (MYBP-C). HCM is mostly an autosomal dominant disorder. The most important histologic features of HCMmyocardium are as follows: • Massive myocyte hypertrophy particularly of transverse myocyte diameters • Myofiber disarray including that of bundles of myocytes, individual myocytes, and contractileelements • Interstitial and replacement fibrosis 2030 Most of the patients can be treated with β blockers to decrease heart rate and contractility.Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators are used in patients with increased risk of ventriculararrhythmias. Some patients can also be treated by surgical excision of the septal muscle or bycarefully controlled septal infarction through a catheter-based infusion of alcohol. question: Which of the following can be prevented by transfusing irradiated RBCs?
explanation: Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevent the incidence of graft versus host disease (GVHD)associated with the transfusion. GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted intoimmunologically compromised recipients and the transferred cells recognize the alloantigens inthe host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem celltransplantation but may occur following transplantation of solid organs too. GVHD maybe of two types: acute and chronic. Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalizedrash), liver( in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But theaffected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes. Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensiveskin damage, with destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemicsclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will beinvolution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also berecurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to thegrafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result inautoantibodies production. Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation, before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence ofGVHD. But irradiation also has its side effects such as recurrence of tumor in leukemic patients,increased incidence of graft failures and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma.

question: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the effect of Glucose-6-PhosphateDehydrogenase deficiency?
explanation: 2032 Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathioneand decreased NADPH. G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt. Defective enzymefunction reduced the ability of red cells to protect themselves against oxidative injuries, therebyincreasing lipid peroxidation and lead to hemolysis. • G6PD reduces NADP to NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate. • This NADPH then provides reducing equivalents needed for conversion of oxidized glutathioneto reduced glutathione. • This reduced glutathione acts as a cofactor in reactions that neutralize compounds such asH2O2, thereby protecting against oxidant injury. • Exposure of G6PD deficient red cells to oxidative stress leads to crosslinking of reactivesulfhydryl groups on globin chains, which then becomes denatured and form membrane-boundprecipitates called ‘Heinz bodies’, thereby producing membrane damage. • When these inclusion bearing RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out theseHeinz bodies. • The resultant cells are called ‘Bite cells’. Clinical features: • Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular • Hemolytic anaemia • Hemoglobinemia • Hemoglobinuria The episode of hemolysis is self-limiting, since only the older RBCs are at risk for lysis, leaving theG6PD-replete younger RBCs in circulation. The recovery phase is heralded by reticulocytosis.

question: Which of the following is not likely to be seen in a patient with Paroxysmal NocturnalHemoglobinuria (PNH)?
explanation: Leukemia is least likely to be seen in patients with Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH). Clinical manifestations of PNH include: • Hemolytic anemia • Pancytopenia • Intermittent hemoglobinuria- acute hemolytic episodes occur at night owing to a slight fall in pHduring sleep • Haemosiderinuria • Venous thrombosis (a leading cause of death in PNH) • Patients diagnosed with PNH can later develop aplastic anemia and vice versa PNH is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycancomplementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of 2033 membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. PNH blood cells are abnormallysusceptible to lysis or injury by complement since they are deficient in three GPI- linked proteinsthat regulate complement activity: • Decay-accelerating factor or CD55 • Membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis or CD59 (Inhibitor of C3 convertase) and • C8-binding protein Diagnosis: • Ham’s test: The abnormal sensitivity of red blood cells, leukocytes, and platelets to complementcan be demonstrated in vitro using red cell lysis at acidic pH. • Flow cytometry detects the red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59. Treatment: Eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody, that prevents the conversion of C5 to C5a has been proveneffective in PNH. The definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

question: What is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of myocarditis?
explanation: An endo-myocardial biopsy is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of myocarditis. Myocarditis can be due to • Infections: Coxsackie A and B, HIV, C.diphtheriae, Ricketssiae, Candida, Protozoa andhelminths. • Immune-mediated reactions: Post-viral, post-streptococcal, drug hypersensitivity (e.g: methyldopa, sulfinamides), transplant rejection, etc., 2035 • Unknown: Sarcoidosis, Giant cell myocarditis Active myocarditis is characterized by an interstitial inflammatory infiltrate associated withdegenerating or apoptotic myocytes.

question: A child presented with bilateral proptosis. From the peripheral smear, he was suspected tohave chloroma. What is the next investigation of choice?
explanation: The next investigation of choice, in a child suspected to have a chloroma, is a bone Synopsisbiopsy. Chloroma, also called myeloid sarcoma, granulocytic sarcoma, or myeloblastoma is anextramedullary tumor that occurs in 2% to 14% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).Frequent sites of involvement are the skin, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, bone, soft tissue,testis, and peritoneum. Isolated orbital involvement of myeloid sarcoma is rare. Proptosis is the most commonpresentation. Other symptoms include lacrimal swelling, conjunctival mass lesion, retinalhemorrhages, ptosis, dystopia. Decreased visual acuity and ocular movement restriction have alsobeen reported. Most cases of chloroma can be diagnosed on peripheral smear examination, which is easilyavailable and is relatively inexpensive. Sometimes it may not be associated with any peripheralsmear abnormality, and hence bone Synopsis aspirate and biopsy should be done to confirmAML. The diagnosis can also be made if Auer rods are detected. Myeloid sarcomas haveimmunophenotypic features that are identical to AML. Although myeloid sarcomas are radiosensitive, they are managed with systemic chemotherapy inmost cases, even in the absence of bone Synopsis involvement. Surgery and/or radiation therapymay be indicated for symptomatic lesions or tumors causing local organ dysfunction orobstruction. The image shows Auer rods contained within myeloblasts. 2036

question: A person working in an industry for a long time developed progressive breathlessness. Thehistopathological image of his lung biopsy is given below. What industry was he most likelyworking in?
explanation: From the clinical history of progressive breathlessness and the histopathological image showingasbestos bodies, ferruginous bodies, and fibrosis, the patient is most likely working in the asbestosindustry. Asbestosis occurs due to the inhalation of crystalline hydrated silicates (asbestos). It ischaracterized by diffuse parenchymal interstitial fibrosis. It usually begins in the lower lobes ofthe lungs and may present with dyspnoea and cough, usually after 20-30 years of exposure. Otherasbestos-related diseases include pleural plaques, recurrent pleural effusions, lung carcinoma, andmesothelioma. Asbestos bodies are a hallmark finding. They appear as golden brown, fusiform, or beaded rods.These are formed when the asbestos fibers are phagocytosed by the macrophages and are coatedby iron-containing proteinaceous material derived from phagocyte ferritin. Similar iron-proteincomplexes coat other inorganic particulates other than asbestos which are termed as ferruginousbodies. The image below shows asbestos bodies. Other options: Option A: Silicosis is due to the inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica) as seen inindividuals employed in sandblasting or rock mining. Macrophages phagocytose inhaled silicaparticles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that causefibroblast recruitment. Subsequently, collagen is deposited in the interstitium. Microscopy reveals coalescent nodules of whorled collagen fibers surrounded by a peripheral zoneof silica-laden macrophages. Shown below is an image of a silicotic nodule with collagen whorls as seen in this condition. 2037 Option C: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coalminers. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, whichaccumulate in the connective tissue. Initially it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis withlittle or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressivemassive fibrosis which is called as complicated coal workers pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes ofthe lungs are commonly involved. Microscopic features consist of coal-laden macrophages, black pigment, and dense collagenousinterstitial fibrosis. The image below shows anthracosis- black pigment engulfed within macrophages as well as in theform of deposits. Option D: Cotton dust causes byssinosis and can induce occupational asthma. 2038

question: A patient presented with complaints of dyspnea on exertion for 1 month. Echocardiographyshowed the presence of mitral stenosis and left ventricular hypertrophy. Identify thehistopathological finding given below and the probable diagnosis.
explanation: The lesion shown in the histopathological slide is Aschoff's body and the most probable diagnosisis rheumatic heart disease (RHD). Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They arecomposed of foci of T lymphocytes, activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells, and occasionalplasma cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoid nuclei withchromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence, they are also calledcaterpillar cells. Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis. During acute rheumatic fever, Aschoffbodies may be found in any of the three layers of the heart that results in pericarditis, myocarditis,or endocarditis. Chronic inflammation leads to diffuse thickening and fibrosis of the valve leaflets, often withcalcific deposits. Fibrinoid necrosis occurs due to inflammation of the endocardium and theleft-sided valves. Over these areas of necrosis, small vegetations called verrucae develop along thelines of closure. Irregular thickenings present in the subendocardium are called MacCallumplaques. In chronic RHD, the mitral valve leaflet is thickened, with commissural fusion and shortening.There is thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords. This can lead to narrowing the mitralorifice, leading to a fish mouth appearance (button hole). Some major manifestations of rheumatic Fever are: • Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints • Pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis, or endocarditis) • Subcutaneous nodules (typically on extensor surfaces of extremities) • Erythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash • Sydenham chorea, a neurologic disorder with involuntary rapid movements Image showing button hole appearance seen in mitral stenosis in case of rheumatic heart disease. 2039 Image show Aschoff bodies seen in RHD. Other options: Option B: Degenerative calcific deposits in the mitral valve typically develop in the fibrousannulus. They are seen grossly as irregular, stony hard, occasionally ulcerated nodules at the baseof the leaflets. Usually, it does not affect valvular function. However, occasionally it can lead toregurgitation, stenosis, or arrhythmias. The image below shows severe calcification of the mitral valve annulus with focally thickenedshortened and fused chordae. Option C: In sarcoidosis, the involved tissues contain well-formed non-necrotizing granulomas.They are composed of aggregates of tightly clustered epithelioid macrophages, often with giantcells, usually without central necrosis. As the lesions become chronic, fibrous rims or hyalinefibrous scars enclose the granulomas. The image below shows non-necrotizing granulomas in the wall of a bronchiole in sarcoidosis. 2040 Option D: In tuberculosis, sites of active involvement of tuberculosis are marked histologically bya characteristic granulomatous inflammatory reaction composed of both caseating andnon-caseating tubercles. Usually, granuloma shows central granular caseation surrounded bymultinucleate giant cells. Central caseation may be absent in non-caseating granulomas. Stainingshould be done to detect acid-fast bacilli when granulomas are present. The image below shows a caseating granulomatous lesion with areas of caseation (on the righthalf) bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes. Image showing non-necrotizing granuloma seen in pulmonary tuberculosis. 2041

question: A patient with lytic lesions on the skull is suspected of a diagnosis of Langerhan cellhistiocytosis. Which of the following is a characteristic finding on electron microscopy?
explanation: The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cellhistiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy. Birbeck granules have a dilated terminal end producing a tennis racket–like appearance.It contains the protein langerin (CD207). It is seen on electron microscopy. The image below shows Birbeck granules on electron microscopy seen in LCH. Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded orgrooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. Birbeck granules areseen in the cytoplasm. The tumor cells specifically express HLA-DR, S-100, and CD1a andlangerin (CD207) markers. 2042 The image below shows histopathological image of Langerhan cells with folded nuclei. Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immaturedendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The mostcommon mutation is BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation. It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly everyorgan, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone Synopsis, or the central nervoussystem. LCH can present as the following clinical entities: • Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease) • Unifocal and multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma)- Thecombination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called theHand-Schüller-Christian triad. • Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis The below image shows lytic lesion of skull seen in LCH. 2043

question: A 60-year-old patient presented with scrotal swelling and ataxia. Which among the followingcould likely be a cause?
explanation: The most likely cause in the following case is Non-Hodgkin lymphoma(NHL). Diffuse large B celllymphoma (DLBCL), a type of NHL is the most common lymphoma. NHL affects the elderly agegroup and extranodal presentation is common. DLBCL can involve CNS, and CNS involvement isparticularly common if there is involvement of the testes, paranasal sinuses, or bone Synopsis aswell. Primary testicular lymphoma is common in NHL when compared to Hodgkin lymphoma. Primarytesticular lymphoma(PTL) is an aggressive and uncommon form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma(NHL)usually affecting the elderly age group(>60y). It typically presents as a painless, firm testicularmass. Constitutional symptoms are uncommon, and if present, warrant a systemic involvement.Metastasis involves the central nervous system (CNS), skin, contralateral testis, and pleuraresulting in local complications. Even though ataxia is seen as a paraneoplastic symptom due to cerebellar degeneration inHodgkin lymphoma, testicular involvement is very rare and so far only 5 cases have beenreported. Hodgkin lymphoma arises in a single node or chain of nodes and spreads first toanatomically contiguous lymphoid tissues. The extranodal presentation is rare. The extranodaldisease can occur at any site like lung, liver, bone, and bone Synopsis is most common if it occurs.The central nervous system and the testis are exceptionally rare sites for Hodgkin's lymphoma.Thus Hodgkin's lymphoma can be ruled out. Other options: A) Glioblastoma multiforme is a highly malignant tumor, common in older adults in the fifth andsixth decades. The most common locations are the frontal and temporal lobes. The tumor mayspread and invade the other hemisphere, resulting in a characteristicbutterfly appearance. Extracranial metastases of malignant gliomas are extremely rare due to: • Absence of a lymphatic system in the brain and spinal cord for systemic dissemination • Dense dura around intracranial veins, preventing the penetration of the tumor 2044 • Lack of nurturing stroma in other organs prevents the proliferation of glioblastoma cells Therefore the tumor metastasizing to the testis is very much unlikely and glioblastoma can beruled out. Image showing MRI(magnetic resonance imaging) of glioblastoma Option D) Testicular cancer is the most common cancer in men aged from 15 to 35 years. Germcell tumors(GCT) account for 90%–95% of cases. Non-seminomatous form (NSGCT) metastasizesto the lungs, liver, central nervous system, and bone in order of frequency. The frequency of brainmetastases is very low, not exceeding 1.2%. Note: This is a controversial question. A more detailed clinical history and examination than whatis provided in the stem are required for us to arrive at a definitive diagnosis.

question: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites presented to you. The gross appearance of his liver is asshown below. Which among the following is true about it?

options.a: Dark areas represent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver tissue
options.b: Dark areas represent viable liver tissue, white areas represent necrosis

explanation: The gross image of the liver shows a nutmeg appearance, seen in heart failure. The dark areasrepresent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver tissue. Nutmeg liver refers to the mottled appearance of the liver which resembles the cut section ofnutmeg. This occurs as a result of hepatic venous congestion following right heart failure. Thedark centrilobular zones reflect sinusoidal congestion. Congestion is seen around the central veinsusually from right-sided heart failure. The pale periportal zones reflect normal or fatty liver tissue. The liver derives its blood supply from the portal venous system and the hepatic artery. The portaltriad constitutes: • Branches of the hepatic artery • Portal vein • Bile duct 2045 The blood from the portal vein and the hepatic artery flow through the intervening sinusoids anddrains into the central vein. The central veins from adjacent lobules form interlobular veins,which then unite as hepatic veins and finally drain into the inferior vena cava. The hepatic lobule is divided into three zones: • Zone 1 is the periportal area • Zone 2 is the intermediate zone • Zone 3 is the area closest to the central vein Right-sided cardiac failure leads to passive congestion of the liver. Left-sided cardiac failure leadsto hypoperfusion and hypoxia of hepatocytes around central veins. The combination ofhypoperfusion and retrograde congestion causes centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis, leading tothis mottled appearance of the liver, known as nutmeg liver. The microscopic image below of a nutmeg liver shows perisinusoidal fibrosis, hepatic venuledilation, and dilation of the sinusoids in zone III.

question: A 6-year-old boy came with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the probablediagnosis, cell, and virus associated with the image given below?
explanation: The probable diagnosis, cell, and virus from the given clinical scenario and the histopathologicalimage are Hodgkin's lymphoma, Reed-Sternberg cells (RS cells), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)respectively. Hodgkin's lymphoma arises in a single lymph node or chain of nodes and spreads first toanatomically contiguous lymphoid tissues. It usually presents as painless lymphadenopathy. Thedistinctive feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma is the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells. RS cells are giant neoplastic cells derived from germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cells.They appear as large cells with multiple nuclei or a single nucleus with multiple nuclear lobes.Each cell contains large inclusion-like prominent nucleoli, and abundant, usually slightlyeosinophilic, cytoplasm, depicting an owl-eye appearance, as shown in the image below. 2046 WHO classifies Hodgkin's lymphoma into 5 subtypes: • Nodular sclerosis: Frequent lacunar cells • Mixed cellularity • Lymphocyte-rich • Lymphocyte depletion • Nodular lymphocyte predominance The first 4 subtypes are considered classical Hodgkin's lymphoma. The RS cells are CD 15+ andCD30+. The lymphocyte predominant type is considered non-classical Hodgkin's lymphoma withCD15-, CD30-, CD20+ and EB -. The image below shows a popcorn cell seen in lymphocytic predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma. TypeRS-cellEB VirusPrognosis 1. Nodular sclerosis (most common in the world)Frequent lacunar cells and occasional diagnostic RS cellsRareVery good 2. Mixed cellularity (most common in India)Frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells70%Good 3.Lymphocyte RichFrequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells40%Very good 4.Lymphocyte depletedReticular variant: frequent diagnostic RS cells and variants and a paucity of background reactive cell 90%(Max)Poorest 5.Lymphocyte predominantL&H variant (Popcorn cell) variants in the background of follicular dendritic cells 0%(Min)Excellent 2047 Other options: Option A: RS cells are diagnostic of Hodgkin's lymphoma, not non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Thehistopathologic findings in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) are varied and depend on the subtype. Option B: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8), alsoknown as Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus. Cutaneous lesions of Kaposi sarcoma are composed ofspindle cells, mostly in the dermis or subcutaneous tissues, with small vessels and slit-like spaceswith red cells. The image shows lesions seen in Kaposi's sarcoma. Option D: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by EBV. The peripheral blood smear shows absolutelymphocytosis with mononucleosis cells which are atypical activated T lymphocytes. They haveabundant cytoplasm with multiple vacuolations and azurophilic granules, and an oval, indented,or folded nucleus and are shown below. 2048 About 5-7% of the cases of infectious mononucleosis can be caused by the cytomegalovirus (CMV),which can also cause pneumonia. CMV-infected pneumocytes with large, intranuclear, basophilicinclusions with haloes at their periphery as well as small, granular cytoplasmic inclusions are seenbelow with an owl-eye appearance.

question: A person was brought to the emergency department with facial swelling, itching, andhypotension following a bee sting. The mentioned clinical features are due to the increase inwhich immunoglobulin?
explanation: The given clinical features suggest type 1 hypersensitivity reaction and are mediated byimmunoglobulin E (IgE). Immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity reactions refer to allergic reactions or allergies. It is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibodyon the surface of mast cells. It occurs in a previously sensitized individual. These reactions are 2049 induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgEproduction in genetically susceptible individuals. Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, andIL-13. These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils. IgE coats mastcells by binding to the FcεRI receptor. Re-exposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgEand FcεRI which in turn causes activation of mast cells releasing powerful mediators. Theprincipal mediators are: • Histamine • Proteases • Prostaglandins • Leukotrienes • Cytokines like TNF, IL-1, and chemokines. The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis tofatal anaphylaxis. It occurs in two phases: • The immediate phase is characterized by vasodilation, vascular leakage, smooth muscle spasm(in asthma), or glandular secretions. These changes occur within minutes after exposure to anallergen and subside in a few hours. • Late-phase reaction is characterized by infiltration of tissues with eosinophils, neutrophils,basophils, monocytes, and CD4+ T cells. Late-phase reaction sets in 2 to 24 hours later and maylast for several days. Image: Sequence of events in immediate (type 1) hypersensitivity.

question: All of the following are associated with massive splenomegaly except :
explanation: 2050 All the above are associated with massive splenomegaly except aplastic anemia. Aplastic anemia is a syndrome of chronic primary hematopoietic failure. This results inpancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia). Important causes include • Alkylating agents, antimetabolites • Benzene • Whole-body irradiation • Viral infections: Hepatitis (unknown virus), Cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Herpes zoster • Fanconi anemia The patient will have • Decreased red blood cells leading to anemia • Decreased white blood cells leading to recurrent infections • Decreased platelets leading to petechiae and ecchymoses. Many other leukemias and lymphomas may have a similar presentation. However, splenomegalyis characteristically absent in these patients. The bone Synopsis is markedly hypocellular. It is largely devoid of hematopoietic cells. Synopsisaspirates yield a dry tap having only fat cells, fibrous stroma, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.Aplasia is best appreciated in Synopsis biopsies. The following image shows a hypocellular boneSynopsis with little hematopoiesis and several fat cells. Stem cell transplantation is the treatment of choice in those with a suitable donor.Immunosuppressive therapy is responsive in old patients or in patients without suitable donors. Other options: Option A- Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with the presence ofBCR-ABL fusion gene translocation mutation. The Synopsis is markedly hypercellular because ofincreased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursor cells. This results in decreasedhematopoiesis within the bone Synopsis. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of 2051 extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mildhepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy. Option C- Hairy cell leukemia is a memory B-cell neoplasm predominantly seen in middle-agedmale patients. It occurs due to activating BRAF mutations. Infiltration of the bone Synopsis, liver,and spleen with tumor cells result in splenomegaly. Sometimes, this can be the only finding in thepatient. Pancytopenia results from Synopsis involvement. Hairy cells have round, oblong, or reniform nuclei and moderate amounts of pale blue cytoplasmwith thread-like or bleb-like extensions. Immunophenotyping shows hairy cell leukemias typicallyexpress the pan-B-cell markers CD19 and CD20 and certain relatively distinctive markers, such asCD11c, CD25, CD103, and annexin A1. Option D- Lymphomas cause splenomegaly due to the infiltration of neoplastic cells in the spleen.

question: A 42-year-old female patient presents with cough, low-grade fever, and hemoptysis.Investigations reveal a cavitary lesion on her right lung apex, which on biopsy reveals caseousnecrosis. The underlying pathophysiology is :
explanation: The clinical scenario with complaints of cough, low-grade fever, hemoptysis is suggestive ofpulmonary tuberculosis. The diagnosis is further supported by a cavitary lesion in the apex of thelung and a biopsy showing caseous necrosis. The pathophysiology is a type 4 hypersensitivityreaction mediated by activated macrophages. Tuberculosis is a chronic pulmonary and systemic disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.Granulomatous inflammation and tissue damage are by Th-1 mediated macrophage activation andkilling of bacteria. Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) released by Th-1 cells is the critical mediator thatactivates the macrophages. This activation differentiates the macrophages into epithelioid cellsthat aggregate to form granuloma. This is a T-cell mediated (Type 4) hypersensitivity reaction. Pulmonary TB due to exogenous (new infection) or endogenous (reactivation of a dormantprimary lesion) infection in a sensitized individual is called post-primary or reactivation orsecondary or adult-type TB. The apical and posterior segments of the upper lobe and superior segments of the lower lobe aremost commonly involved in post-primary TB due to increased ventilation in these segments thanthe lower zones. Patients often present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum,night sweats, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss. Radiological findings include ill-defined opacification in the upper lobes, consolidation, collapse,and cavitation development. • Typically, the disease is parenchymal without nodal enlargement. • Cavitation is a distinguishing feature of postprimary TB. • Typical cavities are thick-walled and irregular. • Air-fluid levels are uncommon in TB. The presence of air-fluid levels indicates superaddedinfections. • Upper-lobe involvement with cavitation and the absence of lymphadenopathy distinguishespostprimary TB from primary TB. The image below shows chest X-ray findings of a post-primary TB with a cavity (black arrows) inthe right upper lobe and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (white triangles) in the apical regions. 2052 Image shows a gross picture of caseous necrosis. Notice the characteristic "cheesy appearance"due to its white appearance of the area of necrosis. Image below shows tuberculoid granuloma associated with caseous necrosis (upper right) andsurrounding epithelioid cells, Langhans' multinucleated giant cells. 2053 Other options: Option A: Enzyme degradation is seen in liquefactive necrosis which is characterized by digestionof the dead cells, resulting in transformation of the tissue into a viscous liquid. It is seen in focalbacterial or fungal infections. Eg: Brain abscess. Option C: Fibrinoid deposition is seen in fibrinoid necrosis. It is seen in immune reactionsinvolving blood vessels with deposition of fibrinoid material which is combination of immunecomplexes and plasma proteins. Eg: Vasculitis syndromes Option D: Sudden cut-off of blood supply causes coagulative necrosis. It is a form of necrosis inwhich the original architecture of dead tissue is preserved with firm texture. Eg: Ischemic injuryin all organs, except the brain.

question: A 45-year-old male patient was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia. Which of the followingis true about intracellular regulation of iron in the above condition?

options.a: Ferritin translation is increased by binding IRP to IRE
options.b: Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE
options.c: Transferrin receptor 1 translation is unaffected by binding IRP to IRE
options.d: Transferrin receptor 1 translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE

explanation: In iron deficiency anemia, ferritin translation is decreased by binding iron regulatory protein toiron response elements. Dietary iron is carried in the blood by transferrin and enters cells via endocytosis, mediated by thetransferrin receptor. Excess iron is stored by binding to ferritin. The levels of transferrin,transferrin receptor (TfR), and ferritin are therefore crucial to cellular iron homeostasis. The synthesis of these three proteins is regulated in response to iron availability and aconitase(enzyme in citric acid cycle). When a cell is depleted of iron, the aconitase enzyme is converted to apoaconitase. Apoaconitaseis identical to iron regulatory protein 1 (IRP-1) and is closely related to IRP-2. It regulates ironmetabolism. The iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) are two cytoplasmic RNA-binding proteins that control ironmetabolism. They bind to regions in the mRNA containing the ferritin and transferrin receptor.These mRNA sequences are part of hairpin structures known as iron response elements (IREs). 2054 • When the IRPs bind to the 5' untranslated IRE sequence in the ferritin mRNA, IRPs blockferritin translation, thus decreasing ferritin. • When IRPs are bound to the 3' end of the untranslated IRE sequence, they stabilize the mRNA,prevent its degradation and increase the copies of transferrin receptor per mRNA molecule. Hence, in iron-deficient cells, iron storage (bound to ferritin) is reduced and iron uptake (viatransferrin receptor) becomes more efficient.
subject: Pathology

question: A 65-year-old male patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy presents to theoutpatient department. His peripheral smear shows the presence of smudge cells. Which ofthe following additional investigations will you do to arrive at a diagnosis?
explanation: An elderly patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy, and a peripheral smear showingthe presence of smudge cells suggest a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. Theclassical immunophenotypic feature of CLL is CD 19+, CD20+, CD 23+, CD5+. Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults,more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, itpresents non specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalizedlymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients. The chromosomal defects in CLL include: • Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis) • Deletion of 11q • Trisomy 12q • Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis) The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) contains small roundlymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may getdisrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of>5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making thepatient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop hemolytic anemia orthrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells. On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with largeractivated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in looseaggregates referred to as proliferation centers. These proliferation centers are pathognomic toCLL when present. Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chroniclymphocytic leukemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combinationof fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressivelymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). The image shows small round lymphocytes and smudge cells seen in CLL. 2055
subject: Pathology

question: Oil red O stain is used in which of the following?
explanation: Oil red O (ORO) stain is used in frozen section. Oil red O stains lipid/ fats and gives a characteristic orange/red appearance. It is used in theunfixed frozen sections as the fixation of fats with other routine processes may lose the lipidcontent. 10% Neutral buffer formaldehyde (NBF) is the preferred fixative in histopathologicalsections staining with Oil red O. Zenker's fixative and Helly's fixative are best avoided duringstaining with ORO. Oil red O stains the lipid in the vacuoles in the pulmonary vasculature. It can be useful inidentifying fat emboli in lung tissue, diagnosing renal cell carcinoma, and sebaceous gland tumorsof the skin. Other stains used for lipids or fats: • Nile blue sulfate. The preferred fixative is formal calcium. • Osmic acid is used in the frozen section. 10% NBF is the preferred fixative • Sudan black B is used in the frozen section. The preferred fixative is 10% NBF. Other Options: Option A: Formalin fixation- Formalin as 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) is the mostcommon fixative used in diagnostic pathology. Option C: Ethyl alcohol- Ideal fixative for cytological smears because they act quickly and givegood nuclear detail. Option D: Glutaraldehyde- Preferred fixative in electron microscopy. The standard solution is a2.5% buffered glutaraldehyde. Image below shows microscopy of a oil red O stained bronchoalveolar lavage sample from apatient with acute lung injury. 2056 The image shows the lipid vesicles in the adipocytes stained using oil-red-O staining.

question: A boy presents with fever, night sweats, and neck swelling. The biopsy of swelling showed astarry sky appearance. What is the most likely genetic abnormality seen in this case?
explanation: The given clinical scenario and the classical histopathological finding of starry sky appearancesuggest the diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma and the most likely genetic abnormality is thetranslocation of the MYC gene on chromosome 8. Burkitt's lymphoma arises from mature germinal center B-cells that express surface IgM, CD19,CD20, CD10, and BCL6. It is divided into endemic and sporadic types, both of which occur mainly in children or youngadults. 2057 • African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma often presents as a mass involving the mandible and mayinvolve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands. • Sporadic (non-endemic) Burkitt lymphoma most often appears as a mass involving theileocecum and peritoneum. • A subset of aggressive lymphomas occurs in individuals infected with HIV. All forms of Burkitt lymphoma are associated with translocations of the MYC gene onchromosome 8 that lead to increased MYC protein levels. Essentially all endemic Burkittlymphomas are latently infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The tumor shows a high mitotic index with numerous apoptotic cells. The nuclear remnants ofthese apoptotic cells are phagocytosed by interspersed benign macrophages. The phagocytes haveabundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic starry sky pattern. Burkitt lymphoma is very aggressive but responds well to intensive chemotherapy. The image below shows the starry sky appearance seen in Burkitt's lymphoma.
subject: Pathology

question: An electron microscopic picture of a cut section of a nerve fiber is given. Identify the areawhich will be affected in the most common variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
explanation: The most common variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome is acute inflammatory demyelinatingpolyneuropathy (AIDP). The area affected in this condition is the myelin sheath (marked as 2 inthe image). 2058 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disease that causes fulminantpolyradiculoneuropathy. It is a T-cell mediated immune response. GBS is usually associated with a history of upper respiratory infection (URI) or acutegastroenteritis (AGE) 1-3 weeks prior. The causative organisms may be Campylobacter jejuni,cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. It presents with the following features: • Ascending motor paralysis (lower limbs > upper limbs) • Sensory deficits may or may not be seen • Deep tendon reflexes - absent • Transient bladder dysfunction - severe cases • Autonomic manifestations - loss of vasomotor control, postural hypotension, cardiacdysrhythmias Histological examination shows inflammation of peripheral nerves, manifested as perivenular andendoneurial infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and a few plasma cells. On electronmicroscopy, an early effect on myelin sheaths is seen. There is segmental demyelination inducedby the actions of activated macrophages. There are several types of Guillain–Barre syndrome: • Demyelinating • Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) - most common • Axonal • Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) • Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN) • Regional GBS syndromes: Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS) 2059
subject: Pathology

question: A 70-year-old patient presented with cough, fatiguability, and weight loss. He was diagnosedwith squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) on bronchoscopy. The resected specimen had a hilarlymph node that was 1cm in size and showed a black pigment. What is the black pigmentlikely to be?
explanation: The black-colored pigment in the hilar lymph node of the resected bronchoscopic specimen islikely to be an anthracotic pigment. The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles. The inhaled carbon particles areengulfed by the lung macrophages and then transported to the hilar lymph nodes.This accumulates and causes the blackening of the lung tissues or anthracosis. It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution withcarbon particles, such as coal mines. It is also the most common exogenous pigment found in thehuman body as a result of air pollution in urban areas. The aggregates of the carbon dust mayinduce fibroblastic reaction or emphysema that may lead to a condition called coal worker'spneumoconiosis. The following image shows anthracosis with deposition of black carbon particles, within thecytoplasm of macrophages. 2065 Option B: Melanin is brown-black in color which occurs as a result of oxidation of tyrosine inmelanocytes, as shown in the following histopathology of a lymph node. 2066 Option C: Lipochrome or lipofuscin (brown lipid) is seen as a yellow-brown pigment inhistopathological sections of the liver and heart of normal aging patients, patients with severemalnutrition, and cancer cachexia. It is derived through lipid peroxidation and indicates freeradical injury and lipid peroxidation. The following image shows a cardiac myocyte with fineyellow-brown lipofuscin granules in the perinuclear region. 2067 Option D: Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment seen in conditionsassociated with iron overload such as hemochromatosis. The following image shows extensiveintra-alveolar hemosiderin deposition following pulmonary hemorrhage.
subject: Pathology

question: A 34-year-old female patient presented to the outpatient department with migratory arthritisand examination revealed a pan-systolic murmur. An echocardiography was performed whichwas suggestive of mitral regurgitation. A biopsy specimen was obtained and the image isprovided below. What is the most likely lesion shown in the histopathology slide?
explanation: The given clinical findings of migratory arthritis, pan-systolic murmur, and mitral regurgitationare suggestive of acute rheumatic fever. The most likely lesion shown in the histopathological slideis Aschoff's bodies. Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They arecomposed of foci of T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump-activated macrophagescalled Anitschkow cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoidnuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence they are also 2068 called caterpillar cells. During acute rheumatic fever, Aschoff bodies may be found in any of the three layers of the heartthat results in pericarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis. Fibrinoid necrosis can occur due to inflammation of the endocardium and the left-sided valves.Over these areas of necrosis, small vegetations can be seen along the lines of closure, calledverrucae. Irregular thickenings called MacCallum plaques can be present In the subendocardium. In chronic RHD, the mitral valve shows leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening,and thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords. Calcification and fibrous bridging of the valvecan lead to narrowing the mitral orifice and giving it a fish mouth appearance.
subject: Pathology

question: A 30-year-old male complained of fatigue for the past 1 year. Examination revealed massivesplenomegaly. His blood workup shows the following findings. Which of the following is themost sensitive investigation in this case?
explanation: The clinical presentation with fatigue, splenomegaly, and the peripheral blood smear findings aresuggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML). The BCR-ABL gene which is specific for CMLis detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization(FISH) or polymerase chain reaction(PCR) basedtests. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence inthe fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CMLfrom other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH)or polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Clinical features: Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism, fatigability, weakness, weight loss, and anorexia.Dragging sensation in the abdomen caused by splenomegaly, or the acute onset of left upperquadrant pain due to splenic infarction. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result ofextensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mildhepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy. 2069 Peripheral blood: • Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consistspredominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, andbasophils. • Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells. • Platelet count is usually increased Bone Synopsis: • Markedly hypercellular Synopsis because of massively increased numbers of maturinggranulocytic precursors. There is usually an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils. • There is also an increase in megakaryocytes and usually include small, dysplastic forms anderythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers. Typically there is anincreased reticulin deposition, but overt Synopsis fibrosis is rare early in the course. • Sea-blue histiocytes - These are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled,green-bluecytoplasm. Other options: Immunophenotyping and flow cytometry: Flow cytometry refers to the measurement of cellularantigens as they flow in a fluid stream. Immunophenotyping is employed using labeled antibodiesagainst specific epitopes of cellular antigens. The technique that is usually used inimmunophenotyping is flow cytometry. It has a limited role in the diagnosis of CML. It is mainlyused in identifying CML blast transformation. LAP score: Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase(LAP) score is decreased in cases of CML. It is onlya first-line test in the diagnosis of CML and the diagnosis needs to be confirmed by other testsincluding bone Synopsis biopsy, molecular diagnostics, and cytogenetic analysis.

question: A girl presents with short stature, webbed neck, thick calves, shield-shaped chest, swelling ofthe ankle, and increased carrying angle. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical presentation of short stature, webbed neck, thick calves, shield-shaped chest, swellingof the ankle, and increased carrying angle is suggestive of Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome occurs due to complete or partial monosomy of X-chromosomes. It produceshypogonadism in phenotypic females. It is the most common sex chromosome abnormality infemales. Important features associated with Turner's syndrome: • Short stature • Webbing of neck • Broad chest and widely spaced nipples • Cubitus valgus • Streak ovaries, infertility, amenorrhea • Peripheral lymphedema at birth 2070 • Low posterior hairline • Poor breast development • Pigmented nevi • Cardiac manifestations – Coarctation of aorta, bicuspid aortic valve • Horse shoe kidney Image showing the features of Turner syndrome Other options: Option B: Important features associated with Down’s syndrome (Trisomy 21) include • Intellectual disability • Congenital heart defects • Epicanthic folds and flat facial profile • Simian crease • Umbilical hernias • Predisposition to leukemia Option C: Important features associated with Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13): • Microphthalmia • Microcephaly and intellectual disability • Cleft lip and palate • Rocker-bottom feet • Cardiac and renal defects Option D: Important features associated with Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18): • Prominent occiput, micrognathia, low set ears 2071 • Intellectual disability • Renal and cardiac malformations • Limited hip abduction, rocker-bottom feet

question: A patient with occupational exposure to benzene presents with repeated infections, easyfatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature. This occupational exposure willpredispose him to which of the following cancers?
explanation: Occupational exposure to benzene predisposes to leukemia. The given clinical history of repeatedinfections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature with benzene exposurepoints towards a diagnosis of leukemia. Benzene is oxidized to an epoxide through hepatic CYP2E1. The epoxide and other metabolitesdisrupt progenitor cell differentiation in the bone Synopsis and lead to Synopsis aplasia and acutemyeloid leukemia. Acute myeloid leukemia is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenicmutations that impede differentiation. This leads to the accumulation of immature myeloid blastsin the Synopsis. The replacement of the Synopsis with blasts produces Synopsis failureand complications related to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. Other options: Option B: Exposure to arsenic and its compounds, asbestos, beryllium and its compounds,chromium compounds, nickel compounds, radon, and its decay products can cause lung cancer. Option C: Exposure to aryl amines, particularly 2-naphthylamine and related compounds,cyclophosphamide, cigarette smoking, irradiation can cause bladder cancer. Option D: Exposure to UV rays, arsenic, and its compounds can cause skin cancer.

question: In iron deficiency anemia, all of the following is increased except
explanation: Transferrin saturation is decreased in iron deficiency anemia. Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise capacity. Cheilosis (fissures atthe corners of the mouth) and koilonychia (spooning of the fingernails) are signs of advancedtissue iron deficiency. Laboratory findings are: • Reduced hemoglobin and hematocrit values. • hypochromia, microcytosis, and poikilocytosis. • serum iron and ferritin levels are low. • The total plasma iron-binding capacity that reflects the elevated transferrin levels is high. • Low serum iron with increased iron-binding capacity results in a reduction of transferrinsaturation to below 15%. • RBC protoporphyrin levels are increased. Protoporphyrin is an intermediate in the hemesynthesis pathway. Under conditions in which heme synthesis is impaired, protoporphyrin 2072 accumulates within the red cell. • Bone Synopsis reveals a mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. The absence ofstainable iron in macrophages is a diagnostically significant finding. Peripheral smear of microcytic hypochromic anemia:

question: Which of the following is a poor prognostic marker of multiple myeloma?
explanation: β-2 microglobulin is a poor prognostic marker of multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm commonly associated with lytic bone lesions,hypercalcemia, renal failure, and acquired immune abnormalities. Poor prognostic factors for multiple myeloma: • Serum β2-microglobulin. It is the single most powerful predictor 2073 • Deletion of 17pITP53 sequences and the translocations t(14;16) and t(14;20) • Polyclonal serum Immunoglobulins • Elevated lactate dehydrogenase • High C-reactive protein • Increased plasma cell proliferative activity • High degree of bone Synopsis replacement • Presence of plasmablastic morphology • Elevated serum soluble receptor for IL6 Multiple myeloma usually presents as destructive plasma cell tumors involving the axial skeleton.The bones most commonly affected in descending order of frequency are the vertebral column,ribs, skull, pelvis, femur, clavicle, and scapula. Radiographically, bone lesions appear as punched-out defects, usually 1 to 4 cm in diameter,and consist of soft, gelatinous, red tumor masses. Radiograph of the skull showing punched out lesions: Morphology: • Malignant plasma cells have a perinuclear clearing due to a prominent golgi apparatus and aneccentrically placed nucleus. • Relatively normal-appearing plasma cells, plasmablasts with vesicular nuclear chromatin and aprominent single nucleolus, or bizarre, multinucleated cells may predominate. • Other cytologic variants include flame cells, Mott cells. • Flame cells have fiery red cytoplasm, Mott cells contain multiple grapelike cytoplasmicdroplets, a variety of other inclusions, including fibrils, crystalline rods, and globules. Theglobular inclusions are referred to as Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear). • Rouleaux formation is characteristic but not specific. High levels of M protein in the bloodcauses red cells to stick to one another in linear arrays in smears leading to rouleaux formation. 2074 Image showing Mott cell: Image showing Russell and Dutcher bodies: Peripheral smear of multiple myeloma: 2075 Bence Jones proteins are excreted in the kidney and causes myeloma kidney. Most myelomas areassociated with more than 3 g/dL of serum Ig and/or more than 6 mg/dL of urine Bence Jonesprotein. The most common monoclonal Immunoglobulin (M protein) is IgG followed by IgA. The clinicopathologic diagnosis of multiple myeloma can be done based on the identification ofclonal plasma cells in the Synopsis and the presence of CRAB criteria (hypercalcemia,renal dysfunction, anemia, and bone lesions).

question: A pap smear taken from a patient revealed hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear borders,and low maturation index involving the whole thickness but did not breach the basementmembrane. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: The hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear borders, and intact basement membrane are allsuggestive of dysplasia. Dysplasia is characterized by the loss in the uniformity of the individual cells and theirarchitectural orientation. The features of dysplasia include: • Pleomorphism • Hyperchromatic nuclei • High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio • Increased mitotic figures When the dysplastic changes involve the entire thickness of the epithelium without breaching thebasement membrane it is considered preinvasive and is termed carcinoma-in-situ. If the tumorinvades the basement membrane it is said to be invasive. Dysplasia can be considered as a precursor to malignant but it does not always progress to cancer.Dysplasia usually occurs in the metaplastic epithelium but all metaplastic epithelium is notdysplastic. Other options: 2076 Metaplasia: It refers to the replacement of one cell type with another type. It is almost alwaysassociated with tissue damage, repair, and regeneration. The most common epithelial metaplasiais columnar to squamous. Carcinoma: In carcinoma, there is the invasion of the basement membrane. Hyperplasia: It refers to the increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ. It can bephysiologic or pathological. Enlargement of the female breast during pregnancy is physiologichyperplasia. Endometrial hyperplasia is an example of pathological hyperplasia.

question: The mother of a 12-year-old girl was worried that her daughter is shorter when comparedwith her classmates. On examination, the child had a webbed neck, low hairline, and shieldchest. A provisional diagnosis of Turner's syndrome was made. Which of the following is alikely finding to be seen in this patient?
explanation: The likely finding seen in a patient with Turner syndrome is bilateral small streak ovaries. Turner syndrome results from complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome. It ischaracterized by hypogonadism in phenotypic females. It is the most common sex chromosomeabnormality in females. Three types of karyotypic abnormalities are seen • Missing an entire X chromosome - this results in a 45X karyotype. • Structural abnormalities of the X chromosomes - isochromosome of the long arm and loss of theshort arm, 46X,i(X)(q10), deletion of portions of both long and short arms that lead tothe formation of a ring chromosome, 46X,r(X), deletion of portions of the short or long arm,46X,del(Xq) or 46X,del(Xp). • Mosaics - they will have 45X along with one or more karyotypically normal or abnormal celltypes. Examples are 45X/46XX, 45X/46XY, 45X/47XXX, 45X/46X,i(X)(q10). Important features associated with Turner's syndrome: • Short stature • Webbing of neck • Broad chest and widely spaced nipples • Cubitus valgus • Streak ovaries • Infertility, amenorrhea • Peripheral lymphedema at birth • Low posterior hairline • Broad chest and widely spaced nipples • Pigmented nevi • Coarctation of aorta There is failure to develop normal secondary sex characteristics at puberty. The genitaliaremain infantile, breast development is inadequate, and there is little pubic hair. Short statureand amenorrhea are of particular importance in establishing the diagnosis in an adult. Other options: 2077 Aortic dissection, subluxation of lens, and mitral valve prolapse are seen in Marfan syndrome.

question: An 18-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with gum bleeding and fever forthe past 2 months. General examination showed pallor and the systemic examination wasunremarkable. Laboratory examination revealed Hb level- 3 gm/dl, TLC- 1500/microL,platelet count- 15000/microL. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and the reticulocyte countis 0.5. Bone Synopsis examination revealed fatty streaks and absent megakaryocytes but noimmature cells. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: The given clinical scenario showing a young male with gum bleeding, fever, pancytopenia, and alow reticulocyte count with bone Synopsis showing fatty streaks and no immature cells issuggestive of idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia. Aplastic anemia is a syndrome characterized by chronic hematopoietic failure and pancytopenia.The common causes include: • Acquired • Idiopathic (most common cause, about 65% of the cases) • Acquired stem-cell defects • Immune-mediated • Chemical agents • Dose-related (alkylating agents, antimetabolites, benzene, chloramphenicol, inorganic arsenals) • Idiosyncratic (chloramphenicol, phenylbutazone, organic arsenicals, carbamazepine,penicillamine, gold salts) • Physical agents • Whole-body irradiation • Viral infections (hepatitis, Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Varicella-Zoster virus) • Inherited • Fanconi anemia • Telomerase defects 2078 Pathogenesis involves an extrinsic immune-mediated suppression of bone Synopsis and anintrinsic abnormality of the stem cells. Clinical features and diagnosis: There is no age or sex predisposition for aplastic anemia. It presents insidiously with features ofpancytopenia such as pallor, petechiae, and ecchymosis. Recurrent infections and fever occur as aresult of neutropenia. Reticulocytopenia is seen and splenomegaly is characteristically absent.Bone Synopsis biopsy is used for diagnosis. Histology: Bone Synopsis aspirate usually results in a dry tap. Examination shows a hypocellular Synopsisdevoid of hematopoietic cells with remnant fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes.Red cells are usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic. The following image shows ahypocellular bone Synopsis with little hematopoiesis and several fat cells. Other options: Option B - Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired disorder resulting fromthe mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), anenzyme that is essential for the synthesis of membrane-associated complement regulatoryproteins. Red cells deficient in these proteins are susceptible to intravascular hemolysis. Patientswith PNH usually present with pancytopenia and reticulocytosis with bone Synopsis biopsyshowing a cellular Synopsis with marked to massive erythroid hyperplasia. Option C - Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of clonal stem cell disorders. It is aconsequence of maturation defects that result in ineffective hematopoiesis with a highpredisposition to conversion to AML. They are characterized by a hypercellular Synopsis withdysplastic cells on bone Synopsis aspirate. Synopsis changes seen in MDS are given in the pearlbelow. Option D - Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and patientsoften present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, malaise, loss ofappetite, and weight loss. 2079

question: A child is presenting with palpable blanching purpura, abdominal pain, and pain in the kneejoint resulting from arthritis. Urine examination showed hematuria and proteinuria. What isthe most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical presentation and the investigations are suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a systemic immune disorder characterized by a purpuric rash,abdominal pain, polyarthralgia, and renal abnormalities. It is most commonly seen in the agegroup of 3-8 years. The patient may present with the following clinical features: • Skin lesions- characteristically involve the extensor surfaces of arms and legs, and also thebuttocks • Abdominal manifestations- include pain, vomiting, and intestinal bleeding. • Renal manifestations- include gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic syndrome, or nephroticsyndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in adults. A rapidly progressive form ofglomerulonephritis is seen in some cases. This condition usually occurs following an upper respiratory tract infection and there is a historyof atopy in one-third of the cases. IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distributionsimilar to that of IgA nephropathy. Microscopic findings: • IgA deposition in the mesangial region. Sometimes there is the deposition of IgG and C3 alongwith IgA. • Renal lesions show focal or diffuse mesangial proliferation, and/or endocapillary proliferation tocrescentic glomerulonephritis. • Skin lesions show subepidermal hemorrhages and necrotizing vasculitis of small vessels. Other options: Option A: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura(ITP): It occurs due to antibody-mediateddestruction of platelets. It can be acute or chronic. Acute ITP is usually self-limiting in nature.Cutaneous bleeding can be in the form of petechiae and ecchymoses. The patient can also havehematuria, melena, or excessive menstrual flow. Option B: Dengue: It is a viral illness caused by the dengue virus. The clinical manifestationsinclude fever, headache, musculoskeletal pain, and rash. The rash which is maculopapular innature begins on the trunk and then spreads centrifugally to the face and extremities. Option C: Churg- Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis): It ischaracterized by eosinophilic vasculitis of multiple organs. The features of this conditioninclude asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, paranasal sinusabnormality, and the presence of eosinophilic vasculitis.
subject: Pathology

question: A 54-year-old patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue, tiredness andcervical lymphadenopathy. The TLC and DLC were normal. No immature cells. A lymph nodebiopsy was performed which shows diffuse effacement of the lymph node architecture, cellswith an indented nucleus, prominent nucleolus, and are atypical. CD10 and BCL2 arepositive. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: The given clinical scenario showing fatigue, tiredness and cervical lymphadenopathy with CD10positive BCL2 positive cells is highly suggestive of follicular lymphoma. 2080 Follicular lymphoma presents at middle age with no sex predilection. The most commonpresenting symptom is painless generalized lymphadenopathy. A lymph node biopsy is adequatefor the diagnosis of follicular lymphoma. Immunophenotyping of the cells showing CD19, CD20,CD10, BCL2 positive, and CD5 negative is suggestive that the cells originate from the germinalcentre. The majority of follicular lymphomas have characteristic (14;18) translocation. This juxtaposes theIGH locus on chromosome 14 and the BCL2 locus on chromosome 18. This chromosomalrearrangement results in the overexpression of BCL2 protein, which is an inhibitor of apoptosisthat contributes to lymphoma cell survival. Histopathology: Lymph nodes exhibit a nodular or nodular and diffuse growth pattern. Two cell types arepredominantly present in varying proportions: • Centrocytes (small cleaved cells) - Small cells with a cleaved nucleus and scant cytoplasm • Centroblasts - Large cells with open nuclear chromatin, several nucleoli, and modest amounts ofcytoplasm In most cases, there is a majority of centrocytes. The peripheral blood smear shows lymphocytosis and bone Synopsis tap reveals paratrabecularlymphoid aggregates. The following image shows a lymph node biopsy in follicular lymphoma: Other options - Option B - Burkitt lymphoma is an aggressive type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). It is alsoknown as small non-cleaved-cell lymphoma and is characterized by the translocation andderegulation of the c-MYC gene on chromosome 8 to chromosome 14 or 22 - t(8:14) ort(8:22). Histopathology of the tumor reveals a starry sky appearance created by apoptotic cells andmacrophages containing clear cytoplasm. Option C - Mycosis fungoides is the most common type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Thehistological hallmark of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides type) is the presence 2081 of Pautrier microabscess. The presence of B-cell markers in the question rules out the differentialof mycosis fungoides. Option D - Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized bythe presence of chimeric BCR-ABL gene which is a result of a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11)translocation (Philadelphia chromosome). The presence of lymphadenopathy in the given scenariorules out the possibility of CML as it is a myeloid disorder.

question: A software engineer presents to the outpatient department with easy fatiguability. He gives ahistory of sitting in front of the computer for 12 - 14 hours. He consumes a lot of junk foodwith very less fruits and vegetables. Hb is 9gm/dl and MCV 120 fl. What is the most likelycause of this patient's anemia?
explanation: The given laboratory values showing anemia and increased MCV are suggestive of megaloblasticanemia. This could be due to cyanocobalamin deficiency or folic acid deficiency. The history ofinadequate intake of fruits and vegetables points towards folic acid deficiency. Dietary sources of Vit-B12 are animal products such as meat, fish, milk, and eggs. Dietary sourcesof folic acid are green vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, asparagus, and broccoli. Megaloblastic anemia can occur due to Vit-B12 or folic acid deficiency. Inadequate intake,intrinsic factor deficiency, pernicious anemia, gastrectomy, malabsorption, ilealresection, alcoholism, anticonvulsants, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, infancy, disseminatedcancer, markedly increased hematopoiesis, folic acid antagonists are some of the causes. Patient can present with anorexia, weight loss, diarrhea, constipation, glossitis, angularcheilosis, reversible melanin skin hyperpigmentation, paresthesias, muscle weakness, dementia,or psychotic disturbances. In megaloblastic anemia, DNA synthesis is impaired that leading to ineffective hematopoiesis anddistinctive morphologic changes. Peripheral blood examination shows oval macrocytes, usually with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis.MCV is usually >100 fL. The normal value of MCV is between 80-100 fL. Most macrocytes lackthe central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is notelevated. The reticulocyte count is low. Neutrophils are larger than normal and show nuclearhypersegmentation with five or more nuclear lobules. Synopsis is markedly hypercellular. Megaloblastic changes are seen at all stages of erythroiddevelopment. There is nuclear-to-cytoplasmic asynchrony, where nuclear maturation is slowerthan cytoplasmic maturation. Granulocytic precursors are seen in the form of giantmetamyelocytes and band forms. Megakaryocytes may be abnormally large with bizarre,multilobate nuclei. Peripheral blood smear showing hypersegmented neutrophil: 2082 Other options: Option A - In cyanocobalamin deficiency, MCV will be increased. But the dietary sourcesof cyanocobalamin are mainly of animal products. In the given clinical scenario thereis inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables. Hence, this is not the answer. Option C - In iron deficiency anemia, MCV will be decreased. Option D - In hereditary spherocytosis, MCV will be normal.
