question: A chronic alcoholic patient presented with increasing abdominal girth. On examination,shifting dullness was present and the liver span was less than 7cm. Histopathologicalexamination revealed the presence of intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in hepatocytes.What is the content of these inclusions?
explanation: The clinical scenario given here describes alcoholic hepatitis. In this condition, there areintracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions called Mallory Denk bodies and they containintermediate filaments. The liver undergoes inflammation and fibrosis in alcoholic hepatitis. This leads to injured andswollen hepatocytes with cleared-out cytoplasm and cytoskeletal damage. These hepatocytes arecalled ballooned hepatocytes. When the cytoskeletal damage is extensive, there is the formation ofMallory Denk/ Mallory hyaline bodies. These are remnants of partially degraded intermediatefilaments and are composed of keratin filaments. Cytoskeletal proteins include intermediate filaments, microfilaments (made up of actin - optionB), and microtubules (option - C). Intermediate filaments provide a flexible scaffold to organize cytoplasm and prevent externalforces from acting on the cell. They are of five types: • Keratin filaments (epithelial cells) • Neuro filaments (neurons) • Desmin filaments (muscles) • Vimentin filaments (connective tissues) 2083 • Glial filaments (glial cells) Fibronectin (option D) is an adhesive glycoprotein. Its presence in cervicovaginal secretions beforerupture of membranes is a possible marker for impending preterm labor. The given image shows intracytoplasmic eosinophilic Mallory bodies.
subject: Pathology

question: A 65-year-old female patient is diagnosed with pure red cell aplasia and a mediastinal mass.Which of the following can be the likely cause?
explanation: The most probable diagnosis for the clinical presentation of mediastinal mass with pure red cellaplasia is thymoma. Thymoma refers to the tumors of the thymic epithelial cells. Most of the thymic tumors occur inthe anterior mediastinum. Clinical features can be chest pain, dyspnea, cough, or superior venacava syndrome. It is associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia, orhypogammaglobulinemia. It is rarely associated with limbic encephalitis, hemolytic anemia,aplastic anemia, and other autoimmune conditions like Sjogren's syndrome. Pure red cell aplasia: It is a Synopsis disorder where the erythroid progenitors are only suppressed.The complete absence of red cell progenitors is seen in severe cases. Causes of pure red cell aplasia: It can be hereditary or acquired. Diamond-Blackfan anemia orcongenital pure red cell aplasia is the hereditary cause. Causes of acquired pure red cell aplasiaare given below: • Cancer • Thymoma • Lymphoid malignancies (eg. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, large granular lymphocytosis) • Paraneoplastic to solid tumors • Connective tissue disorders with immunologic abnormalities 2084 • Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis • Viruses • Persistent B19 parvovirus, hepatitis, adult T cell leukemia virus, Epstein-Barr virus • Drugs • Phenytoin, azathioprine, chloramphenicol, procainamide, isoniazid • Multiple endocrine gland insufficiency • Antibodies to erythropoietin • Idiopathic Other options: Option B: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma can cause pure red cell aplasia but it commonly presents asperipheral adenopathy rather than mediastinal mass. Options C and D: Germ cell tumors and bronchogenic carcinoma are not commonly known to beassociated with red cell aplasia. 2085
subject: Pathology

question: All of the following are seen in anemia of chronic disease except:
explanation: Low serum ferritin levels are not seen in anemia of chronic disease. Anemia of chronic disease is anemia resulting due to chronic diseases which produce systemicinflammation. During chronic inflammation, inflammatory mediators like interleukin - 6(IL-6)stimulate the production of hepcidin from the liver. Hepcidin is an acute phase reactant that 2107 inhibits ferroportin on macrophages and also decreases iron from stores to developing RBCprecursors. This results in decreased proliferation of erythroid progenitors due to impaired ironutilization. By decreasing available serum iron, the body defends itself from certain bacteria(Eg, Hemophilusinfluenza) that require iron for their pathogenicity. The lab findings seen in anemia of chronicdisease are: • Low serum iron • Decreased total iron-binding capacity • Abundant stored iron • Increased hepcidin levels • Increased serum ferritin The chronic illnesses associated with anemia of chronic disease can be grouped into threecategories: • Chronic microbial infections, such as osteomyelitis, bacterial endocarditis, and lung abscess • Chronic immune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis and regional enteritis • Neoplasms, such as carcinomas of the lung and breast and Hodgkin lymphoma Note: Hepcidin is the main regulator of iron absorption which is encoded by the HAMP gene andis defective in hemochromatosis. Given below is an image of iron absorption that shows ferroportin being inhibited by hepcidin atintestinal mucosal cells

question: Neurosecretory bodies are seen in all except
explanation: Neurosecretory bodies are not seen in adrenal cortical tumours. 2108 Most of the adrenocortical neoplasms are aldosterone-producing adenomas. Conn syndromeis primary hyperaldosteronism caused by a solitary aldosterone-secreting adenoma. The clinical features of hyperaldosteronism are secondary hypertension andvarious neuromuscular manifestations resulting from hypokalemia. Microscopically, aldosterone-producing adenomas are found to have eosinophilic, laminatedcytoplasmic inclusions, known as spironolactone bodies, found after treatment with theantihypertensive drug spironolactone. The image given below shows a microscopic image of spironolactone bodies found in adrenaladenomas Other options: Option A: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and they producecalcitonin. They are associated with a point mutation in the RET proto-oncogene and multipleendocrine neoplasias (MEN 2A and 2B). Microscopically, polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma areseen. Electron microscopy reveals neurosecretory granules within the cytoplasm. Option B: Pituitary adenoma may present with visual field abnormalities or pituitary apoplexy(acute haemorrhage into an adenoma). Prolactinoma is the most common type ofhyperfunctioning pituitary adenoma. Histologically, prolactinomas are composed of chromophobecells with cytoplasmic neurosecretory granules. Option C: Adrenal medullary pheochromocytomas are the most common paraganglioma.Extra-adrenal paragangliomas occur in the head and neck at carotid bodies. Microscopically,carotid body tumours contain nests (zellballen) of chief cells. Electron microscopy showswell-demarcated neurosecretory granules.

question: Identify the true statement/s regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney
explanation: True statements regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney are 1, 4. Clear cell carcinoma isthe most common sporadic renal cell cancer and cells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen 2109 and fat. Clear cell cancer arises from the proximal tubular epithelium and usually occurs as solitaryunilateral lesions. Most of the cases are sporadic, but can also occur either in familial forms or in associationwith von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. They are associated with the loss of sequence of the shortarm of chromosome 3. Those with VHL disease inherit a germline mutation of the VHL gene onchromosomal band 3p25 and lose the second allele by somatic mutation. The VHL protein causes the degradation of hypoxia-induced factors (HIFs), which aretranscription factors that contribute to carcinogenesis by stimulating the expression of vascularendothelial growth factor (VEGF) that helps drive tumour cell growth. Histologically, the tumour cells have a rounded or polygonal shape and abundant clear orgranular cytoplasm, which contains glycogen and lipids. Given below is the histopathological image of clear cell carcinoma. Cancerous cells produce various abnormal hormones resulting in paraneoplastic syndrome. Theseinclude polycythemia, hypercalcemia, cushing syndrome, amyloidosis and hypertension. The most common site of metastasis is the lungs and bones. Radical nephrectomy is the treatmentof choice. But T1a(size less than 4cm) tumours are treated by nephron-sparing surgery or partialnephrectomy to preserve renal function. Drugs that inhibit VEGF and tyrosine kinase inhibitorsare used as an adjunct therapy for metastatic disease.

question: The phenomenon of a differential effect of the same gene from different parents is called:
explanation: The phenomenon of a differential effect of the same gene from different parents is called genomicimprinting. Genomic imprinting refers to gene silencing/ inactivation. Here either the maternal or thepaternal allele is inactivated resulting in only one functional allele. It occurs by the process of 2110 epigenetics, where gene expression is lowered by: • DNA methylation • Histone deacetylation Genomic imprinting is best illustrated by two uncommon genetic disorders: Prader-Willisyndrome and Angelman syndrome. The image given below is a child with Prader-Willi syndrome Prader-Willi syndromeAngelMan syndrome Deletion(most common)Paternal chromosome 15Maternal chromosome 15 Uniparental disomy(less common)Maternal disomy(duplication)Paternal disomy(duplication) Clinical featuresElevated ghrelin levels - hyperphagiaTruncal obesitySevere hypotoniaShort statureSmall hands and feet with hypotoniaHypogonadotropic hypogonadismCognitive impairment Short statureSeveremental retardationwith lack of speechStiff arm movementsSpastic, uncoordinated walk (ataxia)SeizuresInappropriate outbursts of laughter (happy puppets) The image given below is a child with Angelman syndrome: 2111 Diagnosis of these syndromes is based on the assessment of the methylation status of markergenes and fluorescence in-situ hybridisation(FISH). Other options: Option A: Gonadal mosaicism is a mutation that occurs only in egg or sperm cells and theindividual will be phenotypically normal. These individuals with gonadal mosaicism can transmitthe disease-causing mutation to the offspring through their mutated gametes. Option C: Anticipation refers to earlier onset of disease or increased severity in succeedinggenerations. This is seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington's disease. Option D: Incomplete penetrance refers to variations in penetrance and expressivity of clinicalfeatures. Not all individuals who inherit the mutant gene show a mutant phenotype. Mnemonic: Prader–Willi Syndrome: Paternal gene deletion - P for P Angelman syndrome: Maternal gene deletion (Mothers are Angels, Maternal gene deletion leadsto Angelman syndrome)

question: Blood transfusion requires screening of donor blood for all of the following infections except:
explanation: Blood transfusion does not requires screening of donor blood for dengue virus infection. Some of the transfusion transmitted infections routienly tested are: • Hepatitis C virus • Human immunodefeciency virus(HIV) • Hepatitis B virus Transfusion-transmitted disease not currently, routinely tested are: 2112 • Hepatitis A virus • Hepatitis E virus • Parvovirus B19 • Dengue fever virus • Malaria • Zika virus

question: Match the microscopic appearance in column A with the type of tumor in column B
explanation: The correctly matched option of the microscopic appearance with the type of tumor is 1-c, 2-d,3-a, 4-b. • Schiller Duval bodies - Yolk sac tumor • Presence of teeth, hair, etc - Teratoma • Signet ring cells - Kruckenberg tumor • Call-Exner bodies - Granulosa cell tumor Schiller Duval bodies are seen in yolk sac tumors. A yolk sac tumor/endodermal sinus tumor is anaggressive malignant germ cell tumor of the ovaries. Most of the yolk sac tumorshave Schiller-Duval bodies and they are pathognomonic. These are glomerulus-like structuresconsisting of a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a space that is also lined by tumorcells. The image given below shows Schiller-Duval bodies seen in yolk sac tumors. Presence of hair, teeth, etc is seen in teratomas. These are germ cell tumors. Theycontain embryonic tissues leading to the differentiation of cells along these pathways. Apartfrom teeth, hair may also contain skin, sebaceous glands, fat, bone, cartilage, etc. 2113 There are three classes of teratomas: • Mature teratomas (eg - dermoid cyst) • Immature teratomas (eg - solid teratoma) • Monodermal highly specialized tumors (eg - Struma ovarii) Given below is the histopathological image of immature teratoma of the ovary, with immaturetissue of the bone (asterisk), cartilage (arrow), and islands of adipose tissue (arrowhead) Signet-ring cells are seen in the Krukenberg tumor. Krukenberg tumor is the carcinoma of thestomach that metastasize to the ovary. Signet ring cells are mucin-producing cells. Theappearance of a signet ring often originates from the gastric mucosa. The image below shows signet-ring cells in the Kruckenberg tumor. Option D: Granulosa cell tumours arise from granulosa cells which form part of the developingovarian follicle. They are unilateral in nature and the mass is cystic and encapsulated. Call-Exner 2114 bodies are seen in granulosa cell tumors. These are gland like small structures with acidophilicmaterial and immature follicles. The image given below shows Call-Exner bodies seen in granulosa cell tumours.

question: A patient suffering from cholelithiasis underwent cholecystectomy. The image of thespecimen is shown below. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis?
explanation: The correct diagnosis in the patient is gallbladder polyp. Gallbladder polyp is a pre-malignant condition that usually presents with biliary colic andcholecystitis. Cholesterol polyps are more common while adenomatous polyps have malignantpotential. Risk factors of malignancy in adenomatous polyp: • Age >60 years • Coexistence of gall stones • The documented increase in size • Size of >10 mm. Polyps less than 1 cm can be followed with serial ultrasonography. The USG given below depictsgallbladder polyps that are fixed and do not cast any acoustic shadow. The polyps larger than 1cm have an increased risk of malignancy and should be treated by performing an opencholecystectomy. 2115 The image below shows an intraoperative photograph of gallbladder polyps. The image given below shows the management of gall bladder polyp 2116 Other options: Options A and D: Cholesterosis or strawberry gallbladder is a condition characterized by acollection of submucous aggregations of cholesterol crystals and cholesterol esters in thegallbladder. The interior of the gallbladder looks like a strawberry with yellow specks. The image given below shows the gross appearance of cholesterosis of the gallbladder Option C: Gallbladder adenocarcinoma is the most common malignancy of the extrahepatic biliarytract. Gallstones are the most important risk factor. Her-2/neu is overexpressed and CA 19-9 isused for monitoring. The most important prognostic factor is the depth of invasion (T-stage). Ongross appearance, they resemble chronic cholecystitis.
subject: Pathology

question: A 15-year-old boy presents with swelling in the upper diaphyseal part of the tibia. X-ray of theswelling showed a periosteal reaction. A histopathological image of the biopsy is given below.Immunohistochemistry was positive for synaptophysin and mic 2. What is the likelydiagnosis?
explanation: 2117 The given clinical scenario along with the image showing small round blue cellsand immunohistochemistry (IHC) positive for synaptophysin and mic-2 point to a likely diagnosisof Ewing sarcoma. Ewing sarcoma is the 2nd most common bone sarcoma in children. The majority of the patientsaffected are usually <20 years of age. It has a slight male predominance. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerusand flat bones of the pelvis. The majority of Ewing sarcomas have a balanced translocationbetween the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 and the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11. Patients present with painful enlarging mass, fever, and anemia. The affected area is usuallytender, swollen, and warm. Laboratory findings may show an elevated WBC count and erythrocytesedimentation rate (ESR). A histopathological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows sheets of uniform, round cells arrangedin Homer-Wright rosettes. These cells are of neuroectodermal origin and have minimal cytoplasmand abundant glycogen. When they are arranged around a central fibrillary core in the form ofclusters, the appearance is termed Homer-Wright rosettes. Immunohistochemistry isusually positive for synaptophysin and mic-2. Given below is the histopathological appearance of Ewing sarcoma. As tumor cells are rich in glycogen, they stain positive for periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stainhowever, they stain negatively for reticulin. The image given below shows PAS staining done in Ewing's sarcoma: 2118 Radiological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows a destructive lesion in the diaphysis of longbones. Deposition of periosteal reaction in layers gives an onion-peel appearance (shown below). Other options: Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignancy of bone. The histologicalfeatures of osteosarcoma include pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundantmitoses. The diagnosis is definitive with the presence of malignant tumor cells producingunmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone arranged in a typically fine, lacelike pattern. Given below is the histopathological image of osteosarcoma: 2119 X-ray shows periosteal reaction and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have asunray appearance as shown below. Option C: Neuroblastoma is a tumor of the sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. It is derivedfrom primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood.On histopathology small round blue cells are seen. These cells are concentrically arranged arounda faintly eosinophilic fibrillary material (neuropil). This appearance is called Homer-Wrightpseudorosettes (shown below). 2120 Option D: Osteoclastoma is also known as a giant cell tumour. The tumor cells are primitiveosteoblast precursors and express high levels of RANKL. Histologically, the tumors consist ofosteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei. These cells are usually present against abackdrop of mononuclear stromal cells. The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of giant celltumour/osteoclastoma: The image below shows an X-ray of a giant cell tumour showing the typical soap bubbleappearance. 2121
subject: Pathology

question: Which of the following is a marker of natural killer cell?
explanation: The marker of the natural killer cells is CD94. It is expressed in natural killer cells and a smallsubset of T lymphocytes. Natural killer cells (NK cells) are essential cells of innate immunity. They act against malignantand virus-infected cells. NK cells are identified by CD16 and CD56 cell surface receptors. NK cells' activity is augmented by interferons and upon activation, they bind to glycoproteinreceptors on the surface of target cells and release perforins. Perforins create pores in themembrane of the target cells. Through these pores, cytotoxic factors like tumor necrosisfactor-beta (TNF-β) enter the cells and destroy them by apoptosis. NK cells express a phenomenon known as antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). Here,NK cells have the capability of killing target cells that are coated by IgG antibodies. The image given below shows the actions of NK cells on cancer cells. 2122 Other options: Option A: CD68 is expressed on macrophages and monocytes. Option B: CD 3 is a T-cell receptor marker. They are involved in the transduction of signals to theT cells when an antigen binds to the T cell receptor. Option C: CD 25 is a component of the IL2 receptor and is important in T cell proliferation andactivation.
subject: Pathology

question: Which of the following conditions is not caused by high-risk strains of humanpapillomavirus?
explanation: Laryngeal papillomatosis is not caused by high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV). It iscaused by low-risk HPV strains 6 and 11. Laryngeal papillomatosis or juvenile papillomatosis is the most common benign neoplasm ofthe larynx in children. It is caused by HPV 6 and 11. It involves supraglottic and glottic regions ofthe larynx. Adult-onset laryngeal papillomatosis involves the anterior part of the vocal cords. It usually occurs between the ages 3–5 years, but less commonly can also occur in men agedbetween 30-50 years. Clinical features include hoarseness or aphonia and respiratorydifficulty. The recurrence rate is high but they rarely transform to SCC. Diagnosis is confirmed by direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Treatment consists of microlaryngoscopy, CO2 laser excision, and topical cidofovir. The image given below shows laryngeal papilloma. 2123 Other options: Cervical cancer, anal cancer and oropharyngeal cancers are caused by high risk HPV types 16 and18.
subject: Pathology

question: A boy presents with recurrent episodes of melena. On examination, there was eczema of theskin with multiple petechiae. His platelet count was low but RBC and WBC counts werewithin normal limits. Which of the following is the diagnostic investigation in this patient?
explanation: The given scenario of recurrent episodes of melena, eczema, and multiple petechiae along withlow platelet counts is suggestive of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. The diagnostic investigation in thispatient is WASP gene mutation testing. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome(WAS) is an X-linked recessive immunodeficiency disorder. It is causedby mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) that primarily affects the Tlymphocytes. Normally, WASp regulates the actin cytoskeleton and thus helps in cell adhesion, migration, andthe formation of synapses between antigen-presenting and target cells. In WAS, there is aprogressive loss of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood resulting in defects in cellularimmunity. The clinical features of WAS are recurrent bacterial infections, eczema, and bleeding dueto thrombocytopenia. Patients with WAS are prone to develop B-cell lymphomas and autoimmunedisorders. The image given below shows eczema seen in WAS 2124 Diagnosis is based on intracellular immunofluorescence analysis of WAS protein (WASp)expression in blood cells. IgM levels in the serum are low, but levels of IgG are usually normal.Reduced-sized platelet is a typical feature of WAS. The only curative treatment is an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Prophylacticantibiotics, immunoglobulin G (IgG) supplementation, and topical treatment for eczema can betried. Gene therapy trials are also under research.
subject: Pathology

question: Which of the following is not a part of innate immunity?
explanation: B lymphocytes are not a part of innate immunity. B lymphocytes are part of adaptive immunity. Innate immunity is an intrinsic mechanism that provides the first line of defence againstinfections. It is non-specific, provides immediate defence against microbes, and helps eliminatedamaged cells. Components of Innate Immunity are: • Epithelial cells - these produce antimicrobial molecules such as alpha-defensins • Macrophages and neutrophils • Dendritic cells - these have receptors that sense microbes and cell damage. They stimulatesecretion of cytokines, which play important role in inflammation and antiviral defence • Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) - these are local tissue lymphocytes that lack T-cell antigenreceptors. They produce inflammatory cytokines during the early phases of immunereactions. Gamma delta T lymphocytes and natural killer (NK) cells belong to this class • Mast cells • Complement pathway - it include complement proteins of alternative and lectin pathways. 2125
subject: Pathology

question: Which of the following disorders is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern?
explanation: Rett syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern. Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder. It is caused due to mutation in the MECP-2gene. The disorder is mostly seen in girls because affected boys usually die in infancy due to adefective single X chromosome. Symptoms of Rett syndrome are microcephaly, developmental delay, autistic-like behavior,cognitive dysfunction, seizures, and repetitive motor actions. Other options: Option B: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is inherited in X linked recessive pattern. Itoccurs due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Typical features include calf musclepseudohypertrophy and Gower's sign (using arms to lift themselves from a seated position).Laboratory investigations show elevated serum creatine kinase levels. Casimersen has beenrecently approved by the FDA for the treatment of DMD. Option C: Huntington's disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is a trinucleotide(CAG) repeat disorder and shows genetic anticipation (earlier onset of disease or increasedseverity in succeeding generations). Patients present with involuntary movements known aschorea. Tetrabenazine is used for treatment. Option D: Tuberous sclerosis also known as Bournville disease is inherited in an autosomaldominant pattern. It occurs due to mutation in TSC1 and TSC2 genes. It is characterized bysubependymal nodules, angiomyolipomas, cafe au lait spots, shagreen patches, and cardiacrhabdomyomas.
subject: Pathology

question: Cell in cell appearance is seen in:
explanation: Cell in cell appearance is seen in entosis. Entosis is a phenomenon where a cell engulfs a cell of the same type. While cells that areinternalised by this mechanism are initially viable. But, the majority of them undergo anon-apoptotic form of cell death. It plays a physiological role in the elimination of cells detachedfrom a surface. Other options: Option A: Necrosis is a pathologic process of irreversible cell death following severe injury. It isassociated with local inflammation due to damaged cell membranes. Some microscopic features ofnecrosis are as follows: • Dilation of mitochondria • Nuclear changes: karyolysis, pyknosis, and karyorrhexis. • Myelin figures replacing dead cells. Option B: Apoptosis is a pathway of programmed cell death. In apoptosis, Mitochondrial anddeath receptor pathways activate caspases resulting in the formation of apoptotic bodies whichare then phagocytosed. 2126 Option C: Necroptosis is a type of cell death which is a hybrid of both necrosis and apoptosis. It isalso called programmed necrosis/caspase-independent programmed cell death(since it does notresult in caspase activation).
subject: Pathology

question: Identify the cell marked in the image below
explanation: The cell marked in the image is a mast cell stained with toluidine blue. Mast cell granules containacid proteoglycan that binds basic blue such as toluidine blue. Mast cells may be difficult to differentiate from lymphocytes in routine, hematoxylin, andeosin-stained sections, and special metachromatic stains (toluidine blue or Giemsa) are used tovisualize their granules. Mast cells are a part of innate immunity and are widely distributed in connective tissues. Theyplay an important role in immediate hypersensitivity and both acute and chronic inflammation. Mast cells express a receptor on their surface that binds to the Fc portion of the IgE antibody.When an antigen binds to IgE antibodies on the surface of the mast cell, they get activated anddegranulate. This results in the release of: • Granule contents: Histamine, chymase, tryptase, heparin. • Lipid mediators: Leucotriene C4, D4, prostaglandin D2, platelet-activating factor. • Cytokines: Tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1 These mediators released from mast cells play an important role in the pathogenesis ofimmediate/type 1 hypersensitivity. The image given below shows the sequence of events in immediate (type 1) hypersensitivity. Some of the important disorders associated with mast cell activity are bronchial asthma, urticaria,mastocytosis, interstitial cystitis and neurofibroma. 2127
subject: Pathology

question: Match the malignancies in column A with the genes in column B
explanation: The correctly matched option is option C 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, and 4-a. Pleomorphic adenoma is associated with chromosomal rearrangements that induceoverexpression of PLAG1. It is the most common salivary gland and lacrimal gland neoplasm.Microscopically, it contains a mixture of ductal (epithelial), myoepithelial, and mesenchymal cells. Burkitt's lymphoma is a non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). It is associated with thetranslocation cMYC gene on chromosome 8 to chromosome 14 or 22 - t(8:14) or t(8:22).Histopathology of the tumour reveals a starry sky appearance. Neuroblastoma is a tumour derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most commonextracranial solid tumour in childhood. They are associated with the translocation nMYC gene. Onhistopathology small round blue cells and Homer-Wright pseudorosettes are seen. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children. It is associatedwith chromosomal rearrangements of the Rb gene. Microscopillay, Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettesare seen. 1. Pleomorphic adenomad. Plag 1 2. Burkitt lymphomac. cMyc 3. Neuroblastomab. nMyc 4. Retinoblastomaa. Rb

question: How does phagolysosome cause cell death?

options.a: Is both intra and extra cellular
options.b: Can fuse with other organelles directly
options.c: Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome

explanation: Phagolysosomes cause cell death by the fusion of lysosomes to form autophagolysosomes. Autophagy is a process in which a cell eats its own contents. Cytoplasmic materials are deliveredand degraded by the lysosome. It is a survival technique of the cell in nutrient deprivation states. The steps are: • An isolation membrane called phagophore is formed and nucleated. • Phagophore is derived from the ER with the help of plasma membrane and mitochondria • A double membrane-bound vesicle is formed from the isolation membrane called theautophagosome • Maturation of the autophagosome by fusion with lysosomes, called autophagolysosome. Apoptosis is a regulated mechanism of eliminating unwanted and damaged cells. It is initiated byenzymes called caspases and is executed by two different pathways. The mitochondrialpathway which is also known as the intrinsic pathway carries out the majority of the apoptosis.The death receptor pathway or the extrinsic pathway is initiated by plasma membrane deathreceptors. Both these pathways combine together and activate the caspase cascade which results 2128 in the final phase of apoptosis. Pyroptosis is a form of apoptosis mediated by fever-inducing cytokine IL-1. A multiproteincomplex called inflammasome is activated when microorganisms enter the cell. It will in turnactivate caspase 1 which cleaves the IL-1 precursor and releases its biologically active form.
subject: Pathology

question: Which of the following features is not observed in pleomorphic adenoma?
explanation: Perineural invasion is not observed in pleomorphic adenoma. Perineural invasion is seen inmalignant salivary gland tumours like adenoid cystic carcinoma. Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary gland and lacrimal gland neoplasm. They arecommonly seen in the parotid. They are painless, slow-growing, mobile, discrete masses withinthe parotid. Histologically, pleomorphic adenoma consists of epithelial and mesenchymal components. • Epithelial components consist of • Ductal cells, myoepithelial cells organized as ducts, acini, irregular tubules, or sheets of cells • Squamous metaplasia with the formation of keratin pearls may be present • Mesenchymal components consist of • Loose myxoid and hyaline tissue containing cartilage (due to chondroid differentiation) and bone The image below shows pleomorphic adenoma of the salivary gland consisting of mixed epithelial(left) and mesenchymal cell components (right). Clinical features • Painless, slow-growing swelling • Lobulated, firm, elastic-to-hard in consistency • Lift the ear lobe 2129 • Free from deeper structures FNAC is the investigation of choice in diagnosing pleomorphic adenoma. Open biopsycontraindicated due to chances of injury to the facial nerve. Surgery is the mainstay of treatment by performing superficial parotidectomy.
subject: Pathology

question: A 60-year-old woman presents with complaints of fatigue and dyspnea for 2 weeks. Onexamination, pallor was seen and hemoglobin was found to be 6 gm/dL. What finding will beseen on peripheral smear?
explanation: Microcytic hypochromic cells will be seen on the peripheral smear. An elderly female presentingwith fatigue and dyspnea with severe anaemia is suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia(IDA). Theperipheral smear of IDA shows microcytic hypochromic red blood cells. Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional disorder in the world. IDA results from dietarydeficiency, impaired absorption, increased requirement and, chronic blood loss. The cause of irondeficiency anaemia in an older man or post-menopausal woman is always gastrointestinal canceruntil proven otherwise. Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, cheilosis (fissures at the corners of themouth) and koilonychia (spooning of the fingernails). Peripheral smear in IDA shows: • Microcytic hypochromic red blood cells with an enlarged zone of central one-third pallor. • Poikilocytes: pencil-shaped RBCs and, target cells. The image given below shows a microcytic hypochromic blood picture in a peripheral smear IDA is treated by giving oral, parenteral and packed cell transfusions depending on the severity ofanaemia. For oral iron replacement therapy, • Up to 200mg of elemental iron is given. 2130 • According to the Anemia Mukt Bharat initiative, adult women need to take 60 mg elemental iron+ 500 mcg folic acid tablets once a week. For parenteral iron therapy, the amount of iron needed by an individual is calculated by theformula: Body weight(kg) x 2.3 x (15 - patient's hemoglobin, g/dL) + 500 or 1000mg (for stores)
subject: Pathology

question: The image below is indicative of which of the following tumors?
explanation: The image shows the characteristic Schiller Duval body consistent with a yolk sac tumor. A yolk sac tumor/endodermal sinus tumor is an aggressive malignant germ cell tumor of theovaries. It originates from embryonal structures of the yolk sac by selective differentiation. It is most oftenly seen in children and young women. It usually presents as abdominaldistention and a palpable pelvic mass. Grossly, the yolk-sac tumor appears yellow, friable (hemorrhagic), and forms solid mass. Most of the yolk sac tumors have Schiller-Duval bodies and they are pathognomonic. These areglomerulus-like structures consisting of a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a spacethat is also lined by tumor cells. The image given below shows Schiller-Duval bodies seen in yolk sac tumors. Yolk-sac tumors are rich in alpha-fetoprotein. Therefore, serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein canserve as a reliable tumor marker in post treatment surveillance. Other options: Option B: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of seminoma. They are unilateral tumorscomposed of vesicular cells and clear cytoplasm. The tumor cells grow in cords or sheets that areseparated by scanty fibrous stroma. They are usually infiltrated by lymphocytes. 2131 Option C: Krukenberg tumor is the carcinoma of the stomach that metastasize to the ovary. It ischaracterized by mucin-producing signet ring cells. The appearance of a signet ring oftenoriginates from the gastric mucosa. The image below shows signet-ring cells in Kruckenberg tumor. Option D: Granulosa cell tumours arise from granulosa cells which form part of the developingovarian follicle. They are unilateral in nature and the mass is cystic and encapsulated. Call-Exnerbodies are seen in granulosa cell tumours. These are gland like small structures with acidophilicmaterial and immature follicles. The image given below shows Call-Exner bodies seen in granulosa cell tumours.

question: In a patient with bare lymphocytic disease, graft vs host reaction does not occur due to:

options.c: MHC class II deficiency on lymphocytes
options.d: MHC class I deficiency on lymphocytes

explanation: 2132 In a patient with bare lymphocytic disease, graft vs host reaction does not occur due to MHC classII deficiency on the lymphocytes. Bare lymphocyte disease occurs due to mutations in transcription factors required for class IIMHC gene expression. This results in the lack of class II MHC molecules, leading to the impaireddevelopment of CD4+ T cells. As these CD 4+ T cells are required for both for cellular immunityand for assisting B cells, class II MHC deficiency results in a combined immuno- deficiency.
subject: Pathology

question: A child presents with multiple skin lesions over the inner thigh and genital areas. It initiallystarted as macule and later developed to become nodules. Some nodules have centralumbilication. The histology of the lesion is shown below. What would be found on biopsy?
explanation: The given clinical scenario and histological image are diagnostic of molluscum contagiosumlesions, which show intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies, called Henderson–Patterson bodies ormolluscum bodies. Infection is usually spread by direct contact, particularly among children and young adults.Multiple lesions occur on the skin and mucous membranes, with a predilection for the trunk andanogenital areas. Individual lesions are firm, pruritic, pink to skin-colored umbilicated papules. Acurd-like material can be expressed from the central umbilication. Smearing this material onto a glass slide and Giemsa staining shows diagnostic molluscumbodies, which are ellipsoid, homogeneous, cytoplasmic inclusions that are found in the cells of thestratum granulosum and the stratum corneum and are up to 35 µm in size. 2133 Other options: Option A: Multinucleate giant cells (called Tzanck cells) are seen in herpes simplex virusinfections. They are formed when individual epidermal cells containing viral inclusions fuse toproduce giant cells. These can be demonstrated by the diagnostic Tzanck test, which is based onthe microscopic examination of the vesicle fluid. Option B: Donovan bodies are seen in donovanosis, caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovanbodies are minute, encapsulated coccobacilli in macrophages, which can be demonstrated inGiemsa-stained smears of the exudate. Option D: Koilocytes are characteristically seen in HPV infections, such as condylomataacuminata. Koilocytes are lining cells that have perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization.
subject: Pathology

question: Investigations of a patient being evaluated for leukemia revealed a WBC count of4,50,000/µL, with eosinophilia and basophilia. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation: A WBC count of 4,50,000/µL with eosinophilia and basophilia indicates a probable diagnosis ofchronic myelogenous leukemia. CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. It is caused by the translocation of ABL gene onchromosome 9 onto BCR gene on chromosome 22, resulting in the formation of the BCR-ABLfusion gene. This chromosomal abnomality, called Philadelphia chromosome, is characteristic ofCML. The resulting BCR-ABL translocation results in the activation of tyrosine kinase that signalspro-growth and pro-survival pathways like RAS and JAK/STAT pathways resulting in theproliferation of hematopoietic stem cells. Patients typically present with a dragging sensation abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenicinfarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. On peripheral smear there is leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000cells/mm3 (neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils),blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells, the platelet count is usually increased. 2134 Basophils and eosinophils are often increased. Other options: Option D: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a hematopoietic progenitor malignancy that causesimmature myeloblast accumulation in the bone Synopsis. Incidence increases with age and peaksafter 60 years of age. The WBC count is about 15,000/µL. Few cases have either <5000 or >1,00,000/µL WBCcount. Clinically, the patients present with symptoms resulting due to pancytopenia (anemia,neutropenia, thrombocytopenia). For acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML) diagnosis, the blast cellcount should be ≥20% in the peripheral blood or bone Synopsis Other distinctive features of AML include • Bone Synopsis/ peripheral smear shows a large, uniform population of cells (myeloblasts) withprominent nucleoli (yellow arrow). It shows the presence of primary cytoplasmic granules • Auer rods: needle-shaped azurophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by the fusion oflysosomes. (black arrow) • Multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell resembling a bundle of sticks known asfaggot cells (seen in peripheral smear). 2135 Option A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) arises from immature B (pre-B) or T (pre-T) cellscalled lymphoblasts. Most cases present with a reduced or normal lymphocyte count. Bloodcounts show anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. Immunohistochemistry for terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive in pre-B andpre-T lymphoblasts. Peripheral smear shows lymphoblasts that have condensed chromatin, lessconspicuous nucleoli, and smaller amounts of cytoplasm which lacks granules as shown below. Option C: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia presents with a mean WBC count of 30*109/L. It isassociated with the deletions of 13q, 11q, 17p, and trisomy 12q. Lymph nodes are diffusely effaced by small lymphocytes with proliferation centers. The imageshows small round lymphocytes and smudge cells seen in CLL. 2136
subject: Pathology

question: Which of the following molecules helps the leukocytes roll over the endothelial cells in thevessels?
explanation: E-selectin, which is present over the endothelium, helps the leukocyte roll over the endothelium. Selectins are of 3 types: L-selectin present on leukocytes, E-selectin present on the endothelium,and P-selectin present in platelets and on the endothelium. The weak rolling action slows down the leukocytes and allows them to bind more firmly to theendothelium with the help of integrins. The recruitment of leukocytes to the site of injury involves the following steps: • Lumen of the vessel to the endothelium: • Margination: Leukocytes assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface because ofthe stasis of blood flow. • Rolling: Leukocytes start rolling on the vessel wall because of signaling molecules from theendothelium. • Adhesion: Leukocytes are attached to the endothelium because of adhesion molecules that areactivated by cytokines. • Transmigration of the leukocytes across the vascular endothelium. • Migration towards a chemotactic stimulus in the extravascular tissues. Other options: Option A: Cadherins are a type of glycoprotein cell adhesion molecule that allows cells to adheretogether. Option B: Platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1), aids in diapedesis, which is themovement of leukocytes through intact endothelium of the capillaries to reach the site of injury. Option D: Cd11a, a molecule from the integrin family, helps firmly adhere the leukocyte to theendothelial cell. 2137
subject: Pathology

question: Identify the given bone Synopsis biopsy instrument.
explanation: The given instrument is a Klima needle. Klima and Salah's needles are reusable bone Synopsis aspiration & biopsy needles, both aremade of stainless steel. Klima needle has a guard that screws along the length of the needle. It hasno side screw. Whereas, Salah's needle has a guard situated 2 cm from the tip and has a sidescrew. The image below shows Klima needle. The image below shows Salah's needle. 2138 Islam and Jamshidi needles have a t-bar at the end for easier maneuvering. Jamshidi needle has atapering end to reduce the crush artefacts in the sample. Islam needle has a core securing device,i.e., its cutting edge is shaped to hold the core of the bone during the procedure. The image below shows the Jamshidi needle. The image below shows the Islam needle. 2139

question: Match the following stains and the tissue.
explanation: The correct match is 1- a, 2- b, 3- d, 4- c. Perl's Prussian blue stain is used in histopathological studies to detect the presence of iron in thespecimen. Iron is stained blue with this stain. It is used in hereditary hemochromatosis to stain liver tissue, which shows hepatocellular iron. Italso stains the iron-laden mitochondria of ring sideroblasts seen in lead toxicity andmyelodysplastic syndrome. The following image shows the blue staining of iron (in the form of hemosiderin) deposited inhepatocytes: 1. Prussian blue staina. Iron 2. PAS stainb. Glycogen 3. Congo red staind. Amyloid 4. Fite- Faraco stainc. Leprosy 2140 PAS stain (Periodic acid Schiff stain) is used for the detection of glycogen in tissues such as theliver, skeletal muscle, etc., and also in tumor cells. The image below shows intense PAS +ve staining of hepatocytes in glycogen storage disorder: The stain used for amyloid deposits is congo red staining, which imparts pink to red color to theamyloid under ordinary light and apple-green birefringence under polarized microscopy. The image shows a congo-red stained biopsy specimen with the following: (A) Focal positive staining (orange-red) of amorphous extracellular material (B) Apple-green birefringence under polarized light 2141 Fite-Faraco stain has been used in cases of leprosy for staining Mycobacterium leprae. It can alsobe used to stain Nocardia. The image below shows acid-fast bacilli inside foamy macrophages:

question: Which of the following statements are true about hereditary spherocytosis?

options.a: Gall stones develop by 4-5 years of age.
options.b: Splenectomy does not protect against developing gall stones.
options.c: At least 25 % cases have a family history of HS.
options.d: High MCH is pathognomonic of HS.

explanation: Among the given statements about hereditary spherocytosis, the true statement is option c– atleast 25% of cases have a familial inheritance (as 75% of cases show an autosomal dominantinheritance pattern) Hereditary spherocytosis is a type of hereditary hemolytic anemia that is mostly inherited in anautosomal dominant pattern. Some of the cases can be autosomal recessive orsporadic. Mutations of the red blood cell surface proteins spectrin and ankyrin can result in 2142 unstable cell membranes, leading to hemolysis. The following mutations have been identified in hereditary spherocytosis: Autosomal dominant (more common): • Ankyrin - most common • Band 3 • β-Spectrin Autosomal recessive: • α-Spectrin • Band 4.2 This disorder can present at a young age with severe jaundice and fatigue. The unconjugatedhyperbilirubinemia predisposes the patient to develop gallstones in early adulthood. Pigmentstones are found in 40-50% of the affected adults. Laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Theperipheral smear will show large spherical red blood cells without central pallor. MCHC (not, MCH) is increased in hereditary spherocytosis; however, it is not pathognomonic as itcould be found in other conditions as well. MCV is mildly decreased because of cellshrinkage. There is mild to moderate anemia, therefore, MCH could be slightly lower. The diagnosis can be confirmed by the acid glycerol lysis test and the eosin-5′-maleimide(EMA)–binding test. There is no specific treatment available besides splenectomy. Spleen is the major site wherespherocytes undergo hemolysis. Hence, splenectomy corrects the anemia and its associatedcomplications, thereby playing a role in preventing gallstones. It is done at 4–6 years of age insevere cases and after puberty in moderate cases. It should be followed up with the appropriateantibiotic and vaccine prophylaxis.

question: B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time due to which phenomenon?
explanation: B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time due to alternative RNA splicing. Alternative RNA splicing is the process by which different proteins are produced from the sameRNA transcript by splicing it in different ways. Mature circulating B cells initially express IgM and IgD antibodies on their surfaces before theyare stimulated to produce specific antibodies. The heavy chains in IgM and IgD are mu (µ)and delta (δ), respectively. The mu and delta genes for these heavy chains are located proximal tothe VDJ encoding regions (i.e., variable, diversity, and joining regions) of the heavy chain locus. Aprimary RNA transcript of this entire region is produced, which then undergoes alternative RNAprocessing, enabling the production of both transmembrane IgM and IgD on B cells. Other options: Options A and C: Somatic hypermutation is a cellular response by which the immune systemadapts to the new foreign elements that confront it. They do so by adding nucleotides in V gene 2143 regions of heavy and light chains, resulting in a better fit of antigen with the antibodies. Thishence increases the affinity of antibodies to antigens. Due to this, the subset of plasma cells withthese improved hypervariable regions are more strongly selected by the antigen and thereforeconstitute a larger part of the population of antibody-producing cells. This process is calledaffinity maturation. Option D: Allelic exclusion is the process by which a cell expresses one of the two alleles of thegene and excludes the other allele. B cells are diploid, therefore, each B cell has six gene segment pools related to antibody chains: • Two heavy-chain pools (one from each parent) and • Four light-chain pools (one κ and one λ from each parent). However, each B cell uses only two of the six gene segment pools: one out of the two heavy-chainpools (maternal and paternal) and one out of the four light-chain pools. Thus, each B cell mustchoose not only between its κ and λ light-chain pools but also between its maternal and paternallight-chain and heavy-chain pools. This process of choosing is by allelic exclusion.

question: Which of the following are true regarding sirtuins?
explanation: The true statements regarding sirtuins are 1, 2, 3, and 4 (option B). Sirtuins are a class of proteins that possess either mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase or deacetylaseactivity. They have been shown to slow down the aging process. Sirtuins promote the expression of several genes whose products increase longevity. These includeproteins that: • Inhibit metabolic activity • Reduce apoptosis • Stimulate protein folding • Inhibit the harmful effects of oxygen-free radicals • Increase insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism (maybe targeted for the treatment ofdiabetes) • Ensure that damaged DNA is not propagated, preventing the accumulation of mutations • Promotes replicative senescence under chronic stress Sirtuins level increases by caloric restriction and are present in red wine. Sirtuins are responsible for an increase in insulin sensitivity. Hence, they can play an importantrole in the treatment of diabetes.

question: Match the following cells with their locations.
explanation: The correctly matched set of the cells and their locations is 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. 2144 Kupffer cells are a component of the mononuclear phagocytic system and are located in the liver. Parietal cells, also called oxyntic cells, are found in the upper half of the gastric glands. They havenumerous mitochondria and are actively involved in the secretion of hydrochloric acid andintrinsic factor - a glycoprotein that aids in the absorption of vitamin B12 from the ileum. Dust cells are macrophages in the walls of the alveoli. They phagocytose dust particles in thealveoli. In CHF these macrophages phagocytose erythrocytes that escape from the capillaries. Thecells acquire a brick-red color and are called heart failure cells. Clara cells are non-ciliated cuboidal epithelial cells that secrete important defense markers andserve as stem cells after injury. These cells make up a larger portion of the epithelial lining in thelater portions of the conducting airway.

question: Which of the following cytokines is not involved in Th1 response?
explanation: The cytokine not involved in TH1 response is IL-4. Dendritic cells and macrophages present antigens to T helper cells (TH) after which theydifferentiate into TH1 and TH2 cells. They are responsible for cell-mediated and humoral immuneresponses, respectively. IL-12 is secreted by macrophages and promotes the proliferation of TH1cells. TH1 cells secrete: • IL-2 which activates natural killer cells (NK cells) and cytotoxic T cells • IFN gamma which stimulates macrophages and is also responsible for delayed hypersensitivityalong with TGF beta. TH2 cells secrete: • IL- 4 stimulates IgE production from B cells • IL- 5 stimulates proliferation of eosinophils and together play a role in helminthic and allergicreactions • IL- 6 promotes proliferation of B cells and production of antibodies.

question: A 19-year-old girl presents with a midline neck swelling that moves on deglutition. USGrevealed a 2 cm x 2 cm nodule on the left lobe of the thyroid, extending into the strapmuscles. The histopathology image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical scenario and the image showing papillae lined by cells with overlapping nucleiand Orphan Annie eye nuclei indicate a diagnosis of papillary carcinoma of thyroid. Papillary carcinoma of thyroid presents as a painless nodule or mass in the neck or cervical nodein women of reproductive age. The risk factors include exposure to ionizingradiation and Hashimoto thyroiditis. It usually presents as a cold nodule on a scan. Histopathological examination shows branchingpapillae and follicles with fibrovascular stalk. Nuclear changes include ground glass or OrphanAnnie eye nuclei, pseudo-inclusions, and nuclear grooves. Psammoma bodies are often present. 2145 Diagnosis can be made based on these nuclear features, even in the absence of papillaryarchitecture. The prognosis is excellent, with a 10-year survival rate in excess of 95%. The image below shows Orphan Annie eye nuclei with central clearing and margination ofchromatin: Other options: Option A: Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is a neuroendocrine tumor that is derived fromparafollicular C cells, that secrete calcitonin. Most of these tumors occur sporadically. Some are associated with familial multiple endocrineneoplasia (MEN) syndrome: MEN 2A and MEN 2B. They frequently present as a neck mass thatmay be associated with cervical lymphadenopathy. With the enlargement of the nodule, patientsmay have dysphagia and dyspnea. Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells which form nests, trabeculae, or follicles.Amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules are present in the stroma. 2146 Calcitonin in the tumor cells and stroma is easily demonstratable by immunohistochemistry. Option B: Follicular carcinoma thyroid on histopathology may show uniform cells forming smallfollicles containing colloid (resembling normal thyroid gland) or sheets of cells without colloid. Anaplastic carcinomas are poorly differentiated thyroid carcinomas with varied morphologyincluding giant cells or spindle-shaped cells or both. There is minimal follicular differentiationwith intratumoral necrosis. 2147 Option C: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presentsduring childhood often noticed after an upper respiratory infection. It represents the persistence of the track of the thyroid gland and can be found adjacent tothe midline. It presents as smooth, fluctuant (cystic) swelling that is often transilluminant.Classically, the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion. Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst and prevent a recurrence.

question: A chronic smoker with a smoking history of 24 packs presents with breathlessness and chestpain. Further investigations revealed the presence of a lung tumor. On staining, cells arepositive for chromogranin. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical scenario of a lung tumor associated with chronic smoking and tumor cells stainingpositive for chromogranin indicates that the most likely diagnosis in this patient is small cellcarcinoma of the lung. 2148 Small cell carcinoma of the lung belongs to the neuroendocrine tumors and originatesfrom neuroendocrine progenitor cells, Kulchitsky cells that line the bronchial epithelium. It is ahighly malignant tumor with a high association with cigarette smoking. It usually arises from themajor bronchi. Histopathology of small cell lung carcinoma shows clusters of small cells which are round, oval, orspindle-shaped, and a prominent nuclear molding. These cells have scant cytoplasm, ill-definedcell borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin (salt and pepper pattern), and absent orinconspicuous nucleoli. The Azzopardi effect is described as basophilic staining of vascular wallsdue to coating by DNA from necrotic tumor cells. Neuroendocrine markers seen in small cell lung carcinoma include: • Chromogranin • Synaptophysin • CD56 Paraneoplastic syndromes associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung are Cushing syndromedue to ACTH production and hyponatremia due to inappropriate ADH secretion. Small cell lungcancer-associated SIADH is due to the ectopic release of antidiuretic hormone. It is associatedwith increased thirst and hyponatremia. Other options: Option A- Adenocarcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumor with differentiation in glands or mucinproduction by the tumor cells. These tumors are commonly found in women and in non-smokers.These tumors are more peripherally located and are smaller. On histopathology, the tumor showsa lepidic pattern of spread with tumor cells crawling along the normal-appearing alveolar septa.The tumor cells are positive for thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) and Napsin A. Option B- Squamous cell carcinoma is found to be more common in men and has a strongassociation with smoking. They have precursor lesions like squamous dysplasia, squamousmetaplasia, or in situ carcinomas. On histopathology, it is characterized by keratinization and/orintercellular bridges. Keratinization occurs in the form of squamous pearls. It is positive for p40and p63 markers. Hypercalcemia is the common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with thistype. Option C- Large cell carcinoma is an undifferentiated malignant epithelial carcinoma. Onhistopathology, the cells are large, with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli with a moderate amountof cytoplasm.

question: A male patient presented with hemoptysis. On examination, hilar mass was present. Thehistopathological image is shown below. Immunohistochemistry revealed that the cells werepositive for p40. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: The given clinical history and the histopathological findings showing keratin pearls are suggestiveof squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly found in men and is strongly associated withsmoking. Squamous cell carcinoma predominantly arises in the central segmental or subsegmentalbronchi. The tumor may grow into the bronchial lumen and produce an intraluminal mass. In 2149 certain cases, the bronchial obstruction may lead to atelectasis or infection. The tumor maypenetrate the wall of the bronchus and infiltrate the peribronchial tissue into the carina or themediastinum. This tumor may be associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like hypercalcemia. The symptomscould include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, lethargy, polyuria, polydipsia, anddehydration. Squamous metaplasia and dysplasia often precede frank squamous cell carcinoma. Carcinomain-situ persists for many years and this may often be recognized on cytologic smears or in BALfluid or brushings. Gross appearance: The tissue is grey-white, firm, with areas of necrosis and hemorrhages. Red oryellow-white mottling and softening may be seen. The necrotic foci may cavitate. Histopathology: They have precursor lesions like squamous dysplasia, squamous metaplasia, or insitu carcinomas. On histopathology, it is characterized by keratinization and/or intercellularbridges. Keratinization occurs in the form of squamous pearls or individual cells with denseeosinophilic cytoplasm. It is positive for p40 and p63 markers.

question: Which of the following is true about proto-oncogenes?
explanation: The true statement about proto-oncogenes is statement 3. ERBB2 amplification (gene thatencodes HER2) is associated with breast cancer, while ERBB 1 mutation (gene that encodesEGFR) is associated with adenocarcinoma of the lung. Other statements: Statement 1: The most common genetic change in GISTs is the gain-of-function mutation of thetyrosine kinase KIT gene. These are present in 75% to 85% of all GISTs. Therefore KIT hasincreased expression in GIST. The second most common mutation results in the activation of platelet-derived growth factorreceptor A (PDGFRA). 2150 Statement 2: KRAS mutation is associated with colon, lung, and pancreatic tumors. Among lungcancers, about 30% of cases of adenocarcinoma have gain of function mutations of the KRASgene. Small cell carcinomas are associated with the inactivation of TP53 and RB genes. Statement 4: PDGFR-β amplification is associated with gliomas and leukemias. PDGF-βoverexpression is associated with astrocytoma. Mutations involved in colon cancer pathogenesis: • Familial adenomatous polyposis usually has mutations involving the APC gene. • HNPCC- majority of the cases have mutations in MSH2 or MLH1. • Adenocarcinomas- the two pathways implicated are the APC pathway and MSI pathway.

question: The given peripheral smear is associated with which of the following leukemias?
explanation: The peripheral smear findings point toward a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The peripheral smear shows smudge cells, increased lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm, andround to slightly irregular nuclei containing clumped chromatin. This large number ofmonotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes is often described as a "convent-girl"appearance. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)/ Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the most commonleukemia among adults in the western world. The differentiating point between CLL and SLL isthat the absolute lymphocyte count is >5000/mm³ in CLL and <5000/mm³ in SLL. The chromosomal defects: • Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis) • Deletion of 11q • Trisomy 12q • Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis) It is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, andanorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are usually seen. Total blood count: • Total leukocyte count is highly variable; leukopenia is seen when the Synopsis is involved. • Hypogammaglobulinemia is common and contributes to increased susceptibility to infections. • 10% to 15% of patients develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia dueto autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells. Findings of peripheral smear: • Predominantly shows small lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm. • Contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is oftendescribed as a convent-girl appearance. 2151 • Smudge cells or basket cells or parachute cells - artifacts of the lymphocytes which are disruptedduring the process of making smears. • Spherocytes (due to coexisting autoimmune hemolytic anemia) and nucleated RBCs (due topremature release of progenitors in face of severe anemia, Synopsis infiltration by the tumor, orboth) Lymph node biopsy: Diffuse effacement of lymph node architecture is seen. Small lymphocytesadmixed with variable numbers of larger activated lymphocytes that often gather in looseaggregates. Proliferation centers containing mitotically active cells are pathognomonic for CLL /SLL. The histopathological image shows small, darker staining lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli,which are typically seen in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). 2152 AML is a hematopoietic progenitor malignancy that causes immature myeloblast accumulation inthe bone Synopsis. Incidence increases with age and peaks after 60 years of age. Clinically, the patients present with symptoms resulting due to pancytopenia (anemia,neutropenia, thrombocytopenia). There is generalized fatigue, bone pain, bleeding tendencies, andan increased risk of recurrent infections. For acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML) diagnosis, theblast cell count should be ≥20% in the peripheral blood or bone Synopsis. Other distinctive features of AML: • Bone Synopsis/ smear shows a large, uniform population of cells (myeloblasts) with prominentnucleoli (yellow arrow). It shows the presence of primary cytoplasmic granules. • Auer rods: needle-shaped azurophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by the fusion oflysosomes. (black arrow) • Multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell resembling a bundle of sticks known asfaggot cells (seen in peripheral smear). 2153 Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) arises from immature B (pre-B) or T (pre-T) cells calledlymphoblasts. Immunohistochemistry for terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positivein pre-B and pre-T lymphoblasts. Peripheral smear shows lymphoblasts that have condensed chromatin, less conspicuous nucleoli,and smaller amounts of cytoplasm which lacks granules as shown below. Chronic myeloid leukemia is characterized by the presence of a Philadelphia chromosomeresulting from reciprocal translocation t(9;22) forming the BCR-ABL fusion gene. They havehypercellular Synopsis due to a massively increased number of maturing granulocytic precursors. The image below shows peripheral smear findings of CML with neutrophils, myelocytes,metamyelocytes, and band cells.

question: Which of the following statements are true about familial adenomatous polyposis?
explanation: 2154 The true statements about familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) are statements 2 and 4 (option-A). Familial adenomatous polyposis is an inherited autosomal dominant disorder presentingnumerous colorectal adenomatous polyps. It is an autosomal dominant disease caused bymutations in the APC gene, which is a regulator in the Wnt signaling pathway. The diagnosis ofFAP requires the presence of at least 100 polyps. Patients are usually teenagers and multiple polyps are visible in the colon during sigmoidoscopy.It is associated with a variety of extraintestinal manifestations including congenital hypertrophy ofthe retinal pigmental epithelium. Colorectal adenocarcinoma occurs in almost all cases before theage of 50. Prophylactic colectomy is recommended in patients with APC gene mutations. The surgeries usedare colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis (IRA), restorative proctocolectomy with an ilealpouch-anal anastomosis (RPC), or total proctectomy and end ileostomy. The first 2 surgeries arepreferred in young patients as it avoids a permanent stoma. Note - FAP along with brain tumors is called Turcot syndrome. FAP along with multiple osteomas,skin, and soft tissue tumors is called Gardner syndrome.

question: Which of the following shows maximum amplitude on thromboelastography?
explanation: The maximum amplitude in thromboelastography represents platelets. A decrease in maximumamplitude signifies a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of platelets. Thromboelastography (TEG) is a non-invasive test that quantifies the ability of whole blood toform a clot. It is useful in intraoperative coagulation status assessment. The dynamic changes inthe viscoelastic properties of a blood sample during the clotting can be detected and quantified bythromboelastography. Underlying coagulation deficiencies show different shapes in the TEG. Theyare shown in the image below: 2155 Advantages of thromboelastography: • Blood coagulability, including coagulation cascade, platelet function, and fibrinolysis can beassessed. • It is a simple bedside test • Can diagnose coagulopathic bleeding • Can be used as a guide in transfusion therapy and decrease the use of blood products • Can detect dynamic changes in blood coagulation during resuscitation • Predict the clinical efficacy of therapeutic agents affecting blood coagulability

question: A man presented with fever, night sweats, and weight loss for 2 months. On examination,non-tender, rubbery lymph nodes were palpable in the supraclavicular and inguinal regionson both sides. Peripheral smear showed the presence of bi-nucleated cells. Which markerswill be seen in this condition?
explanation: The probable diagnosis from the given clinical scenario and the histopathological descriptionis Hodgkin's lymphoma. The bi-nucleated cells are called the Reed-Sternberg cells which are CD15+ and CD30+ (option D- 1 and 2). Hodgkin's lymphoma arises in a single lymph node or chain of nodes and spreads first toanatomically contiguous lymphoid tissues. It usually presents as painless lymphadenopathy. Thedistinctive feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma is the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells. WHO classifies Hodgkin's lymphoma into 5 subtypes: 2156 • Nodular sclerosis: Frequent lacunar cells • Mixed cellularity • Lymphocyte-rich • Lymphocyte depletion • Nodular lymphocyte predominance The first 4 subtypes are considered classical Hodgkin's lymphoma. The RS cells are CD 15+ andCD30+. The lymphocyte predominant type is considered non-classical Hodgkin's lymphoma withCD15-, CD30-, CD20+, and EB -. The image below shows various cells like eosinophils, RS cells, plasma cells, and histiocytes in anFNA specimen of Hodgkin lymphoma: TypeRS-cellEBVirusPrognosis 1. Nodular sclerosis (most common in the world)Frequent lacunar cells and occasional diagnostic RS cellsRareVery good 2. Mixed cellularity (most common in India)Frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells70%Good 3. Lymphocyte RichFrequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells40%Very good 4. Lymphocyte depletedReticular variant: frequent diagnostic RS cells and variants and a paucity of background reactive cell 90%(Max)Poorest 5. Lymphocyte predominantL&H variant (Popcorn cell) variants in the background of follicular dendritic cells 0%(Min)Excellent 2157 Reed-Sternberg cell (RS cell) is the characteristic tumor giant cell of Hodgkin Lymphoma. It isderived from the germinal or post-germinal center B cell. It has a classic owl-eyed appearance dueto the presence of a symmetric or mirror-image bilobed nucleus, with prominent nucleolisurrounded by a clear space. It has the following variants: • Lacunar • Classic • L&H popcorn cells • Pleomorphic • Mononuclear RS cells should be present in a background of non-neoplastic inflammatory cells like lymphocytes,plasma cells, and eosinophils, to make a diagnosis of Hodgkin’s lymphoma. The image given below shows the diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cell, with two nuclear lobes, largeinclusion-like nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm, surrounded by lymphocytes, macrophages, andan eosinophil. The image below shows the Reed-Sternberg cell, mononuclear variant. 2158 The image below shows Reed-Sternberg cell, lacunar variant. This variant has a folded ormultilobated nucleus and lies within an open space, which is an artifact created by disruption ofthe cytoplasm during tissue sectioning. The image below shows the Reed-Sternberg cell, lymphohistiocytic variant. Several such variantswith multiple infolded nuclear membranes, small nucleoli, fine chromatin, and abundant palecytoplasm are present. 2159

question: A 10-year-old boy presented with fatigue. Investigations revealed: Hemoglobin, 9 g/dL; MCV,60 fL; MCH, 20 pg; and serum ferritin, 185 µg/L. The TLC was elevated and showedpredominant lymphocytes and neutrophils. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: The given clinical scenario and the investigation findings are suggestive of microcytichypochromic anemia. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is anemia of chronic disorder. Anemia of chronic disorders more commonly presents as normochromic normocytic anemia thatlater develops into microcytic hypochromic anemia rarely. It is caused due to production oferythrocytes. Anemia of chronic disease is anemia resulting due to chronic diseases which produce systemicinflammation. During chronic inflammation, inflammatory mediators like interleukin - 6(IL-6) stimulate the production of hepcidin from the liver. Hepcidin is an acute phasereactant that inhibits ferroportin on macrophages and also decreases transport of iron from storesto developing RBC precursors. This results in decreased proliferation of erythroid progenitors dueto impaired iron utilization. Other options: Option B: Thalassemia also presents as iron deficiency anemia but it does not have elevatedluekocytosis. Option C: Iron deficiency anemia also presents as microcytic hypochromic anemia. But since thereis deficient iron, the serum ferritin level will also be low. This patient has normal serum ferritinand hence does not have iron deficiency anemia. Note: MCV/RBC count (Mentzer index) can also be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiencyanemia (IDA). MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) arelow in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reducedin IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBCratio. 2160 Option D: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a mutation in β-globin that creates sickle hemoglobin(HbS). It does not present as microcytic hypochromic anemia.

question: Senile atrophy occurs due to ______.
explanation: Senile atrophy is seen when there is a reduced blood supply to a tissue. This reduction in theblood supply occurs in a gradual manner because of slowly progressing atherosclerotic lesions. Atrophy is a process of reduction in the size of a tissue or an organ resulting from a decrease inthe cell size and number. It is a type of cellular adaptation. In this process, there is a decrease inthe synthesis of cellular proteins and an increase in their degradation, mainly mediated by theubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Atrophy can either be physiological or pathological: Physiologic atrophy: • Loss of hormonal stimulation: Atrophy of the uterus after parturition; atrophy of theendometrium, vaginal epithelium, and breast after menopause. • During embryonic development: Certain structures, like the notochord and thyroglossal duct,undergo atrophy during fetal development. Pathologic atrophy: • Disuse Atrophy (decreased workload): e.g., atrophy in a limb that has been immobilizedfollowing a fracture • Denervation atrophy (loss of nerve supply): e.g., skeletal muscle atrophy following nerve injury • Ischemic atrophy: e.g., senile atrophy of the brain and heart due to atherosclerosis • Inadequate nutrition: e.g., severe muscle wasting in marasmus • Pressure atrophy: e.g., atrophy of surrounding uninvolved tissues caused by an enlarging benigntumor

question: Cyclooxygenase plays a role in which pathway?
explanation: Prostaglandins are produced from arachidonic acid present in the membrane phospholipids. Thisprocess is mediated by 2 cyclooxygenases: COX-1 and COX-2. Prostaglandins are produced bymast cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells. COX-1 is commonly found in most tissues. It plays a role in maintaining normal homeostasis. It isalso induced by inflammatory stimuli. COX-2 is found in cells that are involved in inflammatory reactions. The most important prostaglandins in inflammation are PGE2, PGD2, PGF2a, PGI2(prostacyclin), and thromboxane A2. Other options: Options A: Kreb's cycle is also called the citric acid cycle and tricarboxylic acid cycle. It is theterminal pathway for the oxidative catabolism of carbohydrates, amino acids, and fatty acids. 2161 Option C: Leukotrienes are also produced from arachidonic acid with the help of lipoxygenases.

question: Metastatic calcification can be explained by all, except ______.
explanation: Metastatic calcification cannot be explained by vitamin D deficiency. Metastatic calcification isassociated with hypercalcemia, which may be caused by vitamin D intoxication rather thandeficiency. Pathologic calcification is the abnormal tissue deposition of calcium salts, together with smalleramounts of iron, magnesium, and other mineral salts. It is of two types namely metastatic anddystrophic calcification. Metastatic calcification is the deposition of calcium salts in otherwise normal tissues. • Hypercalcemia secondary to some disturbance in calcium metabolism. • Principal causes of hypercalcemia: • Increased secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) • Resorption of bone tissue • Vitamin-D-related disorders- excess or abnormal sensitivity • Renal failure • Aluminum intoxication • Milk-alkali syndrome- due to excess ingestion of calcium Metastatic calcification can be seen in interstitial tissues of the gastric mucosa, kidneys, lungs,systemic arteries, and pulmonary veins.

question: Match the cytokines with the effector cells .
explanation: The correct answer is option B: Cytokines are proteins produced by many cell types (principally activated lymphocytes,macrophages, and dendritic cells, but also endothelial, epithelial, and connective tissue cells) thatmediate and regulate immune and inflammatory reactions. Three subsets of CD4+ T cells secrete different types of cytokines and elicit different types ofinflammation. TH1 cells - activate macrophages by the classical pathway by secreting IFNγ. TH2 cells - recruit and activate eosinophils and are responsible for the alternative pathway ofmacrophage activation by secreting IL4, IL5, and IL13. • IL4 acts on B cells to stimulate class switching to IgE and promotes the development ofadditional TH2 cells. • IL5 is involved in the development and activation of eosinophils, which are essential effectors oftype I hypersensitivity 2162 (discussed later). • IL13 enhances IgE production and acts on epithelial cells to stimulate mucus secretion. Inaddition, TH2 cells (as well as mast cells and epithelial cells) produce chemokines that attractmore TH2 cells, as well as other leukocytes, to the reaction site. It also shares some functionalsimilarities to IL-4 and can thus induce differentiation in dendritic cells. TH17 cells secrete IL17 and other cytokines responsiblefor neutrophils and monocyte recruitment. 1. IL4C. B cells 2. IL5A. Eosinophils 3.IL9B. Mast cells 4. IL13D. Dendritic cells
